Punishment floods limited attention with task-irrelevant thoughts like fear of failure, while reinforcement directs attention to task-relevant cues and what to do correctly
questions.answer_text: Punishment floods limited attention with task-irrelevant thoughts like fear of failure, while reinforcement directs attention to task-relevant cues and what to do correctly
questions.explanation_en: Reinforcement helps athletes attend to task-relevant cues and what to do correctly, whereas punishment tends to flood limited attentional capacity with task-irrelevant cognitions such as fear of failure. Reinforcement is therefore generally preferred, and it is effective across skill levels, not only with elite athletes.
tags: Scientific Foundations - Exam Two

questions.question: An athlete training in the heat is told to drink enough during exercise that his body weight loss stays below the threshold at which performance suffers and heat illness risk climbs. Fluid-related body weight loss during exercise should not exceed roughly:
options: 2% of body weight
5% of body weight
8% of body weight
questions.answer_text: 2% of body weight
questions.explanation_en: Athletes should drink enough during exercise to keep water weight losses under about 2% of body weight, which helps prevent overheating, dehydration, and heat illness while protecting performance. Losses of 5% or more represent substantial dehydration well beyond the recommended limit.
tags: Scientific Foundations - Exam Two

questions.question: An athlete asks about a widely studied, legal ergogenic aid found in coffee and tea that helps both endurance and resistance athletes, but is regulated in a category distinct from most dietary supplements. Which substance fits, and how is it classified?
options: Sodium chloride, classified as a stimulant drug
Caffeine, which is classified as a drug rather than a dietary supplement
Creatine monohydrate, classified as a drug rather than a dietary supplement
questions.answer_text: Caffeine, which is classified as a drug rather than a dietary supplement
questions.explanation_en: Caffeine is a central nervous system stimulant found in coffee, tea, soft drinks, and chocolate and is popular with both aerobic endurance and resistance athletes; unlike most dietary supplements, it is categorized as a drug. Creatine is regulated as a dietary supplement, and sodium chloride is a dietary mineral, not a stimulant drug.
tags: Scientific Foundations - Exam Two

questions.question: An athlete tracking intake wants to convert grams of each macronutrient into calories. Which set of energy values is correct?
options: Carbohydrate 4, protein 9, fat 9 kcal per gram
Carbohydrate 7, protein 4, fat 4 kcal per gram
Carbohydrate 4, protein 4, fat 9 kcal per gram
questions.answer_text: Carbohydrate 4, protein 4, fat 9 kcal per gram
questions.explanation_en: Carbohydrate and protein each provide approximately 4 kcal per gram, while fat provides approximately 9 kcal per gram because fats carry more carbon and hydrogen relative to oxygen. Protein is 4, not 9, kcal per gram (the 7 kcal/g figure belongs to alcohol, not a macronutrient here).
tags: Scientific Foundations - Exam Two

questions.question: A coach wants a nutritional strategy that raises the muscle's capacity to buffer or neutralize the hydrogen ions that accumulate during repeated high-intensity efforts. Which pairing works primarily through that buffering mechanism?
options: Beta-alanine and sodium bicarbonate
Caffeine and creatine monohydrate
Vitamin C and iron
questions.answer_text: Beta-alanine and sodium bicarbonate
questions.explanation_en: Improving buffering capacity through beta-alanine (which raises intramuscular carnosine) and sodium bicarbonate (an alkalinizing agent) can aid performance in activities limited by hydrogen ion buildup. Caffeine acts as a CNS stimulant and creatine works through the phosphagen system, while vitamin C and iron have no primary acid-buffering role.
tags: Scientific Foundations - Exam Two

questions.question: Three athletes ask whether carbohydrate loading is worth it: a marathoner, a 100 m sprinter, and a powerlifter. Carbohydrate loading is most likely to improve performance for which one?
options: The powerlifter, performing single maximal-strength attempts
The marathoner, whose continuous event runs well beyond about 90 minutes
The 100 m sprinter, whose maximal effort lasts under about 10 seconds
questions.answer_text: The marathoner, whose continuous event runs well beyond about 90 minutes
questions.explanation_en: Carbohydrate loading raises pre-event muscle glycogen and benefits continuous aerobic endurance events lasting longer than about 90 minutes (distance running, road cycling, cross-country skiing), where glycogen depletion would otherwise limit late-event performance. It does little for brief, high-power efforts like sprints or maximal lifts, which rely on the phosphagen system.
tags: Scientific Foundations - Exam Two

questions.question: A coach is selecting a sports drink for an athlete training in the heat and wants the electrolyte and carbohydrate content to match the recommended composition. Which option fits?
options: 60 mEq sodium and 30 mEq potassium per liter, with about 1% carbohydrate
No added sodium or potassium, with about 25% carbohydrate
20 to 30 mEq sodium and 2 to 5 mEq potassium per liter, with 5% to 10% carbohydrate
questions.answer_text: 20 to 30 mEq sodium and 2 to 5 mEq potassium per liter, with 5% to 10% carbohydrate
questions.explanation_en: The optimal sport drink contains 20 to 30 mEq of sodium and 2 to 5 mEq of potassium per liter, with carbohydrate at a 5% to 10% concentration. Very high electrolyte loads or a 25% carbohydrate concentration slow gastric emptying and can worsen, not aid, hydration.
tags: Scientific Foundations - Exam Two

questions.question: An athlete weighing anabolic-androgenic steroid use asks you to state the documented health risks accurately. Which option correctly describes adverse effects associated with anabolic steroid abuse?
options: Increased risk of liver tumors and liver damage, unfavorable blood lipid changes, and elevated blood pressure
An improved cholesterol profile alongside lowered blood pressure
No documented effect on either the liver or the cardiovascular system
questions.answer_text: Increased risk of liver tumors and liver damage, unfavorable blood lipid changes, and elevated blood pressure
questions.explanation_en: Documented adverse effects of anabolic steroid abuse include hepatic effects such as increased risk of liver tumors and liver damage, plus cardiovascular effects including unfavorable lipid profile changes and elevated blood pressure, along with endocrine and psychological effects. Steroids worsen, not improve, the lipid profile and blood pressure.
tags: Scientific Foundations - Exam Two

questions.question: Immediately after a heavy resistance session, a healthy younger adult wants the post-training feeding that best drives muscle protein synthesis. Which recommendation fits that acute window?
options: At least 100 grams of protein, regardless of the source
About 20 to 50 grams of a high-quality, high-leucine protein
About 3 to 5 grams of protein from any source
questions.answer_text: About 20 to 50 grams of a high-quality, high-leucine protein
questions.explanation_en: After resistance training, younger individuals should consume about 20 to 50 grams (roughly 8.5 to 20 grams of essential amino acids) of a high-quality, high-leucine protein to maximally stimulate muscle protein synthesis; older adults may need 40 grams or more. A few grams is too little to maximize the response, and 100+ grams offers no added synthesis benefit for a single feeding.
tags: Scientific Foundations - Exam Two

questions.question: You are profiling a Division I athlete for the off-season and decide her primary resistance training goal is strength/power. Why should you commit to ONE primary training outcome per training block rather than chasing strength and muscular endurance at the same time?
options: Concentrating on one outcome per block (emphasis/de-emphasis) lets you give a sufficient, focused stimulus while still maintaining other qualities, instead of diluting the adaptation
Training two qualities at once is biomechanically impossible because the load-repetition relationship only allows a single rep range
Insurance and liability rules prohibit programming more than one fitness characteristic in a block
questions.answer_text: Concentrating on one outcome per block (emphasis/de-emphasis) lets you give a sufficient, focused stimulus while still maintaining other qualities, instead of diluting the adaptation
questions.explanation_en: The book recommends concentrating on only one training outcome per block using an emphasis/de-emphasis approach, while still providing enough stimulus to maintain other qualities for later blocks.
tags: Practical and Applied - Exam One

questions.question: A beginner client just started training and you are choosing which exercises to prioritize. Why do CORE exercises receive priority over assistance exercises when selecting exercises?
options: Because assistance exercises are unsafe for beginners and must be removed entirely
Because core exercises recruit large muscle areas, involve two or more primary joints, and have greater dynamic correspondence (transfer) to sport movements
Because core exercises always use lighter loads, making them easier to coach first
questions.answer_text: Because core exercises recruit large muscle areas, involve two or more primary joints, and have greater dynamic correspondence (transfer) to sport movements
questions.explanation_en: Core exercises recruit one or more large muscle areas and involve multiple primary joints, giving them direct application and dynamic correspondence to sport; that's why they're prioritized.
tags: Practical and Applied - Exam One

questions.question: An athlete's session includes a power clean, a back squat, a barbell row, and biceps curls. Following the recommended exercise order, where should the power clean go and why?
options: Last, so accumulated fatigue forces greater motor-unit recruitment
First, because power exercises place a large neuromuscular and skill demand and are prone to fatigue, so the athlete should perform them while metabolically fresh
It doesn't matter; exercise order has no documented effect on adaptation
questions.answer_text: First, because power exercises place a large neuromuscular and skill demand and are prone to fatigue, so the athlete should perform them while metabolically fresh
questions.explanation_en: Power exercises are performed first because of their high neuromuscular and skill demand and proneness to fatigue; doing them fresh protects technique and reduces injury risk.
tags: Practical and Applied - Exam One

questions.question: You program a core exercise for a trained athlete with a goal of maximal muscular strength. Which load-and-rep prescription fits?
options: About 67-80% of 1RM for 8-12 reps
Less than or equal to 67% of 1RM for 12 or more reps
Greater than or equal to 85% of 1RM for 6 or fewer reps
questions.answer_text: Greater than or equal to 85% of 1RM for 6 or fewer reps
questions.explanation_en: Per table 18.11, strength training in core exercises uses loads of >=85% 1RM for <=6 goal reps; the heavier the load, the fewer reps possible.
tags: Practical and Applied - Exam One

questions.question: A hypertrophy-focused athlete is doing a multijoint exercise (e.g., back squat) and a single-joint assistance exercise (e.g., lateral raise) in the same session. How should rest periods differ between the two?
options: Both get the same 30-second rest because they share the hypertrophy goal
The multijoint exercise gets ~2-3 min while the single-joint exercise gets ~60-90 s, because rest is set by relative load and muscle mass involved
The single-joint exercise needs longer rest (3-5 min) because isolation work is more fatiguing
questions.answer_text: The multijoint exercise gets ~2-3 min while the single-joint exercise gets ~60-90 s, because rest is set by relative load and muscle mass involved
questions.explanation_en: Hypertrophy rest is ~2-3 min for multijoint and 60-90 s for single-joint work; rest is allocated by relative load and amount of muscle mass, not just the overall training goal.
tags: Practical and Applied - Exam One

questions.question: You assigned 3 sets of 6 reps in the bench press. After a few weeks the athlete completes 8 reps in the last set on two consecutive workouts. Per the 2-for-2 rule, what should you do?
options: Increase the load for that exercise at the next training session
Keep the load the same but add two more sets
Drop the load by 10% to manage accumulated fatigue
questions.answer_text: Increase the load for that exercise at the next training session
questions.explanation_en: The 2-for-2 rule: if the athlete can perform 2 or more reps over the goal in the last set for two consecutive workouts, add weight to that exercise next session.
tags: Practical and Applied - Exam One

questions.question: During a depth jump, an athlete pauses noticeably on the ground between landing and the next jump. What happens to the stretch-shortening cycle if this amortization (coupling) phase lasts too long?
options: More elastic energy is stored, making the subsequent jump higher
The stored elastic energy dissipates as heat and the stretch reflex won't enhance concentric force
The Golgi tendon organ is desensitized, increasing force output
questions.answer_text: The stored elastic energy dissipates as heat and the stretch reflex won't enhance concentric force
questions.explanation_en: If the amortization phase is too long, the elastic energy stored during the eccentric phase is lost as heat and the stretch reflex no longer augments the concentric muscle action.
tags: Practical and Applied - Exam One

questions.question: On the continuum of plyometric drills, which of the following is correctly ordered from LOWEST to HIGHEST intensity?
options: Depth jumps, box jumps, jumps in place, skips
Skips (jumps in place), standing jumps, box jumps, depth jumps
Box jumps, depth jumps, multiple hops, standing jumps
questions.answer_text: Skips (jumps in place), standing jumps, box jumps, depth jumps
questions.explanation_en: The intensity continuum runs from low-intensity drills like skips/jumps in place up through standing jumps and box jumps to depth jumps (highest); as intensity rises, volume should fall.
tags: Practical and Applied - Exam One

questions.question: You are prescribing lower-body plyometric volume for a beginner (no experience) doing low-intensity drills. Volume is counted in foot contacts per session. Which range is appropriate for that beginner?
options: Around 80 to 100 foot contacts
Around 120 to 200 foot contacts
Around 100 to 120 foot contacts
questions.answer_text: Around 80 to 100 foot contacts
questions.explanation_en: Per table 19.6, a beginner at low intensity is prescribed roughly 80-100 foot contacts; higher experience and intensity levels permit different volumes, and beginners are not recommended at high intensity.
tags: Practical and Applied - Exam One

questions.question: A 235-pound athlete wants to add high-box depth jumps. What is the appropriate caution, and what is the maximal practical depth-jump box height for effective, safe performance?
options: No cautions apply to heavier athletes; depth jumps up to 60 in. (152 cm) are recommended for everyone
Athletes over 220 lb (100 kg) should approach high-intensity plyometrics and depth jumps from heights >18 in. (46 cm) with caution; a box of about 48 in. (122 cm) is roughly the upper effective limit
Athletes over 220 lb should only ever use boxes taller than 48 in. (122 cm) to overload the tissues
questions.answer_text: Athletes over 220 lb (100 kg) should approach high-intensity plyometrics and depth jumps from heights >18 in. (46 cm) with caution; a box of about 48 in. (122 cm) is roughly the upper effective limit
questions.explanation_en: Athletes weighing over 220 lb (100 kg) should be cautious with high-intensity plyometrics and depth jumps from boxes higher than 18 in.; about 48 in. (122 cm) is near the maximal effective/safe depth-jump height before technique breaks down.
tags: Practical and Applied - Exam One

questions.question: A coach wants to improve an athlete's maximal sprinting speed. Sprint speed is the product of which two variables, and what ultimately underpins maximizing both?
options: Stride length and stride (step) frequency, both underpinned by rapid force production into the ground
Reaction time and arm-swing amplitude, underpinned by flexibility
Ground contact time and body mass, underpinned by aerobic capacity
questions.answer_text: Stride length and stride (step) frequency, both underpinned by rapid force production into the ground
questions.explanation_en: Running velocity is a product of step length and step frequency, and the underlying component to maximizing both is rapid force production applied to the ground.
tags: Practical and Applied - Exam One

questions.question: An athlete tries to run faster by deliberately reaching out and overstriding. Why does overstriding HURT sprint performance?
options: It increases ground contact time, which dampens the stretch-shortening cycle and lowers step frequency
It shortens ground contact time so much that the athlete can't produce force
It increases step frequency but reduces stride length below optimal
questions.answer_text: It increases ground contact time, which dampens the stretch-shortening cycle and lowers step frequency
questions.explanation_en: Overstriding attempts to gain speed via larger ground contact times, which dampens the SSC and lowers step frequency; success comes from high vertical force in a short contact time.
tags: Practical and Applied - Exam One

questions.question: You add overspeed (assisted) sprint training such as towing or downhill running for an advanced athlete. What is the recommended ceiling on the speed increase, and a key drawback?
options: Increases should be limited to <=10%; assisted sprinting can cause chop steps and undesirable braking/overstriding mechanics
Increases should reach 25-30%; there are no documented technique drawbacks
There is no recommended limit; assisted work always improves propulsive force
questions.answer_text: Increases should be limited to <=10%; assisted sprinting can cause chop steps and undesirable braking/overstriding mechanics
questions.explanation_en: Assisted/overspeed increases should be limited to <=10%; pushing beyond can prematurely rush the stance phase, reduce muscle activation/propulsive force, and produce chop steps, leaning back, and overstriding.
tags: Practical and Applied - Exam One

questions.question: Agility differs from simple change-of-direction (COD) ability. What added component defines AGILITY?
options: A predetermined movement pattern executed at maximal speed
A perceptual-cognitive component (responding to a stimulus) combined with change-of-direction ability
Purely greater eccentric strength with no cognitive demand
questions.answer_text: A perceptual-cognitive component (responding to a stimulus) combined with change-of-direction ability
questions.explanation_en: COD is a planned change of direction; agility additionally requires perceptual-cognitive ability, changing direction/velocity/mode in response to a stimulus.
tags: Practical and Applied - Exam One

questions.question: An advanced runner needs work just at race pace to improve lactate threshold and the maximal lactate steady state. Which aerobic endurance method is built around an intensity at or slightly above race pace, corresponding roughly to MLSS?
options: Long, slow (extensive endurance) training
Pace/tempo (threshold) training
Fartlek training
questions.answer_text: Pace/tempo (threshold) training
questions.explanation_en: Pace/tempo (threshold) training uses an intensity at or slightly higher than race pace, corresponding approximately to MLSS, to improve running economy, LT, and MLSS.
tags: Practical and Applied - Exam One

questions.question: You program classic interval training for a runner. Work intervals close to VO2max typically last 3-5 minutes; what work-to-rest ratio is recommended for those intervals?
options: About 1:3, with rest three times the work duration
About 1:1, with the rest interval equal to the work interval
About 3:1, with work three times the rest duration
questions.answer_text: About 1:1, with the rest interval equal to the work interval
questions.explanation_en: For 3- to 5-minute interval work bouts near VO2max, the rest interval should equal the work interval, keeping a 1:1 work-to-rest ratio.
tags: Practical and Applied - Exam One

questions.question: A swimmer's coach wants variety and asks you to describe Fartlek training. Fartlek is best characterized as which of the following?
options: A combination of extensive endurance, pace/tempo, and interval-type efforts (speed play) that challenges all body systems
Continuous training at a single fixed intensity below the lactate threshold
Maximal sprints with full passive recovery and no aerobic component
questions.answer_text: A combination of extensive endurance, pace/tempo, and interval-type efforts (speed play) that challenges all body systems
questions.explanation_en: Fartlek ('speed play') blends extensive endurance with bursts of pace/tempo and interval-type efforts, challenging all systems and helping raise VO2max, LT, economy, and fuel use.
tags: Practical and Applied - Exam One

questions.question: An athlete under heavy psychoemotional and occupational stress keeps getting more intense training. Per Selye's General Adaptation Syndrome, prolonged excessive stress pushes the athlete toward which phase, associated with overreaching/overtraining?
options: The alarm phase
The resistance (adaptation) phase
The exhaustion phase
questions.answer_text: The exhaustion phase
questions.explanation_en: If stress persists too long, the athlete moves into the exhaustion phase of the GAS, where they fail to adapt and most likely experience overreaching or overtraining.
tags: Practical and Applied - Exam One

questions.question: You are planning a training block that is several weeks long. On the periodization hierarchy, what is the cycle that typically lasts two to six weeks, with four weeks being the most common duration?
options: Microcycle
Mesocycle
Macrocycle
questions.answer_text: Mesocycle
questions.explanation_en: A mesocycle lasts several weeks to months (typically 2-6 weeks, most commonly 4); microcycles are usually about a week, and a macrocycle spans months to a year.
tags: Practical and Applied - Exam One

questions.question: You are designing the general preparatory (off-season) phase for a strength athlete. In the traditional periodization model, what are the intensity/volume characteristics and primary goals of the hypertrophy/strength-endurance phase?
options: Low-to-moderate intensity, high volume; goals are to build work capacity and muscle mass as a foundation
Very high intensity (50% to >=93% 1RM), very low volume; goal is to peak performance
Maximal intensity (>=85% 1RM), low volume; goal is maximal strength
questions.answer_text: Low-to-moderate intensity, high volume; goals are to build work capacity and muscle mass as a foundation
questions.explanation_en: The hypertrophy/strength-endurance phase sits early in the preparatory period with low-to-moderate intensity and high volume, building work capacity and muscle mass for later higher-intensity phases.
tags: Practical and Applied - Exam One

questions.question: Two programs are compared: Program A keeps reps fixed but rotates heavy/medium/light loads day to day within a week; Program B gradually raises intensity and lowers volume across successive multi-week blocks. What are these two models called?
options: A is the traditional (so-called linear) model; B is daily undulating periodization
A is daily undulating periodization; B is the traditional (so-called linear) model
Both are parallel models with no meaningful difference
questions.answer_text: A is daily undulating periodization; B is the traditional (so-called linear) model
questions.explanation_en: Daily undulating periodization varies the load (and thus volume-load) across days within the week, while the traditional ('linear') model progressively shifts toward higher intensity and lower volume across blocks.
tags: Practical and Applied - Exam One

questions.question: A coach builds a warm-up using the RAMP model. In the 'Activate and Mobilize' phase, what is the primary focus that distinguishes it from a traditional static-stretching warm-up?
options: Holding end-range positions statically to lengthen individual muscles
Developing movement competency through key patterns like squats and lunges (mobility, not static flexibility)
Maximally raising heart rate before any skill work
questions.answer_text: Developing movement competency through key patterns like squats and lunges (mobility, not static flexibility)
questions.explanation_en: The 5th edition stresses that the Activate/Mobilize phase targets mobility, the capacity to move actively and effectively through movement patterns, not static flexibility of individual muscles.
tags: Practical and Applied - Exam One

questions.question: An athlete needs maximal force and speed output in the activity that immediately follows the warm-up. Which RAMP phase is specifically designed to ramp activity intensity up to competition level and exploit the postactivation effect (treppe/staircase)?
options: Raise
Activate and Mobilize
Potentiate
questions.answer_text: Potentiate
questions.explanation_en: The Potentiate phase uses sport- or capacity-specific activities of progressively increasing intensity; the contractile history (treppe/staircase effect) makes the motor neuron more sensitive, improving subsequent high-force, high-speed performance.
tags: Practical and Applied - Exam One

questions.question: During a hold-relax PNF hamstring stretch, the athlete performs an isometric contraction of the hamstrings against the partner, then relaxes as the partner increases the stretch. The improved ROM after the isometric is primarily attributed to:
options: Autogenic inhibition
Reciprocal inhibition of the quadriceps
Triggering of the stretch reflex
questions.answer_text: Autogenic inhibition
questions.explanation_en: Contracting the muscle being stretched (the hamstrings) and then relaxing produces autogenic inhibition, allowing a greater subsequent passive stretch. The stretch reflex is something you avoid, not trigger, during stretching.
tags: Practical and Applied - Exam One

questions.question: An athlete uses a fast, bouncing sitting toe-touch where each rep pushes farther than the last. Why does the 5th edition caution that this ballistic approach may limit ROM gains compared with dynamic stretching?
options: It cannot raise muscle temperature
It usually triggers the stretch reflex, which keeps the muscle from relaxing
It only works on the upper body
questions.answer_text: It usually triggers the stretch reflex, which keeps the muscle from relaxing
questions.explanation_en: Ballistic stretching typically triggers the stretch reflex, preventing the muscle from relaxing, which can limit ROM. Dynamic stretching is controlled and moderate-paced, avoiding the negative effects associated with ballistic work.
tags: Practical and Applied - Exam One

questions.question: A spotter is asked to spot a flat barbell bench press (an over-the-face exercise). Which grip should the spotter use on the bar?
options: A closed pronated grip wider than the lifter's grip
A supinated grip matching the lifter's grip width
An alternated grip, usually narrower than the athlete's grip
questions.answer_text: An alternated grip, usually narrower than the athlete's grip
questions.explanation_en: For over-the-face barbell exercises the spotter grasps the bar with an alternated grip, usually narrower than the athlete's grip, to safely catch or assist with the load from a higher vantage point.
tags: Practical and Applied - Exam One

questions.question: An experienced lifter asks when breath holding (the Valsalva-type strategy) is acceptable rather than the standard exhale-through-the-sticking-point cue. The 5th edition's general breathing guidance is to:
options: Always hold the breath through every set for spinal support
Exhale through the sticking point and inhale during the less stressful phase for most exercises
Inhale during the concentric phase and exhale during the eccentric phase
questions.answer_text: Exhale through the sticking point and inhale during the less stressful phase for most exercises
questions.explanation_en: For most resistance exercises the athlete should exhale through the sticking point (the hardest part, just after the eccentric-to-concentric transition) and inhale during the less stressful phase. Breath holding is reserved for experienced lifters doing heavy structural exercises.
tags: Practical and Applied - Exam One

questions.question: Which of the following correctly lists the five points of the 'five-point body contact' position for a supine bench exercise?
options: Head, shoulders/upper back, buttocks, right foot, left foot
Head, both hands, buttocks, both feet
Shoulders, hips, both knees, both feet
questions.answer_text: Head, shoulders/upper back, buttocks, right foot, left foot
questions.explanation_en: The five-point body contact position is head, shoulders/upper back, and buttocks firmly on the bench, plus both feet flat on the floor. Maintaining it throughout the lift promotes maximal stability and spinal support.
tags: Practical and Applied - Exam One

questions.question: A new lifter wears a weight belt for every exercise, including biceps curls and lat pulldowns. What is the best coaching guidance?
options: A belt is warranted only for exercises that stress the lower back done with near-maximal or maximal loads; overuse limits trunk-muscle training
Belts are appropriate for all exercises to build the habit
A belt should be worn only for upper-body pressing
questions.answer_text: A belt is warranted only for exercises that stress the lower back done with near-maximal or maximal loads; overuse limits trunk-muscle training
questions.explanation_en: A belt is recommended for exercises stressing the lower back during near-maximal or maximal sets. It is not needed for exercises that do not stress the lower back, and wearing it too often reduces training of the abdominal and lower-back muscles.
tags: Practical and Applied - Exam One

questions.question: You are coaching a power clean. A trainee asks why you will not have a teammate stand by to 'catch' the bar like on the bench press. The best explanation is:
options: One spotter is always enough for a power clean
The spotter should grasp the athlete's wrists during the catch
Power exercises are not spotted; athletes are instead taught how to miss the lift properly
questions.answer_text: Power exercises are not spotted; athletes are instead taught how to miss the lift properly
questions.explanation_en: Power exercises (e.g., power clean, snatch, jerk) are not spotted because of the safety risk to both athlete and spotter; instead athletes are taught how to miss the lift safely.
tags: Practical and Applied - Exam One

questions.question: While watching a deadlift, you see the lifter's hips shoot up faster than the shoulders as the bar leaves the floor. The correct execution is to:
options: Let the hips rise first to protect the knees
Keep the torso-to-floor angle constant so the hips and shoulders rise together, maintaining a neutral spine
Round the upper back to keep the bar closer
questions.answer_text: Keep the torso-to-floor angle constant so the hips and shoulders rise together, maintaining a neutral spine
questions.explanation_en: In the deadlift the lifter extends the hips and knees while keeping the torso-to-floor angle constant; the hips should not rise before the shoulders, and a neutral spine is maintained with the bar kept close to the shins.
tags: Practical and Applied - Exam One

questions.question: An athlete is performing a two-arm kettlebell swing. Where should the hips and the back be at the bottom of the backswing?
options: Hips flexed with the torso nearly parallel to the floor, back in a neutral spine, elbows extended
Hips fully extended with the back rounded to load the lats
Deep squat with the knees fully flexed and torso vertical
questions.answer_text: Hips flexed with the torso nearly parallel to the floor, back in a neutral spine, elbows extended
questions.explanation_en: The kettlebell swing is hip-hinge driven: at the backswing the hips flex until the torso is nearly parallel to the floor with the back neutral and elbows extended; hip extension then propels the bell forward and up to about eye level.
tags: Practical and Applied - Exam One

questions.question: A coach watches an athlete flipping a heavy tire and notices the athlete pulling the tire up with the arms (a lifting motion) instead of driving it. Why is this a dangerous flaw the coach should correct?
options: It overloads the hamstrings and stalls the tire at the floor
It is unsafe only because it raises heart rate too quickly
It places greater load on the biceps (risking biceps injury) and the tire can lose momentum and fall back onto the athlete
questions.answer_text: It places greater load on the biceps (risking biceps injury) and the tire can lose momentum and fall back onto the athlete
questions.explanation_en: Using a lifting rather than pushing motion makes the lifter muscle the tire over, loading the biceps and increasing biceps-injury risk, and the tire can lose momentum and fall backward. The cue is to keep hips low and drive the tire forward, moving with it.
tags: Practical and Applied - Exam One

questions.question: When setting up a reverse sled drag (or forward sled pull), what foot position does the 5th edition recommend to maximize horizontal propulsive force?
options: Feet positioned behind the knees with a vertical trunk
The front foot kept in front of the knees while leaning back with a relatively extended hip
Feet together directly under the hips throughout
questions.answer_text: The front foot kept in front of the knees while leaning back with a relatively extended hip
questions.explanation_en: For the reverse sled drag the athlete leans back, keeps a relatively extended hip, and keeps the front foot in front of the knees throughout the pull to increase the ability to apply propulsive horizontal forces and accelerate the sled.
tags: Practical and Applied - Exam One

questions.question: A strength coach builds a new body-fat assessment device and checks how well its readings line up with same-day DXA scans on the same athletes. What type of validity is being established?
options: Concurrent validity
Predictive validity
Face validity
questions.answer_text: Concurrent validity
questions.explanation_en: Concurrent validity: a new test's scores are correlated with an already-accepted test of the same ability, measured at the same time (this new-body-fat-device-vs-DXA comparison is the textbook's own example of concurrent validity, and 'same-day' is the tell). It is not predictive (that links a score to FUTURE performance). And although DXA is a gold standard, the textbook still classifies validating a new practical test against an accepted test this way as concurrent (criterion validity), not convergent.
tags: Practical and Applied - Exam One

questions.question: Two different testers time the same group of athletes in the 40-yard sprint and consistently disagree with each other's recorded times. Which testing quality is lacking?
options: Objectivity (interrater reliability)
Content validity
Intrasubject variability
questions.answer_text: Objectivity (interrater reliability)
questions.explanation_en: Objectivity, also called interrater reliability or interrater agreement, is the degree to which different raters get the same result on repeated occasions. Disagreement between testers points to poor objectivity, often fixed with a clear scoring system and trained scorers.
tags: Practical and Applied - Exam One

questions.question: You're sequencing a full test battery for a single session. Following the textbook's logical order, which group of tests should be administered FIRST?
options: Maximum power and strength tests (1RM)
Agility tests like the T-test
Nonfatiguing tests like height, vertical jump, and flexibility
questions.answer_text: Nonfatiguing tests like height, vertical jump, and flexibility
questions.explanation_en: The principle is that one test must not impair a later one. Nonfatiguing tests (anthropometry, flexibility, vertical jump) come first, then agility, then max power/strength, sprints, muscular endurance, anaerobic capacity, and finally aerobic capacity.
tags: Practical and Applied - Exam One

questions.question: An athlete completes the T-test by sprinting forward, then shuffling left, right, and back without crossing the feet, touching cone bases by hand. What ability is this test primarily measuring?
options: Maximal aerobic capacity
Lower-body maximal strength
Change of direction / agility
questions.answer_text: Change of direction / agility
questions.explanation_en: The T-test is a change-of-direction (agility) test combining a forward sprint with lateral shuffles in a T-shaped pattern. The best of two trials is recorded to the nearest 0.1 second.
tags: Practical and Applied - Exam One

questions.question: A coach wants to estimate an athlete's back squat 1RM from a load-velocity profile instead of testing it directly. What is the recommendation?
options: The load-velocity profile reliably replaces a direct 1RM test
Directly test the 1RM; the load-velocity estimate tends to overestimate the true 1RM
Use the load-velocity profile only for the bench press, never the squat
questions.answer_text: Directly test the 1RM; the load-velocity estimate tends to overestimate the true 1RM
questions.explanation_en: When the back-squat 1RM is estimated from a load-velocity profile it is highly variable and consistently OVERestimates the athlete's 1RM, so it should not be used for prediction. Direct testing remains the recommended way to determine maximal strength.
tags: Practical and Applied - Exam One

questions.question: A male NCAA Division I athlete's 1RM bench press falls at the 50th percentile on the normative table. How should you interpret this score?
options: Well above average for his group
Average for his group
Well below average for his group
questions.answer_text: Average for his group
questions.explanation_en: On the textbook's percentile descriptors, 90 = well above average, 70 = above average, 50 = average, 30 = below average, and 10 = well below average. A 50th-percentile score is simply average relative to the reference group.
tags: Practical and Applied - Exam One

questions.question: During rehab from an anterior shoulder dislocation, the athletic trainer asks the S&C coach to begin upper-body strengthening, but notes the bench press should be avoided because it can place the shoulder in a vulnerable position. The bench press is best described as what for this athlete?
options: An indication
A contraindication
A closed kinetic chain exercise
questions.answer_text: A contraindication
questions.explanation_en: A contraindication is an activity that is inadvisable or prohibited given the injury. With anterior shoulder instability, the bench press can place the joint in a vulnerable position, making it contraindicated even while other upper-body work is indicated.
tags: Practical and Applied - Exam One

questions.question: An athlete reports that the pain from a muscle strain has resolved and wants to return to full play. Based on the tissue-healing model, why should the S&C professional be cautious?
options: Pain often resolves well before tissue healing is complete, so reduced pain does not confirm it's safe to resume
Pain resolution always means the maturation-remodeling phase is finished
Once the inflammatory phase ends, full healing has occurred
questions.answer_text: Pain often resolves well before tissue healing is complete, so reduced pain does not confirm it's safe to resume
questions.explanation_en: Pain levels typically decrease well before tissue healing reaches the adequate threshold. Athletes may wrongly assume that pain-free means healed, so return-to-play must be judged by healing and objective metrics, not pain alone.
tags: Practical and Applied - Exam One

questions.question: A preseason camp deliberately spikes training volume, causing a short-term performance dip, but after a few days to weeks of recovery the athletes supercompensate and perform better than before. This planned process is best termed what?
options: Nonfunctional overreaching
Overtraining syndrome
Functional overreaching
questions.answer_text: Functional overreaching
questions.explanation_en: Functional overreaching is purposely planned overload causing a brief performance decrement that, after short-term recovery (days to weeks), leads to supercompensation and improved performance. Nonfunctional overreaching only returns to baseline, and overtraining requires long-term impairment.
tags: Practical and Applied - Exam One

questions.question: When choosing tests for a daily athlete-monitoring program to catch impending overtraining, which category of assessment is most appropriate for everyday use?
options: Category I: easy to administer, inexpensive, rapid turnaround, convenient daily
Category III: occasional, intrusive, expensive, long turnaround
Lab-based endocrine panels run weekly
questions.answer_text: Category I: easy to administer, inexpensive, rapid turnaround, convenient daily
questions.explanation_en: Category I tests are daily, easy, inexpensive, and give rapid turnaround (e.g., RPE, resting/recovery HR, HRV, vertical jump), making them suited for routine monitoring. Category III tests are occasional, more intrusive, and slower, so they aren't practical day-to-day.
tags: Practical and Applied - Exam One

questions.question: A new strength and conditioning facility is being built. During which phase of the design process is a reputable architect typically hired, usually through a bid process?
options: The predesign phase
The design phase
The construction phase
questions.answer_text: The predesign phase
questions.explanation_en: The predesign phase consists of a needs analysis, feasibility study, and master plan formation; hiring the architect (often via a low-bid process) is the final step of this phase, before the design phase begins.
tags: Practical and Applied - Exam One

questions.question: When planning the total area of a strength and conditioning facility, what is the recommended minimum amount of floor space per individual, counting all athletes, staff, and other persons present?
options: 50 square feet (4.6 m2) per person
100 square feet (9.3 m2) per person
200 square feet (18.6 m2) per person
questions.answer_text: 100 square feet (9.3 m2) per person
questions.explanation_en: The recommended minimum is 100 square feet (9.3 m2) per individual, including all athletes, strength and conditioning professionals, and any additional staff present. Having enough space matters more for the training environment than having extra specialized equipment.
tags: Practical and Applied - Exam One

questions.question: A coach is laying out a weight room and wants main walkways that allow safe traffic flow and ADA wheelchair access. What is the recommended width for these main walkways?
questions.explanation_en: Racks and machines are best lined up in rows running the length of the facility, creating two or three main walkways that should be 5 to 7 feet (1.5-2.1 m) wide. This supports safety, clear access to exits, and ADA-required wheelchair access. (Note: a separate minimum of 3 feet, 0.9 m, applies between individual pieces of equipment.)
tags: Practical and Applied - Exam One

questions.question: A facility will program box jumps, vertical jumps, and weightlifting. What ceiling height is recommended to give athletes enough clearance to comfortably perform most of these activities?
questions.explanation_en: A recommended ceiling height of 12 to 14 feet (3.7-4.3 m) accommodates the athlete plus the space needed for jumping and explosive lifting. Some exercises, like overhead medicine ball throws, may need additional clearance or an alternate space.
tags: Practical and Applied - Exam One

questions.question: In the law of negligence, how is the standard of care for a strength and conditioning professional best described?
options: The degree of caution and prudence a reasonable person would exercise in similar situations
The highest level of skill possessed by any expert in the field
Whatever level of care the athlete agrees to in a signed waiver
questions.answer_text: The degree of caution and prudence a reasonable person would exercise in similar situations
questions.explanation_en: Standard of care is the degree of caution and prudence a reasonable person would exercise in similar situations. The strength and conditioning professional is expected to act according to their education, training, and certification.
tags: Practical and Applied - Exam One

questions.question: An athlete is recovering from a knee injury and asks the strength coach whether she is medically cleared to resume training. According to scope of practice, who is responsible for providing that medical clearance?
options: The strength and conditioning professional, based on a movement screen
The sports medicine staff (e.g., athletic trainer, physician, or physical therapist)
The athletic director after reviewing the athlete's file
questions.answer_text: The sports medicine staff (e.g., athletic trainer, physician, or physical therapist)
questions.explanation_en: It is not within the strength and conditioning professional's scope of practice to diagnose or evaluate a medical condition. Only the sports medicine staff can grant medical clearance; the coach then collaborates with them to modify workouts as needed.
tags: Practical and Applied - Exam One

questions.question: Per NSCA Strength and Conditioning Professional Standards and Guidelines (Guideline 3.1), which set of recommended professional-to-participant supervision ratios is correct?
options: 1:10 junior high school, 1:15 high school, 1:20 college
1:5 junior high school, 1:10 high school, 1:15 college
1:15 junior high school, 1:20 high school, 1:25 college
questions.answer_text: 1:10 junior high school, 1:15 high school, 1:20 college
questions.explanation_en: Guideline 3.1 recommends professional-to-participant ratios of 1:10 (junior high school), 1:15 (high school), and 1:20 (college), along with at least 100 ft2 of floor space per participant. Ratios should be increased (more supervision) for complex movements or low-training-age athletes.
tags: Practical and Applied - Exam One

questions.question: A strength coach notices a frayed cable on a machine, makes a mental note of it, but does not post an 'Out of Order' sign or remove it; an athlete is later injured using it. This scenario most directly illustrates which legal concept?
options: Assumption of risk
Sovereign immunity
Negligence
questions.answer_text: Negligence
questions.explanation_en: This is the textbook's example of negligence: the coach had a duty to fix the cable or post a sign, breached that duty by failing to act, and that failure proximately caused a foreseeable injury. Negligence requires duty, breach, causation, and damages.
tags: Practical and Applied - Exam One

questions.question: A 22-year-old soccer player joins your program. He has competed at a high level for six years, but his intake questionnaire and a movement screen show only about seven weeks of unstructured lifting and poor barbell technique. Using resistance training status to set his starting point, how should you classify him and prescribe initial frequency and training stress?
options: Advanced; four or more sessions per week at high training stress since he is an elite competitor
Beginner; roughly one to two sessions per week at low training stress while technique is taught
Intermediate; three to four sessions per week at moderate training stress because his years of sport count as training age
questions.answer_text: Beginner; roughly one to two sessions per week at low training stress while technique is taught
questions.explanation_en: Resistance training status reflects weight room experience and lifting skill, not sport experience or competitive level. Under two months of training with minimal skill classifies an athlete as a beginner, who should start with low frequency (about one to two days per week) and low training stress while learning technique.
tags: Practical and Applied - Exam Two

questions.question: In a muscular strength program, a lifter finishes a heavy multijoint core lift and then moves to lateral shoulder raises loaded at a 12RM. A newer coach wants to give the raises the same rest the core lift received. What rest length actually fits the lateral raise, and on what basis?
options: At least 5 minutes, because single-joint work still demands full neuromuscular recovery
The same 2 to 5 minutes as the core lift, because the whole session shares one strength goal
About 1 minute, because rest is set by the relative load and muscle mass of that specific exercise, both of which are low here
questions.answer_text: About 1 minute, because rest is set by the relative load and muscle mass of that specific exercise, both of which are low here
questions.explanation_en: Rest between sets is assigned by the relative load and amount of muscle mass involved in each exercise, not by the overall program goal. A light single-joint assistance lift such as a 12RM lateral raise needs only about 1 minute of rest even inside a strength program.
tags: Practical and Applied - Exam Two

questions.question: A trained athlete's block is centered on maximal strength, and the back squat is the core lift. You want the load and repetition prescription to land squarely in the maximal strength zone rather than drifting toward hypertrophy. Which prescription fits?
options: At least 85 percent of 1RM for about 6 or fewer repetitions
About 67 to 80 percent of 1RM for 8 to 12 repetitions
About 60 to 67 percent of 1RM for 12 to 15 repetitions
questions.answer_text: At least 85 percent of 1RM for about 6 or fewer repetitions
questions.explanation_en: Maximal strength on core exercises is trained with loads of at least 85 percent of 1RM for roughly 6 or fewer repetitions. The moderate-load, higher-rep ranges target hypertrophy and muscular endurance instead.
tags: Practical and Applied - Exam Two

questions.question: You are building a hypertrophy-focused day around multijoint lifts and want each core exercise's load and rep scheme to sit in the middle of the hypertrophy zone, not bleed into the strength or endurance zones. Which prescription fits?
options: Below 67 percent of 1RM for more than 15 repetitions
About 67 to 80 percent of 1RM for 8 to 12 repetitions
About 85 to 90 percent of 1RM for 3 to 5 repetitions
questions.answer_text: About 67 to 80 percent of 1RM for 8 to 12 repetitions
questions.explanation_en: Hypertrophy is emphasized with moderate loads of roughly 67 to 80 percent of 1RM for about 8 to 12 repetitions, balancing mechanical tension against enough volume. Heavier low-rep work targets strength, and very light high-rep work targets muscular endurance.
tags: Practical and Applied - Exam Two

questions.question: During a power block you are programming for a shot putter, whose event is a single explosive effort. You want the load and rep scheme that maximizes power for a single-effort movement. Which prescription is recommended?
options: About 75 to 85 percent of 1RM for 3 to 5 repetitions performed explosively
30 to 50 percent of 1RM for 10 to 12 repetitions performed explosively
80 to 90 percent of 1RM for 1 to 2 repetitions performed explosively
questions.answer_text: 80 to 90 percent of 1RM for 1 to 2 repetitions performed explosively
questions.explanation_en: Single-effort power events are trained with about 80 to 90 percent of 1RM for 1 to 2 repetitions performed explosively. Multiple-effort power uses a lower load, about 75 to 85 percent of 1RM, for 3 to 5 repetitions.
tags: Practical and Applied - Exam Two

questions.question: In a power phase you load the power clean to 80 percent of 1RM. The athlete clearly could grind out five or six reps, but you cap the set at three. A teammate asks why you are leaving reps 'in the tank.' What is the real reason for stopping short?
options: To keep bar velocity high so the set trains power instead of degrading into slow, fatiguing grinding reps
To accumulate the most time under tension possible on each set
To ensure the set reaches muscular failure on a heavy compound lift
questions.answer_text: To keep bar velocity high so the set trains power instead of degrading into slow, fatiguing grinding reps
questions.explanation_en: Power development depends on high movement velocity. The earliest reps at a given load are the fastest, so a power set uses fewer reps than the load would allow in order to keep every rep explosive rather than slow and grinding.
tags: Practical and Applied - Exam Two

questions.question: A cross country runner enters a preseason block whose primary resistance training aim is muscular endurance. You want the core-lift load and rep prescription to match that aim and not slide toward strength or power. Which prescription fits?
options: 85 percent or more of 1RM for 6 or fewer repetitions
67 percent or less of 1RM for 12 or more repetitions
75 to 85 percent of 1RM for 3 to 5 repetitions
questions.answer_text: 67 percent or less of 1RM for 12 or more repetitions
questions.explanation_en: Muscular endurance is trained with light loads of 67 percent or less of 1RM for many repetitions, 12 or more per set. The heavier low-rep options correspond to power and strength goals respectively.
tags: Practical and Applied - Exam Two

questions.question: To save time, a coach has an athlete perform a set of front squats immediately followed by a set of overhead presses with only brief rest between them, then repeats. A colleague calls this a compound set. What is the method actually called, and what is its main benefit?
options: Circuit training, whose main benefit is maximizing the metabolic conditioning effect
A compound set, which stacks two exercises for the same muscle group to pre-exhaust it
An alternating (push-pull) arrangement, which lets one region recover while the other works and improves time efficiency
questions.answer_text: An alternating (push-pull) arrangement, which lets one region recover while the other works and improves time efficiency
questions.explanation_en: Alternating an upper-body and a lower-body exercise with brief rest is a push-pull (alternating muscle-group) arrangement: one region recovers while the other trains, improving time efficiency. It is not a compound set (two exercises for the same muscle group), and a superset specifically pairs opposing agonist and antagonist muscles.
tags: Practical and Applied - Exam Two

questions.question: A coach logs a session of 3 sets of 10 back squats at 100 kg and computes the volume-load. A second coach did full-range squats while this athlete used a shortened partial range, yet both logged the identical numbers. What is the volume-load, and what does this measure fail to capture?
options: 3,000 kg; it fails to capture actual bar displacement, so partial and full-range squats show the same value
1,000 kg; it fails to capture the number of sets performed
30 repetitions; it fails to capture the load that was lifted
questions.answer_text: 3,000 kg; it fails to capture actual bar displacement, so partial and full-range squats show the same value
questions.explanation_en: Volume-load equals sets times reps times weight, so 3 x 10 x 100 kg is 3,000 kg. Because it multiplies only weight by repetitions, it ignores bar displacement (range of motion), so a partial-range and a full-range squat with the same sets, reps, and load produce identical volume-load.
tags: Practical and Applied - Exam Two

questions.question: You are prescribing low-intensity lower-body plyometric drills for a beginner and need to record the session's volume in the appropriate unit. How should lower-body plyometric volume be expressed?
options: As the number of sets carried to technical failure
As foot contacts per session
As total minutes of jumping per session
questions.answer_text: As foot contacts per session
questions.explanation_en: Lower-body plyometric volume is counted as foot contacts per session, each instance a foot or the feet contact the surface. Bounding drills may instead be quantified by distance covered.
tags: Practical and Applied - Exam Two

questions.question: You are ordering boxes for depth jumps and box jumps and want a height range that allows a meaningful eccentric stimulus without pushing athletes past the height where landing mechanics break down. Which height range is recommended?
options: 2 to 12 inches (5 to 30 cm)
12 to 60 inches (30 to 152 cm)
6 to 42 inches (15 to 107 cm)
questions.answer_text: 6 to 42 inches (15 to 107 cm)
questions.explanation_en: Plyometric boxes should range from 6 to 42 inches (15 to 107 cm), with a nonslip top and a stable base. Heights near the top of this range give a large eccentric overload; going much higher tends to break down landing technique and raise injury risk.
tags: Practical and Applied - Exam Two

questions.question: An athlete is running a circuit-style muscular endurance program with light loads and high repetitions, and you want the between-set rest to reinforce the endurance stimulus rather than allow full recovery. Which rest length fits?
options: 30 seconds or less
2 to 5 minutes
2 to 3 minutes
questions.answer_text: 30 seconds or less
questions.explanation_en: Muscular endurance programs use very short rest periods, often 30 seconds or less, to deliberately limit recovery when light loads are lifted for many repetitions. Longer rests correspond to hypertrophy (2 to 3 minutes) and strength or power (2 to 5 minutes).
tags: Practical and Applied - Exam Two

questions.question: You are setting weekly resistance training frequency for a trained athlete who is currently in the off-season and building a base before the season starts. Based on frequency guidelines by sport season, which weekly range is appropriate?
options: 1 to 3 sessions per week
4 to 6 sessions per week
3 to 4 sessions per week
questions.answer_text: 4 to 6 sessions per week
questions.explanation_en: For a trained athlete, recommended frequency by sport season is 4 to 6 sessions per week in the off-season, 3 to 4 in the preseason, 1 to 3 in-season, and 0 to 3 postseason during active rest. The off-season allows the highest frequency.
tags: Practical and Applied - Exam Two

questions.question: A distance runner wants to accumulate time near VO2max to raise aerobic power and asks you to program classic interval training specifically (not HIIT). Which combination of intensity, work-bout length, and work-to-rest ratio defines interval training?
options: Below the lactate threshold, performed continuously for about 30 to 120 minutes
Greater than VO2max, short bouts of about 30 to 90 seconds, roughly a 1:5 work-to-rest ratio
Close to VO2max, work bouts of about 3 to 5 minutes, roughly a 1:1 work-to-rest ratio
questions.answer_text: Close to VO2max, work bouts of about 3 to 5 minutes, roughly a 1:1 work-to-rest ratio
questions.explanation_en: Interval training uses work bouts near VO2max lasting about 3 to 5 minutes at roughly a 1:1 work-to-rest ratio, which lets the athlete accumulate time near VO2max. Greater-than-VO2max short bouts at about 1:5 describe HIIT, and continuous submaximal work describes long slow distance training.
tags: Practical and Applied - Exam Two

questions.question: A coach is deciding between HIIT and standard interval training and needs to explain how HIIT differs on intensity, work duration, and work-to-rest ratio. Which description correctly captures HIIT relative to standard intervals?
options: HIIT is performed above VO2max with shorter work bouts of about 30 to 90 seconds and roughly a 1:5 work-to-rest ratio
HIIT is performed below VO2max with longer work bouts and about a 1:1 work-to-rest ratio
HIIT uses the same intensity and bout length as interval training but with a much longer relief period
questions.answer_text: HIIT is performed above VO2max with shorter work bouts of about 30 to 90 seconds and roughly a 1:5 work-to-rest ratio
questions.explanation_en: HIIT uses shorter work bouts of about 30 to 90 seconds at intensities greater than VO2max with a longer relief period, roughly a 1:5 work-to-rest ratio. Standard interval training is near VO2max for about 3 to 5 minutes at roughly 1:1.
tags: Practical and Applied - Exam Two

questions.question: A coach notes that the back squat loads the spine and requires the lifter to keep a rigid torso and neutral spine so posture is stabilized against the load throughout the lift. Within the exercise classification system, which category best fits the back squat on that basis?
options: A single-joint assistance exercise
A structural exercise
A power exercise, because any barbell squat is defined by explosive intent
questions.answer_text: A structural exercise
questions.explanation_en: A core exercise that loads the spine directly or indirectly and requires muscular stabilization of posture during the lift is classified as a structural exercise. A structural exercise performed very quickly or explosively is further classified as a power exercise, but a standard back squat is simply structural.
tags: Practical and Applied - Exam Two

questions.question: A sprint coach is contrasting the low, forward-leaning drive an athlete uses coming out of the blocks with the tall, upright running he does once he has reached full speed. These two portions of the sprint are best labeled as which phases?
options: The braking phase and the recovery phase
The amortization phase and the concentric phase
The acceleration phase and the maximal-velocity phase
questions.answer_text: The acceleration phase and the maximal-velocity phase
questions.explanation_en: Sprinting requires the ability to accelerate and then reach maximal velocity. The acceleration phase (drive out of the blocks) and the maximal-velocity phase (upright top-end running) use different body positions and produce vertical and horizontal ground reaction forces of differing magnitude.
tags: Practical and Applied - Exam Two

questions.question: You are outlining the preparatory (off-season) period for a traditionally periodized athlete and need to describe its characteristic training emphasis. Which combination correctly characterizes that period?
options: Low to moderate intensity with high volume, emphasizing hypertrophy and strength endurance
Moderate intensity with sport-specific technique and tactics as the primary focus
High intensity with very low volume and peaking work as the main emphasis
questions.answer_text: Low to moderate intensity with high volume, emphasizing hypertrophy and strength endurance
questions.explanation_en: The preparatory/off-season period uses high volume at lower intensity to build a base, hypertrophy, and strength endurance, with a low technical and tactical emphasis. Intensity rises and volume falls as competition approaches.
tags: Practical and Applied - Exam Two

questions.question: A team-sport athlete faces a competitive period spanning several months, and the goal is to retain strength and power while managing the fatigue of frequent competition. How is a maintenance program for such a prolonged competitive period generally characterized?
options: Maximal volume and maximal intensity held constant every week to prevent detraining
Moderate to high intensity of about 85 to 93 percent of 1RM at low to moderate volume
High volume at low intensity below 60 percent of 1RM to minimize joint stress
questions.answer_text: Moderate to high intensity of about 85 to 93 percent of 1RM at low to moderate volume
questions.explanation_en: During a prolonged competitive period, a maintenance program is marked by moderate to high intensity, about 85 to 93 percent of 1RM, at low to moderate volume, with loads modulated microcycle to microcycle around the competition schedule.
tags: Practical and Applied - Exam Two

questions.question: A coach tapers an athlete before a competition and observes performance rise above baseline in the days that follow. Using the fitness-fatigue paradigm, how is preparedness best described, and why does the taper work?
options: Preparedness is the sum of fitness and fatigue, which rise together and remain permanently elevated after training
Preparedness is the fatigue component alone, so reducing load simply removes fatigue while fitness stays fixed
Preparedness is the fitness component minus the fatigue component; because fatigue dissipates faster than fitness, reducing load lets preparedness rise
questions.answer_text: Preparedness is the fitness component minus the fatigue component; because fatigue dissipates faster than fitness, reducing load lets preparedness rise
questions.explanation_en: Each training bout produces both fitness and fatigue, and preparedness is their net effect (fitness minus fatigue). Because fatigue dissipates faster than fitness, reducing the training load during a taper lets preparedness climb above baseline.
tags: Practical and Applied - Exam Two

questions.question: A coach wants to make an athlete faster and is deciding what to target in training. Sprint speed is the product of which two variables, and what primarily drives improvement in both?
options: Stride length and stride rate (frequency), improved mainly by applying greater force during the brief ground-contact time
Reaction time and flexibility, improved mainly through static stretching
Body mass and limb length, improved mainly by adding external load
questions.answer_text: Stride length and stride rate (frequency), improved mainly by applying greater force during the brief ground-contact time
questions.explanation_en: Sprint speed equals stride length times stride frequency. Faster sprinters direct larger forces into the ground during a brief stance phase, which lengthens the stride while a high stride rate is maintained.
tags: Practical and Applied - Exam Two

questions.question: Setting up for a heavy deadlift, a lifter positions one hand so the palm faces the body and the other so the palm faces away, specifically to stop the bar from rolling out of the hands as the load gets heavy. Which grip is being used?
options: A neutral grip
An alternated grip
A supinated grip
questions.answer_text: An alternated grip
questions.explanation_en: An alternated grip places one hand pronated (palm facing away) and the other supinated (palm facing the body). It is commonly used on heavy pulling movements such as the deadlift to keep the bar from rolling and improve grip security.
tags: Practical and Applied - Exam Two

questions.question: Working through a RAMP warm-up, a coach reaches the final segment right before performance and uses specific, increasingly intense movements at competition intensity to exploit a postactivation potentiation effect. Which RAMP phase is this?
options: Activate and Mobilize
Raise
Potentiate
questions.answer_text: Potentiate
questions.explanation_en: The Potentiate phase uses specific, progressively more intense movements to bring activity up to competition intensity and take advantage of postactivation potentiation right before the main activity. Raise elevates body temperature and heart rate early, and Activate and Mobilize targets key muscles and ranges of motion in between.
tags: Practical and Applied - Exam Two

questions.question: An athlete asks whether adding a block of static stretching to the pre-competition warm-up will help him jump and sprint better. How is the current evidence on static stretching in a warm-up best summarized with respect to subsequent performance?
options: It is equivocal, and several reviews suggest it can compromise force and power performance
It reliably improves force and power output when done before performance
It has been shown to have no measurable effect on any performance variable
questions.answer_text: It is equivocal, and several reviews suggest it can compromise force and power performance
questions.explanation_en: The literature on static stretching in warm-ups is equivocal, and a number of reviews report negative effects on force production and power. That is why dynamic warm-ups are generally favored before performance.
tags: Practical and Applied - Exam Two

questions.question: A coach is explaining how to execute the concentric phase of a power clean and, separately, what training through a full range of motion does to flexibility. Which statement is correct on both counts?
options: Flexibility is unaffected by full-ROM training, and the concentric phase of an explosive lift should follow a fixed 3-second tempo
Flexibility is maintained or improved through full-ROM training, and the concentric phase of an explosive lift should be accelerated to maximal speed while keeping control and form
Flexibility decreases with full-ROM training, so the concentric phase of an explosive lift should be slowed deliberately to protect the joint
questions.answer_text: Flexibility is maintained or improved through full-ROM training, and the concentric phase of an explosive lift should be accelerated to maximal speed while keeping control and form
questions.explanation_en: Training through a full range of motion maintains or even improves flexibility. For explosive movements such as the power clean, the bar should be accelerated to maximal speed during the concentric phase while control and proper form are maintained.
tags: Practical and Applied - Exam Two

questions.question: Checking a lifter's hand placement on the bar, you see the thumb resting alongside the fingers on the same side of the bar rather than wrapped around it. You correct it to a closed grip. Why is wrapping the thumb around the bar preferred over that open or false grip?
options: It is only necessary for supinated grips and can be skipped on pronated grips
It increases the range of motion available at the wrist during the lift
It keeps the bar from slipping out of the hands, improving control and safety
questions.answer_text: It keeps the bar from slipping out of the hands, improving control and safety
questions.explanation_en: In a closed grip the thumb is wrapped around the bar, securing it in the hand. In an open or false grip the thumb sits alongside the fingers, which allows the bar to slip out more easily and is less safe, regardless of whether the grip is pronated or supinated.
tags: Practical and Applied - Exam Two

questions.question: You are spotting an athlete doing heavy dumbbell chest presses. During the last rep her elbows begin to buckle and the dumbbells drift toward her face and chest. To have the best chance of stopping the weights before they strike her, where should your hands already be positioned?
options: At her wrists or on the forearms just below the wrists
At the elbows, so you can push the upper arms back up as they bend
Under the dumbbells themselves, cupping the plates from below
questions.answer_text: At her wrists or on the forearms just below the wrists
questions.explanation_en: Dumbbells are spotted at the forearms near the wrists, closest to the load, so the spotter can actually arrest the weights. Spotting at the elbows leaves the spotter unable to stop the dumbbells from continuing toward the athlete once the elbows collapse.
tags: Practical and Applied - Exam Two

questions.question: A beginner is setting up for a standard barbell exercise and asks you how far apart to place the hands as a starting default. Absent a specific reason to go wider or narrower, what should you tell him?
options: As wide as he can comfortably reach to increase leverage
Roughly shoulder-width apart
Hands touching in the center of the bar for maximum control
questions.answer_text: Roughly shoulder-width apart
questions.explanation_en: Grip widths are described as common, wide, and narrow, but the common default for most exercises places the hands approximately shoulder-width apart to keep the load balanced on the bar. Widest-possible or hands-together grips are special cases, not the default.
tags: Practical and Applied - Exam Two

questions.question: During a training session an athlete asks you to stand behind him and 'catch' the bar on his power cleans the same way you would guide the bar back to the rack on a failed bench press. How should you respond?
options: Position two spotters, one at each end of the bar, to share the load
Agree and prepare to catch, since any lift performed with heavy weight must be spotted
Decline, because explosive lifts are not spotted; the safer approach is coaching him to miss or dump the bar cleanly
questions.answer_text: Decline, because explosive lifts are not spotted; the safer approach is coaching him to miss or dump the bar cleanly
questions.explanation_en: Because of the speed of the movement, explosive lifts such as the power clean are not spotted; a spotter cannot safely intervene and would be endangered. Instead the athlete is taught to miss the lift by dropping or pushing the bar away safely.
tags: Practical and Applied - Exam Two

questions.question: A single competent spotter can comfortably handle the weight on an athlete's incline press. A newer staff member suggests adding a second and third spotter 'to be safe.' Why is using just the one capable spotter generally the better choice here?
options: Every added spotter is one more person who must sync timing with the lifter and the others, raising the odds of a coordination error
Facility standards prohibit using more than one spotter on any lift
A lone spotter can generate more rescue force than several spotters combined
questions.answer_text: Every added spotter is one more person who must sync timing with the lifter and the others, raising the odds of a coordination error
questions.explanation_en: When one spotter can handle the load, one is preferred: each additional spotter has to coordinate with the lifter and every other spotter, and each added person increases the chance of a timing or technique error. Multiple spotters are reserved for loads a single person cannot manage.
tags: Practical and Applied - Exam Two

questions.question: You are correcting an athlete's stance before a set of standing overhead presses done free of any rack or support. Which foot setup gives the most stable base for this ground-based standing lift?
options: A very wide stance with the weight shifted back onto the heels
Feet slightly wider than hip width, with both the heels and the balls of the feet pressing into the floor
Feet close together directly beneath the hips to stack the joints
questions.answer_text: Feet slightly wider than hip width, with both the heels and the balls of the feet pressing into the floor
questions.explanation_en: Standing free-weight exercises call for the feet slightly wider than hip width with both the heels and the balls of the feet in contact with the floor, creating a stable base. A narrow stance or loading only the heels undermines that base.
tags: Practical and Applied - Exam Two

questions.question: An experienced lifter with clean squat mechanics plateaus at lockout. You decide to hang chains from the bar for his back squats. What effect are you counting on, and why does his training background matter here?
options: The chains make the bottom heaviest and the top lightest, which makes them ideal for teaching brand-new beginners
The chains keep resistance constant through the range, so any lifter's experience level is irrelevant
The chains load the top of the squat, where he is strongest, and unload the bottom; the added instability means this suits a lifter who already has solid technique
questions.answer_text: The chains load the top of the squat, where he is strongest, and unload the bottom; the added instability means this suits a lifter who already has solid technique
questions.explanation_en: Chains add resistance near the top of the lift, where leverage and strength are greatest, and unload the bottom, helping match the load to the strength curve. Because the swinging implements add instability, they are appropriate for athletes who already have solid technique.
tags: Practical and Applied - Exam Two

questions.question: A coach wants to strengthen an athlete's midsection and assumes only dedicated isolation core drills like crunches will do it. Compared with those isolation drills, how do ground-based lifts such as squats and deadlifts affect the anatomical core?
options: They tend to activate the core to a similar or greater degree while training it to stiffen and transmit force through the kinetic chain
They bypass the core almost entirely because the trunk stays rigid throughout
They recruit the core less than isolation work because the bracing limits trunk motion
questions.answer_text: They tend to activate the core to a similar or greater degree while training it to stiffen and transmit force through the kinetic chain
questions.explanation_en: Ground-based free-weight lifts activate the core similarly to or more than isolation exercises, and they train the core to stiffen and transfer force through the kinetic chain in a more sport-relevant way than isolation drills do.
tags: Practical and Applied - Exam Two

questions.question: An athlete asks you to program his heavy squats and cleans on a wobble board and stability ball to 'build more power.' Based on how unstable surfaces affect force production, how should you advise him?
options: It raises force output and is therefore ideal for peak power development
Unstable-surface work tends to reduce force output, so it fits rehab and prehab better than maximizing strength and power
It leaves force output unchanged, so it can simply replace conventional free-weight training
questions.answer_text: Unstable-surface work tends to reduce force output, so it fits rehab and prehab better than maximizing strength and power
questions.explanation_en: The nervous system limits force output when the base is unstable, so training on unstable surfaces can markedly lower the force produced. That makes it useful for rehabilitation and prehab but poorly suited to maximizing strength and power.
tags: Practical and Applied - Exam Two

questions.question: A coach measures an athlete's vertical jump on Monday and again on Thursday under identical conditions, then examines how closely the two sets of scores agree. Any gap between them is treated as measurement error. Which quality of the test is she evaluating?
options: How thoroughly the test covers the components of the ability being measured
How well the test predicts a future performance outcome
How consistently the test reproduces the same score across repeated administrations
questions.answer_text: How consistently the test reproduces the same score across repeated administrations
questions.explanation_en: Administering the same test twice under identical conditions and comparing the scores evaluates test-retest reliability, the consistency or repeatability of the measure.
