The difference between the two sets of scores represents measurement error. Predictive coverage and content coverage are forms of validity, not reliability.
tags: Practical and Applied - Exam Two

questions.question: A coach builds an 'agility' test as a fully pre-planned course: athletes memorize every cut ahead of time and never have to react to a stimulus. A panel of experts concludes it fails to measure agility as the sport actually demands it. Which quality is most directly missing?
options: The extent to which the test covers the defining components of the ability measured
The degree to which different testers would score it the same way
The consistency of the score when the test is repeated
questions.answer_text: The extent to which the test covers the defining components of the ability measured
questions.explanation_en: Content validity is the expert judgment that a test covers the relevant components of the quality being measured. An 'agility' test with no perceptual-cognitive or reactive component omits a defining part of agility, so content validity is what it lacks. Scorer agreement and repeatability are separate qualities.
tags: Practical and Applied - Exam Two

questions.question: Before adopting a new fitness battery, a program director convenes sport experts to judge whether the tests collectively cover every relevant physical ability the sport requires, and in the right proportions. Which quality are the experts establishing?
options: Whether the tests simply appear relevant to the athletes at first glance
The extent to which the battery samples all relevant component abilities in appropriate proportions
The degree to which battery scores correlate with an already-accepted test of the same abilities
questions.answer_text: The extent to which the battery samples all relevant component abilities in appropriate proportions
questions.explanation_en: Content validity is the experts' assessment that testing covers all relevant subtopics or component abilities in appropriate proportions, which for sport means every ability the sport demands. Correlating with an accepted test is concurrent validity, and surface plausibility is face validity.
tags: Practical and Applied - Exam Two

questions.question: You are running an athlete through progressively heavier attempts to find her 1RM back squat. She just completed a submaximal warm-up attempt and is a couple of loads away from her likely max. How much rest is recommended before this next non-maximal attempt versus before an attempt that is close to her maximum?
options: At least 5 minutes before non-maximal attempts and about 10 minutes before near-maximal attempts
About 30 seconds before non-maximal attempts and roughly 1 minute before near-maximal attempts
At least 2 minutes before non-maximal attempts and 3 minutes before near-maximal attempts
questions.answer_text: At least 2 minutes before non-maximal attempts and 3 minutes before near-maximal attempts
questions.explanation_en: For multiple-trial 1RM testing, allow at least 2 minutes of rest between attempts that are not close to the maximum and at least 3 minutes between attempts that are near the maximum. Shorter rests leave residual fatigue; much longer rests are not what the protocol specifies.
tags: Practical and Applied - Exam Two

questions.question: A testing session pairs a maximal test of the phosphagen system with a maximal test of the anaerobic glycolytic system. To keep fatigue from one from contaminating the other, how much recovery does each respectively require?
options: About 3 to 5 minutes after the phosphagen test and at least 1 hour after the anaerobic glycolytic test
About 1 hour after the phosphagen test and about 3 minutes after the anaerobic glycolytic test
About 30 seconds after each is enough because both are short in duration
questions.answer_text: About 3 to 5 minutes after the phosphagen test and at least 1 hour after the anaerobic glycolytic test
questions.explanation_en: A maximal phosphagen-system test needs roughly 3 to 5 minutes for full recovery, whereas a maximal anaerobic glycolytic test needs at least 1 hour. The glycolytic test's long recovery is why it should be sequenced so it does not fatigue later tests.
tags: Practical and Applied - Exam Two

questions.question: An athletic trainer is managing an athlete's acute ankle sprain in the first day or two and wants an approach that reflects the current move away from the older PRICE model, which the field revised because strict rest was not producing the best outcomes. Which strategy fits that updated thinking?
options: Applying heat and deep tissue massage to the area on the first day
POLICE: protection, optimal loading, ice, compression, and elevation
Strict immobilization of the joint for no less than two weeks
questions.answer_text: POLICE: protection, optimal loading, ice, compression, and elevation
questions.explanation_en: The evidence-based shift replaced the 'rest' of PRICE (protection, rest, ice, compression, elevation) with 'optimal loading' in POLICE, because controlled early loading rather than complete rest tends to yield better outcomes and faster recovery. Prolonged immobilization and early heat/massage run counter to this.
tags: Practical and Applied - Exam Two

questions.question: An athlete tears a muscle acutely and reports pain, swelling, and redness at the site. During roughly what window does this initial healing phase last, and which physiological change is characteristic of it?
options: Roughly six months, characterized by full return of the tissue's original strength
Roughly two months, characterized by realignment of collagen and rising tissue strength
Roughly the first 72 hours, characterized by increased inflammatory cells and decreased collagen synthesis
questions.answer_text: Roughly the first 72 hours, characterized by increased inflammatory cells and decreased collagen synthesis
questions.explanation_en: The inflammatory response phase typically lasts about 72 hours and is marked by pain, swelling, redness, an influx of inflammatory cells, and decreased collagen synthesis. Collagen realignment and rising strength belong to the later repair and remodeling phases, which unfold over weeks to months.
tags: Practical and Applied - Exam Two

questions.question: You are guiding an athlete through the early healing phase after a medial collateral ligament (MCL) sprain of the knee. Knowing which loading direction most directly stresses that ligament, which type of movement should you avoid for now?
options: Frontal-plane, valgus-loading movement such as a lateral box jump or side shuffle
Closed-chain sagittal loading such as a leg press
Straight-ahead sagittal-plane movement such as an easy jog
questions.answer_text: Frontal-plane, valgus-loading movement such as a lateral box jump or side shuffle
questions.explanation_en: The MCL resists valgus (frontal-plane) stress at the knee, so frontal-plane movements like lateral box jumps and side shuffles load the injured ligament most and are avoided in early healing, then reintroduced in later phases. Straight-ahead jogging and leg pressing do not impose the same valgus stress.
tags: Practical and Applied - Exam Two

questions.question: A preseason camp deliberately overloads training volume for a couple of weeks. Performance dips briefly, then rebounds above baseline once athletes recover within days to a few weeks. How is this planned response best classified relative to a more severe state that would take weeks to months to resolve?
options: Ordinary acute fatigue that bears no relationship to the overtraining continuum
Functional overreaching, in contrast to nonfunctional overreaching
Overtraining syndrome, in contrast to functional overreaching
questions.answer_text: Functional overreaching, in contrast to nonfunctional overreaching
questions.explanation_en: Functional overreaching is intentionally programmed: a short-term performance decrement is followed by recovery within days to weeks and a supercompensation rebound. Nonfunctional overreaching is more severe and takes longer to resolve, and overtraining syndrome involves long-term impairment lasting weeks to months or more.
tags: Practical and Applied - Exam Two

questions.question: Two athletes are diagnosed with different forms of overtraining syndrome: a powerlifter whose case traces to chronically high training intensity, and a marathoner whose case traces to accumulated high volume. Which mapping of these forms is correct?
options: Both cases are the same condition, since the sympathetic and parasympathetic labels are interchangeable
The powerlifter has volume-driven parasympathetic overtraining; the marathoner has intensity-driven sympathetic overtraining
The powerlifter has intensity-driven sympathetic overtraining; the marathoner has volume-driven parasympathetic overtraining
questions.answer_text: The powerlifter has intensity-driven sympathetic overtraining; the marathoner has volume-driven parasympathetic overtraining
questions.explanation_en: Sympathetic overtraining is intensity-driven and more typical of strength and power athletes, whereas parasympathetic overtraining is volume-driven and more typical of endurance athletes who accumulate large training volumes. The two forms are distinct, not interchangeable.
tags: Practical and Applied - Exam Two

questions.question: You are advising on HVAC setpoints for a new weight room and want athletes comfortable enough to train at a high quality. Which range should you target as the optimal training temperature?
options: 68 to 74 degrees F (20 to 23 degrees C)
58 to 64 degrees F (14 to 18 degrees C)
78 to 84 degrees F (26 to 29 degrees C)
questions.answer_text: 68 to 74 degrees F (20 to 23 degrees C)
questions.explanation_en: An appropriate weight-room range is about 68 to 78 degrees F, with an optimal target near 68 to 74 degrees F (20 to 23 degrees C). A room that is too cold or too hot degrades training quality, so both the low-50s/60s and high-70s/80s ranges are outside the recommendation.
tags: Practical and Applied - Exam Two

questions.question: A facility manager is installing wall mirrors along the dumbbell area and wants to keep dropped or rolling weights from striking and shattering them. What is the recommended minimum height for the bottom edge of the mirrors above the floor?
options: At least 48 inches (122 cm) above the floor
At least 20 inches (51 cm) above the floor
At least 6 inches (15 cm) above the floor
questions.answer_text: At least 20 inches (51 cm) above the floor
questions.explanation_en: Mirrors should sit a minimum of 20 inches (51 cm) above the floor so dropped or rolling weights are less likely to strike and shatter them. The 6-inch figure is the separate recommendation for clearance between a mirror and adjacent equipment, not its height off the floor.
tags: Practical and Applied - Exam Two

questions.question: A facility will train athletes for weightlifting competition and needs regulation lifting platforms. Consistent with competition rules, how should each platform be constructed?
options: As an all-foam matted surface for maximum cushioning
As a single wooden surface across the entire platform
With a wooden middle section and rubber outer sections
questions.answer_text: With a wooden middle section and rubber outer sections
questions.explanation_en: In line with weightlifting competition rules, platforms have a wooden middle section where the lifter stands and rubber outer sections. Inlaid platforms are also preferred over raised ones because they remove a tripping hazard. An all-wood or all-foam surface does not meet the standard.
tags: Practical and Applied - Exam Two

questions.question: You are laying out a resistance-training area with racks, barbells, and dumbbells and need enough room for both the athlete and a spotter to move safely around each station. What is the minimum recommended spacing between pieces of equipment?
options: 3 feet (0.9 m) between each piece
7 feet (2.1 m) between each piece
1 foot (0.3 m) between each piece
questions.answer_text: 3 feet (0.9 m) between each piece
questions.explanation_en: Racks, barbells, and dumbbells should have at least 3 feet (0.9 m) of space between them so the athlete and spotter can move safely, with additional clearance where multiple spotters are used. One foot is too tight, and 7 feet exceeds the stated minimum.
tags: Practical and Applied - Exam Two

questions.question: While setting environmental controls for a strength and conditioning facility, you want to hold humidity low enough to limit microbial growth and equipment rust in areas where athletes are active. What upper limit should relative humidity not exceed?
options: It should never drop below 75%
It should not exceed 60%
It should be maintained at exactly 90%
questions.answer_text: It should not exceed 60%
questions.explanation_en: In any space where physical activity occurs, relative humidity should not exceed 60%. Staying below that level limits bacterial and microbial growth and reduces rust and equipment damage; holding it at 90% or above, or forcing it to stay above 75%, would worsen those problems.
tags: Practical and Applied - Exam Two

questions.question: An injured athlete sues a strength and conditioning professional, alleging negligence. For the claim to succeed, the plaintiff must prove four specific elements by a preponderance of the evidence. Which set lists those four elements?
options: Liability, insurance coverage, a signed waiver, and proximate cause
Intent, malice, damages, and consent
Duty, breach of that duty, causation, and damages
questions.answer_text: Duty, breach of that duty, causation, and damages
questions.explanation_en: Negligence is a tort with four elements: a duty owed, a breach of that duty, causation linking the breach to the harm, and damages, each proven by a preponderance of the evidence. Intent and malice belong to other torts; liability, insurance, and waivers are not the elements themselves.
tags: Practical and Applied - Exam Two

questions.question: An athlete signed an assumption-of-risk waiver before starting a program. He is later hurt in a way that a court finds was caused by the strength and conditioning professional's negligence. What protection does the signed waiver actually provide in that situation?
options: It may fail to shield the professional from liability, because the injury was caused by negligence
It fully bars any liability, no matter how the professional acted
It shifts all liability onto the supervising athletic trainer
questions.answer_text: It may fail to shield the professional from liability, because the injury was caused by negligence
questions.explanation_en: An assumption-of-risk waiver acknowledges the inherent risks of an activity, but it may not protect the professional when the injury results from negligence. Waivers do not excuse negligent conduct, and they do not transfer that liability to a third party.
tags: Practical and Applied - Exam Two

questions.question: A high school athlete returning from a concussion asks his strength coach to sign off that he is medically cleared to resume contact practice. Under the NSCA's defined scope of practice for the strength and conditioning professional, what is the appropriate action?
options: Issue the clearance himself so the athlete does not miss training time
Recognize that clearance is outside his expertise and refer the athlete to the appropriate professional
Leave the decision entirely to the athlete's own judgment
questions.answer_text: Recognize that clearance is outside his expertise and refer the athlete to the appropriate professional
questions.explanation_en: The scope of practice requires the strength and conditioning professional to recognize the boundaries of his expertise and to consult with or refer to the appropriate professional, such as a physician, for matters like medical clearance. Providing clearance personally, or deferring to the athlete, falls outside that scope.
tags: Practical and Applied - Exam Two

questions.question: In the 5th-edition fiber-type classification, which fiber type is described as red, with high myoglobin content?
options: Type IIx (fast-twitch glycolytic)
Type I (slow-twitch oxidative)
Type IIa, but never Type I
questions.answer_text: Type I (slow-twitch oxidative)
questions.explanation_en: Type I (slow) fibers are RED because of high myoglobin and dense capillaries; Type IIx are white (low myoglobin) and Type IIa are intermediate (white/red). A common mnemonic error is to flip this and call slow fibers 'white.'
tags: Full Mixed Review

questions.question: The complete oxidation of one molecule of blood glucose yields a NET of how many ATP?
options: 38 ATP
32 ATP
4 ATP
questions.answer_text: 32 ATP
questions.explanation_en: Using current P/O ratios (NADH = 2.5 ATP, FADH2 = 1.5 ATP) the 5th edition lists ~32 ATP net from blood glucose (and 34 from muscle glycogen). The older figure of 38 used the outdated NADH = 3 convention.
tags: Full Mixed Review

questions.question: Glycolysis that begins with muscle glycogen nets more ATP than glycolysis beginning with blood glucose because:
options: Glycogen contains more carbon per molecule
Free glucose must be phosphorylated by hexokinase at the cost of 1 ATP, whereas glycogen-derived glucose is already phosphorylated
Glycogen bypasses the electron transport chain
questions.answer_text: Free glucose must be phosphorylated by hexokinase at the cost of 1 ATP, whereas glycogen-derived glucose is already phosphorylated
questions.explanation_en: Trapping free blood glucose in the cell costs an ATP (hexokinase step). Glycogen-derived glucose is already phosphorylated, so the 5th edition lists 34 ATP from glycogen vs 32 from blood glucose.
tags: Full Mixed Review

questions.question: At the very onset of all-out exercise, which energy system predominates?
options: Oxidative (aerobic) system
Phosphagen (ATP-PCr) system
Fast glycolysis
questions.answer_text: Phosphagen (ATP-PCr) system
questions.explanation_en: The phosphagen system is highly active at the start of ALL exercise regardless of intensity because it resynthesizes ATP fastest (creatine kinase). It has the lowest capacity, so it dominates only the first few seconds.
tags: Full Mixed Review

questions.question: Per the sliding-filament theory, which regions of the sarcomere get SMALLER during contraction?
options: The A-band only
The H-zone and the I-band
Only the A-band, while sarcomere length is unchanged
questions.answer_text: The H-zone and the I-band
questions.explanation_en: As actin slides toward the center, the H-zone and I-band shorten while the A-band (myosin filament length) stays constant. The whole sarcomere shortens.
tags: Full Mixed Review

questions.question: Calcium binding to which protein exposes the myosin-binding sites on actin?
options: Tropomyosin
Troponin
Titin
questions.answer_text: Troponin
questions.explanation_en: Ca2+ binds troponin, which pulls tropomyosin off the active sites so myosin crossbridges can attach. Tropomyosin is the 'door' covering the sites when calcium is low.
tags: Full Mixed Review

questions.question: Most human limb movements, such as the elbow flexion of a biceps curl, operate with which lever type?
options: First-class lever, at mechanical advantage
Third-class lever, at mechanical disadvantage
Second-class lever, at mechanical advantage
questions.answer_text: Third-class lever, at mechanical disadvantage
questions.explanation_en: Third-class levers (muscle force applied between the fulcrum and the resistance) are most common in the body and work at a mechanical disadvantage - the muscle produces more force than the load, trading force for speed and range of motion.
tags: Full Mixed Review

questions.question: The maximal force a muscle can exert is most directly proportional to its:
options: Volume
Cross-sectional area
Resting length
questions.answer_text: Cross-sectional area
questions.explanation_en: Maximal contractile force is proportional to cross-sectional area (the 2nd power of linear dimensions), not volume (3rd power). That is why, as body size increases, body mass rises faster than strength.
tags: Full Mixed Review

questions.question: At a given velocity, which muscle action produces the greatest force?
options: Concentric
Eccentric
Concentric at high velocity
questions.answer_text: Eccentric
questions.explanation_en: Force capability is greatest eccentrically, then isometric, then concentric. Torque can even rise with increasing eccentric velocity, the opposite of the concentric force-velocity relationship.
tags: Full Mixed Review

questions.question: An athlete moves from the first transition period (the strength/power phase) into the competitive period of a traditional periodization model. Compared with the first transition period, training during the competitive period typically involves:
options: Higher training volume and lower intensity to build a work-capacity base
Further increased intensity with decreased volume, plus a sharp rise in sport-specific skill and tactical practice
Roughly the same intensity and volume, held constant to avoid any detraining
questions.answer_text: Further increased intensity with decreased volume, plus a sharp rise in sport-specific skill and tactical practice
questions.explanation_en: Across the periodization periods, volume falls as intensity rises. Moving from the first transition (strength/power phase: low to very high loads at low volume) into the competitive period, the aim is to further increase strength and power by raising intensity while decreasing volume (peaking can reach >=93% of the 1RM at very low volume), and time spent on sport-specific skills and tactics increases dramatically (5th ed, ch 22). Building a base with high volume and low intensity belongs to the preparatory/off-season period.
tags: Full Mixed Review

questions.question: Which best describes cortisol's role relevant to resistance training?
options: An anabolic hormone that builds contractile protein
A catabolic signal hormone for carbohydrate metabolism, with greater catabolic effect on Type II fibers
A hormone whose main action is suppressing fat oxidation
questions.answer_text: A catabolic signal hormone for carbohydrate metabolism, with greater catabolic effect on Type II fibers
questions.explanation_en: Cortisol is the primary signal hormone for carbohydrate metabolism - it promotes gluconeogenesis, raises proteolytic enzymes, and inhibits protein synthesis, hitting Type II fibers hardest. It does NOT suppress fat oxidation (insulin does).
tags: Full Mixed Review

questions.question: In men, testosterone is secreted primarily from:
options: The adrenal medulla
Leydig cells in the testes
The anterior pituitary
questions.answer_text: Leydig cells in the testes
questions.explanation_en: Testosterone comes mainly from the Leydig cells of the testes (also ovaries in women and the adrenal glands), then travels bound to globulin and albumin to target tissues.
tags: Full Mixed Review

questions.question: Which factor has the GREATEST effect on the magnitude of excess post-exercise oxygen consumption (EPOC)?
options: Exercise intensity
Time of day
The athlete's standing height
questions.answer_text: Exercise intensity
questions.explanation_en: Intensity has the greatest effect on EPOC, although both higher intensity and longer duration increase it. EPOC is the elevated post-exercise oxygen uptake that restores the body after the oxygen deficit incurred at onset.
tags: Full Mixed Review

questions.question: A consistent fiber-type shift with chronic endurance (or resistance) training is:
options: Type I converting to Type IIx
Type IIx shifting toward the more oxidative Type IIa
Type IIa converting to Type I
questions.answer_text: Type IIx shifting toward the more oxidative Type IIa
questions.explanation_en: Training shifts fibers from the least oxidative Type IIx toward Type IIa. Detraining can cause a Type IIx 'overshoot.' True Type I Type II conversion is not well supported.
tags: Full Mixed Review

questions.question: The minimal essential strain (MES) that initiates new bone formation is approximately:
options: About one-tenth of the force needed to fracture the bone
Equal to the force needed to fracture the bone
About double the fracture force
questions.answer_text: About one-tenth of the force needed to fracture the bone
questions.explanation_en: MES is roughly 1/10 of the bone's fracture force. Loading above MES (an osteogenic stimulus) recruits osteoblasts to deposit new bone matrix that mineralizes as hydroxyapatite.
tags: Full Mixed Review

questions.question: Complete oxidation of ONE triglyceride molecule yields approximately how many ATP?
options: Over 300 ATP
Exactly 38 ATP
About 100 ATP
questions.answer_text: Over 300 ATP
questions.explanation_en: The 5th edition states a triglyceride (glycerol + three fatty acids) yields 'over 300 ATP.' Notes citing 463 ATP use the outdated NADH = 3 convention.
tags: Full Mixed Review

questions.question: Yerkes-Dodson's inverted-U hypothesis predicts that as arousal increases, performance:
options: Increases continuously (more is always better)
Improves to an optimal point, then declines with further arousal
Is unaffected by arousal level
questions.answer_text: Improves to an optimal point, then declines with further arousal
questions.explanation_en: The inverted-U: arousal helps performance up to an optimal level, beyond which more arousal hurts it. Drive theory, by contrast, predicts a linear increase with arousal.
tags: Full Mixed Review

questions.question: An athlete's belief in their capability to perform a SPECIFIC task in a SPECIFIC situation is called:
options: Trait anxiety
Self-efficacy
Intrinsic motivation
questions.answer_text: Self-efficacy
questions.explanation_en: Self-efficacy is task- and situation-specific perceived capability and influences activity choice, effort, and persistence. Self-confidence is the broader belief that one can perform a desired behavior.
tags: Full Mixed Review

questions.question: Removing an aversive stimulus in order to increase the likelihood of a desired behavior is:
options: Positive reinforcement
Negative reinforcement
Positive punishment
questions.answer_text: Negative reinforcement
questions.explanation_en: Negative reinforcement increases a behavior by taking away something aversive. Reinforcement (positive or negative) increases behavior; punishment decreases it.
tags: Full Mixed Review

questions.question: Which goal type is most within an athlete's control and the recommended emphasis?
options: Outcome goals, such as winning the event
Process goals, such as executing specific technique cues
Outcome and process goals are equally controllable
questions.answer_text: Process goals, such as executing specific technique cues
questions.explanation_en: Process goals focus on actions the athlete controls (effort, technique). Outcome goals depend on opponents and others, so they are largely outside the athlete's control.
tags: Full Mixed Review

questions.question: The correct order of Fitts and Posner's stages of motor learning is:
options: Automatic, then associative, then cognitive
Cognitive, then associative, then autonomous (automatic)
Associative, then cognitive, then automatic
questions.answer_text: Cognitive, then associative, then autonomous (automatic)
questions.explanation_en: Learners progress from the cognitive stage (effortful, conscious) to the associative stage (refining) to the autonomous/automatic stage (little conscious attention needed).
tags: Full Mixed Review

questions.question: The recommended daily protein intake for STRENGTH athletes is approximately:
options: 0.8 g/kg/day
1.4-2.0 g/kg/day
3.5-4.0 g/kg/day
questions.answer_text: 1.4-2.0 g/kg/day
questions.explanation_en: Strength athletes target roughly 1.4-2.0 g/kg/day (endurance athletes ~1.2-2.0). The general adult RDA is 0.8 g/kg/day.
tags: Full Mixed Review

questions.question: Which plant-based protein is noted as containing all nine essential amino acids?
options: Rice
Soy
Peanuts
questions.answer_text: Soy
questions.explanation_en: Soy is cited as the only plant-based source containing all nine essential amino acids, making it a complete protein.
tags: Full Mixed Review

questions.question: A common creatine supplementation protocol is:
options: 2 g/day for 30 days with no loading
A loading dose of ~20-25 g/day (or 0.3 g/kg/day) for ~5 days, then ~2 g/day maintenance
A single 0.3 g/kg dose just before competition
questions.answer_text: A loading dose of ~20-25 g/day (or 0.3 g/kg/day) for ~5 days, then ~2 g/day maintenance
questions.explanation_en: Loading ~20-25 g/day (0.3 g/kg/day) for ~5 days saturates muscle creatine stores, followed by ~2 g/day (0.03 g/kg/day) maintenance.
tags: Full Mixed Review

questions.question: Sodium bicarbonate works as an ergogenic buffer by:
options: Lowering blood pH to speed glycolysis
Raising blood pH, which increases the gradient driving H+ out of muscle cells
Directly supplying ATP to the muscle
questions.answer_text: Raising blood pH, which increases the gradient driving H+ out of muscle cells
questions.explanation_en: Sodium bicarbonate raises blood pH, increasing the pH gradient between inside and outside the cell so H+ leaves working muscle faster. Roughly 0.3 g/kg 60-90 min before high-intensity exercise; it can cause GI distress.
tags: Full Mixed Review

questions.question: The Adequate Intake (AI) for water is approximately:
options: 3.7 L/day for men and 2.7 L/day for women
1 L/day for everyone
5 L/day for men and 4 L/day for women
questions.answer_text: 3.7 L/day for men and 2.7 L/day for women
questions.explanation_en: Water AI is ~3.7 L/day (men) and ~2.7 L/day (women). A fluid loss exceeding 2% of body weight signals inadequate replacement.
tags: Full Mixed Review

questions.question: The glycemic index ranks a carbohydrate against a reference food (glucose or white bread) assigned a value of:
questions.explanation_en: GI compares a food's ~2-hour blood-glucose response to a reference food (glucose or white bread = 100). Glycemic load additionally accounts for the amount of carbohydrate per serving.
tags: Full Mixed Review

questions.question: To maximize muscle protein synthesis after resistance training in young adults, the recommended protein dose is about:
options: 5-10 g of any protein
20-25 g of high-quality, leucine-rich protein
60-80 g of protein
questions.answer_text: 20-25 g of high-quality, leucine-rich protein
questions.explanation_en: About 20-25 g of high-quality, high-leucine (~2-3 g leucine) protein maximizes MPS in young individuals; older adults may need 40+ g. The 'anabolic window' is heavily debated.
tags: Full Mixed Review

questions.question: A 'core' exercise (as opposed to an assistance exercise) is best defined as one that:
options: Targets the abdominal muscles specifically
Recruits one or more large muscle areas, crosses two or more primary joints, and receives priority
Uses only body weight
questions.answer_text: Recruits one or more large muscle areas, crosses two or more primary joints, and receives priority
questions.explanation_en: Core exercises recruit large muscle areas across 2+ primary joints (e.g., squat, bench press) and get priority for their direct sport application. Assistance exercises are smaller, often single-joint.
tags: Full Mixed Review

questions.question: For improving power output in exercises that can be heavily loaded, the most effective intensity range is roughly:
options: Always 100% 1RM
questions.explanation_en: For heavily loadable resistance exercises, ~75-90% 1RM is most effective/practical for power. Rest 2-5 minutes between sets when training single-effort power.
tags: Full Mixed Review

questions.question: The '2-for-2 rule' directs you to increase load when an athlete can perform:
options: 2 reps over the goal on the last set in 2 consecutive workouts
2 total workouts within 2 weeks
2 sets of 2 reps at a new maximum
questions.answer_text: 2 reps over the goal on the last set in 2 consecutive workouts
questions.explanation_en: The 2-for-2 rule: if the athlete completes 2 or more reps beyond the rep goal on the last set in 2 consecutive sessions, increase the weight.
tags: Full Mixed Review

questions.question: Order these training cycles from LONGEST to shortest:
options: Microcycle > mesocycle > macrocycle
Macrocycle > mesocycle > microcycle
Mesocycle > macrocycle > microcycle
questions.answer_text: Macrocycle > mesocycle > microcycle
questions.explanation_en: Macrocycle (months to a year) > mesocycle (2-6 weeks) > microcycle (several days to ~2 weeks).
tags: Full Mixed Review

questions.question: The preparatory (off-season) period is characterized by:
options: High intensity, low volume, sport-specific work
Low intensity, high volume to build a conditioning base
Peaking with very low volume
questions.answer_text: Low intensity, high volume to build a conditioning base
questions.explanation_en: The preparatory/off-season period uses low intensity and high volume to develop a conditioning base, raising the athlete's tolerance for later, more intense training.
tags: Full Mixed Review

questions.question: Complex training takes advantage of postactivation potentiation by pairing:
options: A high-load strength exercise followed by a biomechanically similar explosive/plyometric exercise
Two antagonist exercises back-to-back
Steady-state cardio with static stretching
questions.answer_text: A high-load strength exercise followed by a biomechanically similar explosive/plyometric exercise
questions.explanation_en: Complex training follows a heavy strength exercise with a similar explosive (stretch-shortening-cycle) movement to exploit postactivation potentiation.
tags: Full Mixed Review

questions.question: A frequently cited strength prerequisite before an adult performs lower-body depth jumps is a back-squat 1RM of at least:
options: 1.0x body weight
1.5x body weight
2.5x body weight
questions.answer_text: 1.5x body weight
questions.explanation_en: A common guideline is a squat 1RM of ~1.5x body weight before lower-body (depth/box) plyometrics. Depth-jump box heights run ~16-42 in (norm 30-32 in); use <18 in for athletes over 220 lb.
tags: Full Mixed Review

questions.question: The recommended MINIMUM recovery between plyometric training sessions is:
options: 12-24 hours
48-72 hours
A full week
questions.answer_text: 48-72 hours
questions.explanation_en: 48-72 hours between plyometric workouts optimizes adaptation while minimizing injury risk.
tags: Full Mixed Review

questions.question: The defining difference between 'change of direction' and 'agility' is that agility:
options: Is simply slower than change of direction
Adds a response to a stimulus (a perceptual-cognitive component)
Only occurs in a straight line
questions.answer_text: Adds a response to a stimulus (a perceptual-cognitive component)
questions.explanation_en: Change of direction is pre-planned; agility requires reacting to a stimulus, combining perceptual-cognitive ability with change-of-direction ability.
tags: Full Mixed Review

questions.question: Which is generally considered the BEST single indicator of aerobic endurance performance?
options: VO2max
Maximal lactate steady state
Resting heart rate
questions.answer_text: Maximal lactate steady state
questions.explanation_en: The hierarchy given is maximal lactate steady state > lactate threshold > VO2max as an indicator of aerobic endurance performance.
tags: Full Mixed Review

questions.question: In PNF stretching, the first phase always begins with:
options: A 6-second maximal isometric contraction
An initial ~10-second passive, relaxed stretch
A ballistic bounce at end range
questions.answer_text: An initial ~10-second passive, relaxed stretch
questions.explanation_en: PNF (hold-relax or contract-relax) always starts with a ~10-second passive relaxed stretch, then the contraction phase, then a longer relax.
tags: Full Mixed Review

questions.question: Relaxation that occurs in the SAME muscle that was just actively contracted (e.g., before stretching it) is called:
options: Reciprocal inhibition
Autogenic inhibition
The stretch reflex
questions.answer_text: Autogenic inhibition
questions.explanation_en: Autogenic inhibition is relaxation in the same muscle experiencing increased tension (GTO-mediated). Reciprocal inhibition is relaxation of the OPPOSING muscle while the agonist contracts.
tags: Full Mixed Review

questions.question: When spotting a dumbbell chest fly, the spotter's hands should be placed near the athlete's:
options: Wrists
Forearms, close to the elbows
The dumbbells themselves
questions.answer_text: Forearms, close to the elbows
questions.explanation_en: Spot the dumbbell fly at the forearms near the elbows - not the wrists and not the dumbbells - for the best control and safety.
tags: Full Mixed Review

questions.question: Interval training to develop the phosphagen (ATP-PCr) energy system uses near-maximal (90-100%) efforts of about 5 to 10 seconds. According to the textbook's interval-training table, the appropriate work-to-rest ratio is approximately:
questions.explanation_en: The 5th ed interval-training table (ch 3) pairs each energy system with a work-to-rest ratio: phosphagen (90-100%, ~5-10 s) = 1:12 to 1:20; fast glycolysis (15-30 s) = 1:3 to 1:5; fast glycolysis + oxidative (1-3 min) = 1:3 to 1:4; oxidative (>3 min) = 1:1 to 1:3. Short maximal efforts need long rest so phosphagens can replenish, hence the large 1:12 to 1:20 ratio.
tags: Full Mixed Review

questions.question: Compared with a high-bar back squat, a low-bar squat (more forward trunk lean) tends to place:
options: More torque on the knees and less on the hips
More torque on the hips and less on the knees
Equal torque on the hips and knees
questions.answer_text: More torque on the hips and less on the knees
questions.explanation_en: Greater forward lean (low-bar) lengthens the moment arm at the hips, so hip torque rises and knee torque falls. The more upright high-bar squat shifts torque toward the knees.
tags: Full Mixed Review

questions.question: In a test battery, which tests should be administered BEFORE the others?
options: Aerobic capacity tests
Non-fatiguing tests and maximal power/strength tests, before fatiguing anaerobic and aerobic capacity tests
Local muscular endurance tests
questions.answer_text: Non-fatiguing tests and maximal power/strength tests, before fatiguing anaerobic and aerobic capacity tests
questions.explanation_en: Sequence: non-fatiguing -> agility -> max power/strength -> sprints -> muscular endurance -> fatiguing anaerobic capacity -> aerobic capacity. Fatiguing tests go last so they don't contaminate power and skill measures.
tags: Full Mixed Review

questions.question: Sympathetic overtraining syndrome is MOST associated with:
options: Endurance athletes and high training volume
Strength/power athletes and high training intensity
Beginners only
questions.answer_text: Strength/power athletes and high training intensity
questions.explanation_en: Sympathetic OTS is intensity-driven and develops first, more common in younger strength/power athletes. Parasympathetic OTS is volume-driven, more common in endurance athletes, and represents the later culmination.
tags: Full Mixed Review

questions.question: Functional overreaching (FOR) differs from nonfunctional overreaching (NFOR) in that FOR:
options: Causes months-long performance loss
Causes a short-term performance dip that can supercompensate into gains after an appropriate taper
Always progresses to overtraining syndrome
questions.answer_text: Causes a short-term performance dip that can supercompensate into gains after an appropriate taper
questions.explanation_en: FOR is a short-term (days-weeks) decrement that can rebound into gains after a taper. NFOR is a weeks-to-months stagnation/decrement; overtraining syndrome lasts months or more.
tags: Full Mixed Review

questions.question: During the acute inflammatory phase of tissue healing (first ~2-3 days), the strength coach should:
options: Aggressively load the injured tissue to drive adaptation
Avoid exercise that directly stresses the injured area while maintaining cardiorespiratory fitness and surrounding function
Stop all physical activity completely
questions.answer_text: Avoid exercise that directly stresses the injured area while maintaining cardiorespiratory fitness and surrounding function
questions.explanation_en: In the inflammatory phase, protect the injured structure (avoid directly stressing it) while maintaining cardiorespiratory fitness and the function of surrounding, uninjured areas.
tags: Full Mixed Review

questions.question: Recommended professional-to-participant supervision ratios tighten for younger athletes. The HIGH-SCHOOL ratio is:
questions.explanation_en: Junior high 1:10, high school 1:15, college 1:20 (adults/elite can be higher). Younger, less experienced athletes need closer supervision.
tags: Full Mixed Review

questions.question: Which four elements must all be present to establish negligence?
options: Duty, breach of duty, proximate cause, and damages
Intent, motive, opportunity, and harm
Contract, payment, service, and refund
questions.answer_text: Duty, breach of duty, proximate cause, and damages
questions.explanation_en: Negligence = a duty to act, a breach of that duty (failing the standard of care), proximate cause (reasonably foreseeable), and resulting damages.
tags: Full Mixed Review

questions.question: The general planning guideline for resistance-training floor space is approximately:
options: ~25 sq ft per athlete
~100 sq ft per athlete
~400 sq ft per athlete
questions.answer_text: ~100 sq ft per athlete
questions.explanation_en: Plan for roughly 100 sq ft per athlete in the resistance-training area, with walkways over 36 in (over 48 in in circuit areas) and air exchanged 8-12 times per hour.
tags: Full Mixed Review

questions.question: An athlete performs a standing dumbbell biceps curl. At the elbow, the biceps inserts close to the joint axis while the dumbbell is held far out at the hand. To hold the weight static at 90 degrees of flexion, what is true about the force the biceps must produce relative to the weight of the dumbbell?
options: The biceps must produce a force greater than the weight of the dumbbell because the muscle's force arm is shorter than the resistance arm
The biceps produces a force equal to the dumbbell's weight because torque is conserved across the joint
The biceps produces less force than the dumbbell's weight because the elbow gives the muscle a mechanical advantage greater than 1
questions.answer_text: The biceps must produce a force greater than the weight of the dumbbell because the muscle's force arm is shorter than the resistance arm
questions.explanation_en: The elbow during curling is a third-class lever: the muscle (effort) inserts between the axis and the resistance, so its force arm (moment arm) is shorter than the resistance arm. Mechanical advantage = force arm / resistance arm < 1, so the muscle must produce MORE force than the external load to balance torque. The trap is the third option ('mechanical advantage greater than 1') - third-class levers favor range of motion and speed, not force, so MA is always less than 1 and the muscle is at a force disadvantage.
tags: Hardest Mode

questions.question: A coach wants to compare the torque produced about the knee at two points in a leg extension. The quadriceps tendon force is identical at both points, but at point A the perpendicular distance from the knee axis to the line of muscle pull is larger than at point B. What does this tell you about the muscular torque at the two points?
options: Torque is greater at point A because torque equals muscle force times the perpendicular distance (moment arm)
Torque is greater at point B because a shorter moment arm concentrates the force closer to the axis
Torque is equal at both points because the muscle force did not change
questions.answer_text: Torque is greater at point A because torque equals muscle force times the perpendicular distance (moment arm)
questions.explanation_en: Torque = force x moment arm, where the moment arm is the PERPENDICULAR distance from the axis of rotation to the line of action of the force. With equal force, the larger moment arm (point A) yields greater torque. The trap is the second option: a shorter moment arm produces LESS torque, not more - 'closer to the axis' reduces the lever, it does not concentrate force. The third option ignores that moment arm, not just force, sets torque.
tags: Hardest Mode

questions.question: Two volleyball players leave the ground with the exact same takeoff velocity and reach the same jump height. Player 1 used a deep, slow countermovement applying a moderate ground reaction force over a longer time; Player 2 used a shallow, quick countermovement applying a much larger force over a shorter time. Which principle best explains how both achieved the same takeoff velocity?
options: The force-velocity relationship, because higher force always permits a higher movement velocity
The Frank-Starling mechanism, because greater stretch yields a more forceful contraction
The impulse-momentum relationship, because the product of force and time (impulse) equals the change in momentum, and both produced the same impulse
questions.answer_text: The impulse-momentum relationship, because the product of force and time (impulse) equals the change in momentum, and both produced the same impulse
questions.explanation_en: Impulse (force x time) equals the change in momentum (mass x velocity change). Identical takeoff velocity for the same mass means identical change in momentum, so both jumps required the same impulse - achievable as big force x short time OR smaller force x longer time. The trap force-velocity choice describes the inverse relationship between contraction force and shortening velocity within a muscle, not how two jumpers reach equal velocity. Frank-Starling is a cardiac stretch-tension mechanism, irrelevant here.
tags: Hardest Mode

questions.question: An athlete performs the lowering (return) phase of a standing cable chest fly: starting with the handles pressed together in front of the chest, the arms open outward to the sides under control until they are wide. During this controlled opening, which muscle action is occurring at the shoulder?
options: The shoulder adductors (pectoralis major, latissimus dorsi) contract eccentrically, lengthening under load to control the arms moving into abduction
The shoulder abductors (deltoid) contract concentrically to spread the arms apart
The shoulder adductors contract concentrically to open the arms
questions.answer_text: The shoulder adductors (pectoralis major, latissimus dorsi) contract eccentrically, lengthening under load to control the arms moving into abduction
questions.explanation_en: On the return phase the cable resistance is pulling the arms apart (toward abduction), and the prime movers of the fly - the shoulder ADDUCTORS (pectoralis major, lat) - lengthen while still generating force to control that motion, so they work eccentrically. The trap is the deltoid (abductors): they would be the concentric mover if the cable were resisting you in the other direction, but here gravity/the cable open the arms and the adductors brake it. A concentric adductor action would bring the arms back together, not open them.
tags: Hardest Mode

questions.question: Slow-motion video shows a baseball pitcher's throwing arm during the follow-through, immediately after release: the arm has just rapidly internally rotated to deliver the pitch and must now be decelerated before the shoulder reaches its end range. Which muscles act eccentrically to brake the arm?
options: The external rotators of the posterior rotator cuff (infraspinatus, teres minor), lengthening under load to decelerate the internal rotation
The internal rotators (subscapularis, pectoralis major), eccentrically slowing the arm
The middle deltoid, concentrically abducting the arm
questions.answer_text: The external rotators of the posterior rotator cuff (infraspinatus, teres minor), lengthening under load to decelerate the internal rotation
questions.explanation_en: The forceful motion that launches the pitch is rapid internal rotation, driven concentrically by the internal rotators. Decelerating it falls to the antagonist working eccentrically - the EXTERNAL rotators of the posterior cuff (infraspinatus, teres minor) lengthen under load to brake the arm and protect the joint, which is why posterior-cuff eccentric strength is emphasized in throwers. The trap is the internal rotators: they PRODUCE the internal rotation concentrically, they do not brake it. The deltoid is not the decelerator here.
tags: Hardest Mode

questions.question: A lifter slowly lowers into the bottom of a back squat under control. At the hip, which muscle action is occurring as the lifter descends?
options: The hip extensors (gluteus maximus, hamstrings) are contracting eccentrically to control hip flexion
The hip flexors (iliopsoas) are contracting concentrically to pull the lifter down
The hip extensors are contracting concentrically to lower the body
questions.answer_text: The hip extensors (gluteus maximus, hamstrings) are contracting eccentrically to control hip flexion
questions.explanation_en: Descending into a squat is hip FLEXION occurring against gravity. Gravity supplies the flexing force, so the muscles working are the antagonists - the hip EXTENSORS - lengthening eccentrically to brake the descent. The trap is the hip flexors contracting concentrically: gravity, not the hip flexors, drives the descent, so the flexors are largely passive while the extensors do the controlling work. Concentric hip extension happens on the way UP, not down.
tags: Hardest Mode

questions.question: During the first roughly 10 seconds of an all-out sprint relying on the phosphagen system, what happens to intramuscular ATP and phosphocreatine (PCr) concentrations?
options: Both ATP and PCr fall dramatically in parallel
PCr stays nearly constant while ATP is markedly depleted
ATP stays nearly constant while PCr is markedly depleted
questions.answer_text: ATP stays nearly constant while PCr is markedly depleted
questions.explanation_en: ATP concentration is fiercely defended and stays nearly constant even during maximal effort, because the creatine kinase reaction rapidly rephosphorylates ADP using PCr. PCr is the buffer that gets drained - it can drop substantially in seconds. The trap is picking ATP as the substance depleted: a large fall in ATP would compromise the cell, so the body sacrifices PCr to keep ATP stable. The third option reverses the actual physiology.
tags: Hardest Mode

questions.question: A strength coach is classifying the dominant energy system for a single effort that lasts about 2 minutes at high intensity (for example, a 800 m run sustained near maximal pace). Which energy system contribution best describes this effort?
options: Almost entirely phosphagen, because the effort is maximal
Almost entirely oxidative, because it lasts longer than one minute
A roughly balanced contribution from fast glycolysis and oxidative metabolism
questions.answer_text: A roughly balanced contribution from fast glycolysis and oxidative metabolism
questions.explanation_en: Energy system contribution is judged by the DURATION of the effort. Efforts of about 1 to 3 minutes draw on a mix of fast glycolysis and oxidative metabolism, with the crossover occurring within this window. The trap 'almost entirely oxidative' is wrong because the glycolytic system is still contributing heavily near the 2-minute mark - oxidative does not fully dominate until efforts well beyond 3 minutes. Phosphagen is essentially spent after roughly 10 seconds.
tags: Hardest Mode

questions.question: A basketball point guard repeatedly performs all-out 5-second drives separated by jogging and standing. Generically the sport is 'aerobic' over a 40-minute game, but each explosive drive itself is fueled mostly by which system?
options: The oxidative system, because the overall game is long
The phosphagen system, because each individual burst is very short and near-maximal
Fast glycolysis, because basketball is a power sport
questions.answer_text: The phosphagen system, because each individual burst is very short and near-maximal
questions.explanation_en: Classify by the duration of the described action, not the sport label. A 5-second near-maximal burst is fueled predominantly by the phosphagen system. Intermittent sprint sports are anaerobic bursts riding on an aerobic base - the aerobic system helps replenish PCr between efforts, but it does not power the burst itself. The trap 'oxidative because the game is long' confuses total game time with the brief effort. Fast glycolysis would dominate efforts more in the 15 to 30 second range.
tags: Hardest Mode

questions.question: A coach programs 10-second maximal sled sprints. The training GOAL is to maximize speed and power output on every rep, with each rep as crisp as the first. Which work-to-rest ratio best fits this goal?
options: About 1:3 to 1:5 (short rest), so the athlete trains under fatigue
About 1:1, to keep the session time-efficient
About 1:12 to 1:20 (full recovery, roughly 2 to 3 minutes rest), so PCr is nearly fully restored before each rep
questions.answer_text: About 1:12 to 1:20 (full recovery, roughly 2 to 3 minutes rest), so PCr is nearly fully restored before each rep
questions.explanation_en: For a speed and power goal, each rep must be high quality, which requires near-full PCr restoration between efforts - a long work-to-rest ratio of about 1:12 to 1:20 (roughly 2 to 3 minutes rest after a 10-second sprint). The trap is the short 1:3 to 1:5 ratio: that incomplete recovery is deliberately used to train anaerobic/glycolytic CAPACITY (forcing work before PCr refills), which degrades power output - the opposite of a speed-power goal.
tags: Hardest Mode

questions.question: A different coach uses the same 10-second sprints but now wants to build anaerobic (glycolytic) capacity and tolerance to fatigue, deliberately starting each rep before PCr is fully restored. Which work-to-rest ratio fits this goal?
options: About 1:12 to 1:20, full recovery between reps
About 1:3 to 1:5, incomplete recovery between reps
About 1:25, extended recovery to keep quality high
questions.answer_text: About 1:3 to 1:5, incomplete recovery between reps
questions.explanation_en: An anaerobic/glycolytic CAPACITY goal calls for incomplete recovery, around 1:3 to 1:5, so the athlete begins each rep before PCr fully refills, taxing glycolysis and fatigue tolerance. The trap is the long 1:12 to 1:20 ratio - that full recovery is for a speed-power QUALITY goal and would not stress the glycolytic system the way capacity training requires. Note the same 10-second sprint serves opposite goals depending only on the rest interval.
tags: Hardest Mode

questions.question: Compared with Type I fibers, Type IIx (fast-twitch) muscle fibers are best characterized by which combination?
options: Higher mitochondrial density, greater fatigue resistance, and slower contraction velocity
Greater capillary density, higher myoglobin content, and faster contraction velocity
Higher force output per cross-sectional area, faster contraction velocity, and lower fatigue resistance
questions.answer_text: Higher force output per cross-sectional area, faster contraction velocity, and lower fatigue resistance
questions.explanation_en: Type IIx fibers contract fastest, produce high force/power, and fatigue quickly; they have relatively low mitochondrial density, capillarization, and myoglobin. The correct answer pairs fast velocity + high force + low fatigue resistance. The first option describes Type I traits (oxidative, fatigue-resistant, slow). The third option mixes Type I oxidative features (capillary density, myoglobin) with fast velocity, an internally inconsistent trap that cannot coexist in IIx.
tags: Hardest Mode

questions.question: As an athlete progressively increases the force of a muscle contraction, how does the neuromuscular system grade the force output, according to the size principle?
options: Lower-threshold (smaller) motor units are recruited first, then higher-threshold units are added, and firing rate increases
High-threshold motor units are recruited first because they produce the most force
Individual fibers are partially activated to a degree matching the required force
questions.answer_text: Lower-threshold (smaller) motor units are recruited first, then higher-threshold units are added, and firing rate increases
questions.explanation_en: By the size principle, motor units are recruited in order of increasing size: low-threshold (small, Type I) units first, then progressively larger high-threshold (Type II) units as force demand rises, with rate coding (increased firing frequency) adding further force. The trap second option reverses recruitment order. The third option violates the all-or-none law - a fiber cannot be partially activated; once its motor unit fires, all of its fibers contract fully, and force is graded by recruitment and rate coding, not partial fiber activation.
tags: Hardest Mode

questions.question: For the cross-bridge cycle of the sliding-filament model to proceed (attachment, power stroke, detachment, and reattachment), which two things are both required?
options: Calcium ions to expose actin binding sites and ATP to power the stroke and detach the cross-bridge
Calcium ions and lactate, which together drive the power stroke
ATP alone, since calcium is only needed for relaxation
questions.answer_text: Calcium ions to expose actin binding sites and ATP to power the stroke and detach the cross-bridge
questions.explanation_en: Excitation releases Ca2+ from the sarcoplasmic reticulum; Ca2+ binds troponin, moving tropomyosin to expose actin's myosin-binding sites. ATP is then required both to energize the power stroke and to detach myosin from actin so the cycle can repeat. The trap third option is a common error: ATP is needed for detachment AND relaxation, but Ca2+ is essential to INITIATE contraction, not just relaxation. Lactate plays no direct role in the cross-bridge cycle.
tags: Hardest Mode

questions.question: Two muscles have the same physiological cross-sectional area, but Muscle A has highly pennate fibers at a steep angle while Muscle B has fibers running parallel to the line of pull. What is the trade-off for the pennate Muscle A?
options: Greater maximal force potential but a lower maximal shortening velocity
Greater maximal shortening velocity but lower force potential
Both greater force and greater shortening velocity, with no trade-off
questions.answer_text: Greater maximal force potential but a lower maximal shortening velocity
questions.explanation_en: Pennation packs more sarcomeres in parallel per unit area, increasing physiological cross-sectional area and thus force potential, but the fibers are shorter and angled, reducing maximal shortening velocity and the proportion of fiber force transmitted along the tendon. So pennate muscle favors force over speed. The trap second option reverses this (that describes the longer parallel fibers of Muscle B). The third option ignores the inherent force-versus-velocity trade-off of architecture.
tags: Hardest Mode

questions.question: Based on the force-velocity relationship of muscle, in which condition can a muscle generate the GREATEST force?
options: During a fast concentric (shortening) action, because speed adds momentum
During an eccentric (lengthening) action against a high load
At its maximal unloaded shortening velocity
questions.answer_text: During an eccentric (lengthening) action against a high load
questions.explanation_en: Force capability is highest during ECCENTRIC actions, where a muscle can resist loads exceeding its maximal isometric force; force then decreases as concentric shortening velocity increases, and is lowest at maximal (unloaded) shortening velocity. The trap first option is the classic error - faster concentric shortening actually produces LESS force, not more, per the force-velocity curve. The third option describes the point of essentially zero force production.
tags: Hardest Mode

questions.question: During the early weeks (first few weeks) of a previously untrained person's resistance-training program, strength often improves substantially before any meaningful change in muscle size. What primarily accounts for these initial gains?
options: Rapid myofibrillar hypertrophy adding contractile proteins
Neural adaptations such as increased motor unit recruitment, rate coding, and synchronization
An immediate rise in resting testosterone concentration
questions.answer_text: Neural adaptations such as increased motor unit recruitment, rate coding, and synchronization
questions.explanation_en: Early strength gains in novices are predominantly NEURAL - greater agonist recruitment, increased firing rate (rate coding), improved synchronization, and reduced antagonist co-activation - and precede measurable hypertrophy, which becomes the dominant driver only later. The trap is hypertrophy, which lags behind neural changes in the first weeks. A chronically elevated resting testosterone level is not the mechanism for the rapid early improvements.
tags: Hardest Mode

questions.question: After several months of well-designed aerobic endurance training, which set of cardiovascular and peripheral adaptations would you expect?
options: Increased mitochondrial density and capillary density, a widened arterial-venous oxygen difference, and a rightward shift of the lactate threshold
Decreased stroke volume with a higher resting heart rate to maintain cardiac output
Reduced capillary density but greater reliance on the phosphagen system
questions.answer_text: Increased mitochondrial density and capillary density, a widened arterial-venous oxygen difference, and a rightward shift of the lactate threshold
questions.explanation_en: Chronic aerobic training increases mitochondrial number/density, capillary density, and the a-vO2 difference (more oxygen extracted per unit blood), raises maximal stroke volume (lowering resting heart rate), and shifts the lactate threshold to the right (higher intensity before lactate accumulates). The trap second option is backward - stroke volume INCREASES and resting heart rate DECREASES with training. The third option contradicts the well-established increase in capillarization and oxidative capacity.
tags: Hardest Mode

questions.question: Immediately following an acute bout of high-volume, multi-joint resistance exercise with short rest periods, which hormonal response pattern is most expected in a young trained male?
options: Acute increases in testosterone, growth hormone, and cortisol
An acute decrease in growth hormone and cortisol with no change in testosterone
A selective acute rise in cortisol only, with testosterone and growth hormone unchanged
questions.answer_text: Acute increases in testosterone, growth hormone, and cortisol
questions.explanation_en: A demanding resistance bout (large muscle mass, high volume, short rest) acutely elevates testosterone, growth hormone, and cortisol together; these transient post-exercise spikes are part of the anabolic/catabolic signaling environment. The trap second option reverses the GH and cortisol responses - both rise, they do not fall. The third option wrongly isolates cortisol; the acute response is broad, not selective.
tags: Hardest Mode

questions.question: A parent asks whether starting their healthy 11-year-old on a properly supervised, appropriately loaded resistance-training program will stunt the child's growth. Based on current evidence, what is the most accurate response?
options: Yes, resistance training should be avoided before puberty because it compresses the growth plates and stunts height
No, properly designed and supervised resistance training does not stunt growth; epiphyseal plate injury risk is associated with improper technique or maximal/excessive loads, not appropriate training
Yes, but only if the child uses machines instead of free weights
questions.answer_text: No, properly designed and supervised resistance training does not stunt growth; epiphyseal plate injury risk is associated with improper technique or maximal/excessive loads, not appropriate training
questions.explanation_en: There is no credible evidence that properly designed, supervised, age-appropriate resistance training stunts growth; it is recognized as safe and beneficial for youth. The real risk to the epiphyseal (growth) plate comes from improper technique or maximal/excessive loading, not from resistance training per se. The trap first option repeats the persistent growth-stunting myth. The third option invents a free-weight prohibition that is not the issue - supervision and appropriate loading are.
tags: Hardest Mode

questions.question: When comparing average muscular strength between men and women, which statement most accurately reflects the textbook position?
options: Men are stronger than women in both absolute terms and when strength is expressed relative to lean body mass, across all muscle groups equally
Women are stronger than men in absolute terms but weaker relative to lean body mass
On an absolute basis men are generally stronger, but when strength is expressed relative to lean body mass (especially lower body) the differences shrink markedly
questions.answer_text: On an absolute basis men are generally stronger, but when strength is expressed relative to lean body mass (especially lower body) the differences shrink markedly
questions.explanation_en: Men typically have greater ABSOLUTE strength largely due to greater muscle mass, but when strength is normalized to lean body mass the sex difference narrows considerably, and lower-body relative strength can be quite similar; upper-body differences tend to remain larger. The trap first option overstates the gap by claiming it persists equally relative to lean mass across all muscles - normalization reduces it. The third option is simply false on the absolute comparison.
tags: Hardest Mode

questions.question: During an open-skill play, a point guard dribbles up the court while simultaneously tracking five defenders, two cutting teammates, and the shot clock to decide where the play goes. According to Nideffer's model, which attentional style is this player primarily using?
options: Broad-external
Broad-internal
Narrow-external
questions.answer_text: Broad-external
questions.explanation_en: Broad-external = taking in MANY cues that exist OUT in the environment (defenders, teammates, clock), which is exactly what reading a developing play requires. Broad-internal is the trap: that style is for analyzing or strategizing using many of one's OWN thoughts/plans, not scanning the live environment. Narrow-external would be locking onto a single external target (like a free-throw rim).
tags: Hardest Mode

questions.question: A golfer stands over a putt and concentrates exclusively on a single feel cue - the smooth tempo of her own backswing - shutting out everything else. Which attentional quadrant best describes this focus?
options: Broad-internal
Narrow-internal
Narrow-external
questions.answer_text: Narrow-internal
questions.explanation_en: Narrow-internal = focusing on ONE internal cue (a single swing thought / kinesthetic feel of her own movement). Narrow-external is the trap: that would be fixing on one cue out in the environment, such as a spot on the green or the hole - but tempo of her own backswing is an internal kinesthetic cue, not an environmental one. Broad-internal would involve juggling many of her own thoughts at once.
tags: Hardest Mode

questions.question: A placekicker blocks out the crowd and rush and zeroes in solely on a single spot on the goalpost as his aiming point. Which attentional style is he using?
options: Narrow-internal
Narrow-external
Broad-external
questions.answer_text: Narrow-external
questions.explanation_en: Narrow-external = locking onto ONE cue that is OUT in the environment (the spot on the goalpost). The trap is narrow-internal, which would apply if he were focused on one of his own bodily/mental cues rather than an external target; the aiming spot is external. Broad-external would mean scanning many environmental cues at once, which he is deliberately avoiding.
tags: Hardest Mode

questions.question: A powerlifter must produce a maximal, simple deadlift, while a few platforms over a gymnast attempts a complex, precise beam routine. Compared to the powerlifter, the gymnast's optimal arousal level for peak performance should be:
options: Higher, because more total muscle activation is needed
Lower, because the task is complex and requires fine motor control
Identical, because optimal arousal is the same for all athletes
questions.answer_text: Lower, because the task is complex and requires fine motor control
questions.explanation_en: Per the inverted-U principle, complex tasks demanding fine motor control and coordination (beam routine) have a LOWER optimal arousal level than simple, gross-force tasks (deadlift). The trap (higher arousal) confuses 'needs precision' with 'needs more drive'; high arousal degrades fine, complex skills. 'Identical for all' ignores that optimal arousal varies by task complexity (and by individual, per IZOF).
tags: Hardest Mode

questions.question: A 19-year-old female distance runner reports fatigue and heavy training volume. Of the following, which nutritional concern is MOST characteristically associated with female endurance athletes and warrants screening?
options: Iron deficiency, which can impair oxygen transport and endurance performance
Vitamin C toxicity from too much fruit in the diet
Excess dietary protein causing kidney damage in healthy athletes
questions.answer_text: Iron deficiency, which can impair oxygen transport and endurance performance
questions.explanation_en: Iron deficiency is especially common in female endurance athletes (losses plus high demand) and impairs oxygen-carrying capacity, hurting endurance - the textbook flags it for screening. Vitamin C 'toxicity' from fruit is the trap: it is water-soluble and not a realistic concern here. Excess protein causing kidney damage in healthy athletes is a common myth, not an established textbook risk, and is unrelated to this presentation.
tags: Hardest Mode

questions.question: A basketball player reports that for the first three quarters her heart was pounding and her muscles felt tense, but those physical symptoms faded once play settled in; meanwhile she kept worrying about disappointing her coach right through the final minutes. Which best characterizes her anxiety?
options: Somatic anxiety that persisted and cognitive anxiety that dissipated
Somatic anxiety that dissipated at the start of play and cognitive anxiety that persisted
Trait anxiety, which is situation-specific and short-lived
questions.answer_text: Somatic anxiety that dissipated at the start of play and cognitive anxiety that persisted
questions.explanation_en: Somatic (physical) anxiety - pounding heart, tense muscles - typically peaks pre-competition and dissipates once performance begins, while cognitive anxiety (worry) can persist throughout. Option A reverses the two (the classic trap). Trait anxiety is a stable personality disposition, not a short-lived, situation-specific state, so C mislabels both the type and its time course.
tags: Hardest Mode

questions.question: An athlete tells the strength coach his main aim this season is to 'win the conference championship.' To make the goal more effective, the coach should steer him toward which type of goal?
options: A process goal he can control, such as completing his prescribed sprint mechanics drills each session
A more ambitious outcome goal, such as winning the national title
An outcome goal tied to beating a specific rival
questions.answer_text: A process goal he can control, such as completing his prescribed sprint mechanics drills each session
questions.explanation_en: Process (and performance) goals focus on controllable actions the athlete executes, which is why they are emphasized over outcome goals. Winning a championship is an outcome goal - the LEAST controllable (depends on opponents, luck). Both B and C are traps because they are still outcome goals (just bigger or more specific); raising the stakes does not fix the core problem of low controllability.
tags: Hardest Mode

questions.question: A young athlete who used to train enthusiastically just for the love of the sport is now paid a cash bonus by a sponsor for every win. Over the season his enjoyment and self-driven effort decline. This illustrates that:
options: Tangible extrinsic rewards can undermine intrinsic motivation
Extrinsic rewards always strengthen intrinsic motivation
Intrinsic and extrinsic motivation are unrelated and never interact
questions.answer_text: Tangible extrinsic rewards can undermine intrinsic motivation
questions.explanation_en: Tangible extrinsic rewards (cash per win) can shift the athlete's perceived reason for participating from internal enjoyment to the reward, undermining intrinsic motivation - the documented effect here. 'Always strengthen' is the trap: rewards perceived as controlling often reduce, not boost, intrinsic drive. 'Never interact' is false because the whole point is that the two motivation types influence each other.
tags: Hardest Mode

questions.question: A coach wants to build a returning athlete's self-efficacy before a key competition. According to Bandura, which strategy will have the STRONGEST effect?
options: Repeatedly telling the athlete 'I know you can do it' (verbal persuasion)
Structuring training so the athlete accumulates successful past performance accomplishments
Having the athlete watch a similar teammate succeed (vicarious experience)
questions.answer_text: Structuring training so the athlete accumulates successful past performance accomplishments
questions.explanation_en: Bandura ranks past performance accomplishments (mastery experiences) as the STRONGEST source of self-efficacy - actually succeeding builds the most durable confidence. Verbal persuasion is the classic trap: it is one of the WEAKER sources. Vicarious experience (modeling) helps but is weaker than one's own mastery, so B beats both alternatives.
tags: Hardest Mode

questions.question: A diver's body is calm but he is consumed by worrisome, negative thoughts about failing his next dive - a clear cognitive-anxiety problem. Which psychological technique is BEST matched to this type of anxiety?
options: Progressive muscle relaxation to reduce muscular tension
Thought stopping and positive self-talk / imagery to address the worry
Deep diaphragmatic breathing to lower heart rate
questions.answer_text: Thought stopping and positive self-talk / imagery to address the worry
questions.explanation_en: Cognitive anxiety (worry, negative thoughts) is best treated with cognitive techniques like thought stopping, positive self-talk, and imagery. The trap answers (progressive muscle relaxation and breathing) are SOMATIC techniques - they target physical tension and are matched to somatic anxiety, not to a mind racing with worry. Matching the intervention to the anxiety type is the key principle.
tags: Hardest Mode

questions.question: A sport dietitian needs to estimate daily energy needs for a very lean, muscular 80 kg male athlete with about 8 kg of fat mass. Which approach does the textbook favor for this athlete, and roughly what is the first step?
options: Apply a flat 15-20 kcal per pound of body weight as the standard textbook method
Estimate resting metabolic rate with the Cunningham equation [500 + (22 x fat-free mass in kg)], then multiply by a physical activity level coefficient
Use total body weight in the Cunningham equation, ignoring body composition
questions.answer_text: Estimate resting metabolic rate with the Cunningham equation [500 + (22 x fat-free mass in kg)], then multiply by a physical activity level coefficient
questions.explanation_en: The textbook estimates energy needs as RMR x a physical-activity (PAL) coefficient; the Cunningham equation - 500 + (22 x fat-free mass kg) - is preferred for lean, muscular athletes because it is driven by fat-free mass. The trap is the 'flat kcal per pound' table, which is not the RMR-times-activity method the book teaches. Using total body weight (C) defeats the purpose of an FFM-based equation.
tags: Hardest Mode

questions.question: A strength athlete already eating about 1.6 g of protein per kg of body weight asks whether doubling his protein to 3.2 g/kg will add proportionally more muscle. The best evidence-based answer is:
options: Yes - muscle gain increases roughly linearly with protein intake, so more protein means more muscle
No - athlete protein needs fall in roughly the 1.2 to 2.0 g/kg range (strength athletes toward the upper end), and intakes well above that do not produce proportionally more muscle
No - because excess protein is toxic and he should drop below 1.0 g/kg
questions.answer_text: No - athlete protein needs fall in roughly the 1.2 to 2.0 g/kg range (strength athletes toward the upper end), and intakes well above that do not produce proportionally more muscle
questions.explanation_en: The 5th edition recommends roughly 1.2 to 2.0 g/kg of protein depending on the sport and training program, with strength/power athletes typically toward the upper end (about 1.5 to 2.0 g/kg). At 1.6 g/kg he is already within the recommended range, so once needs are met more protein does not build proportionally more muscle (training stimulus and total energy/carbohydrate matter). 'More protein = more muscle' is the linear trap. Option C overcorrects with a false toxicity claim and a sub-need recommendation.
tags: Hardest Mode

questions.question: An endurance athlete finishes a depleting two-hour session and wants to maximize muscle glycogen resynthesis. Which post-exercise carbohydrate strategy is best supported?
options: Consume high-glycemic-index carbohydrate soon after exercise
Consume low-glycemic-index carbohydrate and delay intake several hours to 'spread out' refueling
Avoid carbohydrate and rely on protein alone to rebuild glycogen
questions.answer_text: Consume high-glycemic-index carbohydrate soon after exercise
questions.explanation_en: High-glycemic-index carbohydrate soon after exercise speeds glycogen resynthesis by driving a rapid glucose/insulin response when muscle is most receptive. The trap (low-GI plus delay) slows refueling and wastes the window of elevated glycogen-storage capacity. Protein alone (C) cannot replace the carbohydrate that glycogen is built from, though some protein with carbohydrate can help.
tags: Hardest Mode

questions.question: A coach insists athletes only need to drink 'when they feel thirsty' and that a couple percent of body-weight loss is harmless. Which statement most accurately corrects this?
options: Thirst is a reliable real-time gauge, so drinking only to thirst fully prevents performance loss
Thirst lags behind actual fluid deficit, and a loss of roughly 2% of body weight can already impair performance
Athletes should drink as much plain water as possible at all times to stay maximally safe
questions.answer_text: Thirst lags behind actual fluid deficit, and a loss of roughly 2% of body weight can already impair performance
