questions.question: Testosterone and cortisol are lipophilic and can pass through the plasma membrane. Because of this property, where do their receptors have to be located to transmit the signal?
options: Anchored on the outer surface of the cell membrane
Inside the cell, in the cytosol or nucleus
Only in the bloodstream, on carrier binding proteins
questions.answer_text: Inside the cell, in the cytosol or nucleus
questions.explanation_en: Steroid hormones are lipophilic and diffuse across the membrane to bind intracellular (cytosolic or nuclear) receptors that then act on DNA; membrane-surface receptors are used by non-lipophilic hormones.
tags: Chapter 4 quiz: Endocrine Responses to Resistance Exercise and Training

questions.question: Growth hormone and insulin are polypeptides that cannot cross the cell membrane. Given that limitation, how must they transmit their signal into the cell?
options: By diffusing through the membrane to cytosolic receptors
By binding DNA directly inside the nucleus
By binding membrane-surface receptors that trigger secondary messengers
questions.answer_text: By binding membrane-surface receptors that trigger secondary messengers
questions.explanation_en: Non-lipophilic polypeptide hormones cannot cross the membrane, so they bind membrane-surface receptors and rely on secondary messenger cascades; direct DNA binding and membrane diffusion are steroid-hormone traits.
tags: Chapter 4 quiz: Endocrine Responses to Resistance Exercise and Training

questions.question: The anterior pituitary releases ACTH, which travels in the blood to stimulate cortisol secretion. Which structure actually produces and releases the cortisol in response?
options: The adrenal cortex
The anterior pituitary
The adrenal medulla
questions.answer_text: The adrenal cortex
questions.explanation_en: The adrenal cortex produces and releases cortisol in response to ACTH; the adrenal medulla secretes catecholamines, and the anterior pituitary is the source of ACTH, not cortisol.
tags: Chapter 4 quiz: Endocrine Responses to Resistance Exercise and Training

questions.question: A chronically overtrained, underfed athlete shows elevated protein breakdown and gluconeogenesis with suppressed muscle growth. Which hormone, catabolic and anti-anabolic, best accounts for this pattern?
options: Testosterone
Cortisol
Insulin-like growth factor-1
questions.answer_text: Cortisol
questions.explanation_en: Cortisol is the primary catabolic and anti-anabolic hormone, promoting protein breakdown and gluconeogenesis especially when chronically elevated; testosterone and IGF-1 are anabolic.
tags: Chapter 4 quiz: Endocrine Responses to Resistance Exercise and Training

questions.question: An athlete progresses from a light warm-up load to a near-maximal load on the same lift. According to the size principle, what happens to motor unit recruitment, and what does this imply for adaptation?
options: Only slow-twitch fibers are activated no matter how heavy the load gets
Fewer motor units are recruited at higher loads to conserve energy
Progressively more and larger fast-twitch motor units are recruited, and only recruited fibers adapt
questions.answer_text: Progressively more and larger fast-twitch motor units are recruited, and only recruited fibers adapt
questions.explanation_en: Under the size principle, heavier loads recruit progressively more and larger fast-twitch motor units to meet force demand, and only the fibers actually recruited receive the training stimulus.
tags: Chapter 4 quiz: Endocrine Responses to Resistance Exercise and Training

questions.question: When designing a program to maximize muscle growth, a coach wants to leverage the body's primary anabolic hormones. Which group represents those hormones?
options: Testosterone, growth hormone, and IGF-1
Calcitonin, aldosterone, and prolactin
Cortisol, epinephrine, and glucagon
questions.answer_text: Testosterone, growth hormone, and IGF-1
questions.explanation_en: Testosterone, growth hormone, and IGF-1 are the primary anabolic hormones driving muscle growth and remodeling; the other groups are catabolic or serve non-anabolic regulatory roles.
tags: Chapter 4 quiz: Endocrine Responses to Resistance Exercise and Training

questions.question: After a rise in circulating growth hormone, most of the endocrine IGF-1 that appears in the blood is synthesized where?
options: Skeletal muscle exclusively
The liver
The adrenal medulla
questions.answer_text: The liver
questions.explanation_en: Systemic IGF-1 is mainly produced by the liver in response to the 22 kD GH isoform; skeletal muscle also makes local IGF-1 from mechanical stress, but not exclusively, and the adrenal medulla makes catecholamines.
tags: Chapter 4 quiz: Endocrine Responses to Resistance Exercise and Training

questions.question: A common misconception is that heavy lifting will make women bulky like men. Considering circulating testosterone, women naturally have roughly what fraction of the amount found in men?
options: About 25-30%
About 50%
About 5-10%
questions.answer_text: About 5-10%
questions.explanation_en: Women have only about 5-10% of the circulating testosterone found in men, largely due to the absence of testes; the higher fractions overstate the difference.
tags: Chapter 4 quiz: Endocrine Responses to Resistance Exercise and Training

questions.question: Comparing several session designs by their acute post-workout hormonal surge, which one tends to produce the LARGEST rise in both anabolic and catabolic hormones?
options: Moderate loads around 8-10RM with short (1-2 min) rest and higher volume
Single-joint isolation exercises using very light loads
Heavy 1-3RM loads with rest periods over 3 minutes
questions.answer_text: Moderate loads around 8-10RM with short (1-2 min) rest and higher volume
questions.explanation_en: Higher-volume work at moderate loads with short rest creates the greatest metabolic demand and largest acute hormonal surges; heavy low-rep long-rest work has low metabolic demand, and light isolation work does little.
tags: Chapter 4 quiz: Endocrine Responses to Resistance Exercise and Training

questions.question: The lock-and-key model is used to explain why a given hormone affects only certain tissues. What does the model actually describe?
options: Receptors physically lock onto one another to amplify a signal
A hormone must precisely match its specific receptor to trigger a response
Hormones are locked inside binding proteins and are never released to act
questions.answer_text: A hormone must precisely match its specific receptor to trigger a response
questions.explanation_en: The lock-and-key model describes how a specific hormone (key) must fit its specific receptor (lock) to produce an effect, explaining target-tissue specificity.
tags: Chapter 4 quiz: Endocrine Responses to Resistance Exercise and Training

questions.question: A hormone bound to a carrier protein in the blood is temporarily inactive yet the arrangement benefits the athlete. What is the primary role of these binding proteins?
options: They convert steroid hormones into peptide hormones
They permanently block the hormone so it can never act on tissue
They extend the hormone's half-life and protect it from degradation until released
questions.answer_text: They extend the hormone's half-life and protect it from degradation until released
questions.explanation_en: Binding proteins act as temporary storage that protects hormones from degradation and extends their half-life until they are released to the free, active fraction; they do not permanently block or chemically convert hormones.
tags: Chapter 4 quiz: Endocrine Responses to Resistance Exercise and Training

questions.question: As part of the fight-or-flight response to intense exercise, epinephrine and norepinephrine surge into the blood. Which structure is their primary source?
options: The adrenal medulla
The thyroid gland
The anterior pituitary
questions.answer_text: The adrenal medulla
questions.explanation_en: The adrenal medulla secretes the catecholamines epinephrine, norepinephrine, and dopamine; the thyroid and anterior pituitary secrete different hormones.
tags: Chapter 4 quiz: Endocrine Responses to Resistance Exercise and Training

questions.question: After prolonged high insulin exposure, a person's tissues respond less to the same insulin level because receptor number or sensitivity has fallen. This adaptation is called what?
options: Receptor upregulation
Receptor downregulation
Cross-reactivity
questions.answer_text: Receptor downregulation
questions.explanation_en: Receptor downregulation reduces receptor number or sensitivity after chronic overstimulation, with insulin resistance as a classic example; upregulation is the opposite response.
tags: Chapter 4 quiz: Endocrine Responses to Resistance Exercise and Training

questions.question: Some hormones do not directly build muscle but must be present at normal levels for anabolic hormones to work, enabling the underlying metabolic reactions. Which pair plays this permissive role?
options: Cortisol and aldosterone
Estradiol and progesterone
Insulin and thyroid hormones
questions.answer_text: Insulin and thyroid hormones
questions.explanation_en: Insulin and thyroid hormones act permissively, enabling the metabolic and chemical reactions that support muscle growth; cortisol is catabolic and the other listed hormones are not described as permissive here.
tags: Chapter 4 quiz: Endocrine Responses to Resistance Exercise and Training

questions.question: Studies measuring the growth hormone response to a resistance session by immunoassay usually track a particular isoform that rises with total work and short rest. Which isoform is this?
options: The 22 kD isoform
The 44 kD aggregate
There is only one form of GH
questions.answer_text: The 22 kD isoform
questions.explanation_en: Resistance exercise raises the 22 kD GH isoform, the form most studies measure, and it is sensitive to total work and short rest; GH actually exists in multiple isoforms and aggregates.
tags: Chapter 4 quiz: Endocrine Responses to Resistance Exercise and Training

questions.question: A lab reports both total and free testosterone for an athlete. What distinguishes the free fraction, and why does it matter physiologically?
options: It is always higher than total testosterone after exercise
It is the small unbound portion that can directly interact with target tissue
It is the portion permanently bound to sex hormone-binding globulin
questions.answer_text: It is the small unbound portion that can directly interact with target tissue
questions.explanation_en: Free testosterone (roughly 0.5-2% of total) is the unbound fraction able to interact directly with target tissues; the bound portion is not the free fraction, and free can never exceed total.
tags: Chapter 4 quiz: Endocrine Responses to Resistance Exercise and Training

questions.question: A coach wants a session that acutely elevates serum testosterone. Which combination of program variables is recommended to achieve that?
options: A single set to failure followed by 5-minute rest periods
Small-muscle isolation exercises, light loads, and very long rest
Large-muscle-group exercises, heavy resistance, moderate-to-high volume, and short rest
questions.answer_text: Large-muscle-group exercises, heavy resistance, moderate-to-high volume, and short rest
questions.explanation_en: Large-muscle-group lifts, heavy resistance, moderate-to-high volume, and short rest acutely raise serum testosterone; isolation/light/long-rest and single-set/long-rest schemes do not provide the needed stimulus.
tags: Chapter 4 quiz: Endocrine Responses to Resistance Exercise and Training

questions.question: Cortisol is usually cast as purely catabolic, yet an acute post-session rise is not entirely harmful. Which beneficial process does that acute cortisol increase support?
options: Helping clear damaged proteins and aiding tissue remodeling
Directly synthesizing new contractile proteins
Permanently downregulating androgen receptors
questions.answer_text: Helping clear damaged proteins and aiding tissue remodeling
questions.explanation_en: An acute cortisol rise helps clear damaged proteins, assists muscle remodeling, and helps maintain blood glucose; it does not directly build contractile protein and does not permanently downregulate androgen receptors.
tags: Chapter 4 quiz: Endocrine Responses to Resistance Exercise and Training

questions.question: Two athletes have similar resting testosterone levels, but one gains muscle much faster on the same program. Which principle best explains why blood hormone concentration alone does not determine the outcome?
options: Blood hormone level by itself fully dictates the tissue response
The number and sensitivity of receptors strongly determine the actual effect
Receptors are fixed and do not adapt to training
questions.answer_text: The number and sensitivity of receptors strongly determine the actual effect
questions.explanation_en: The actual tissue effect depends heavily on receptor availability and sensitivity, which adapt to training; muscle can grow even without large changes in circulating hormone levels.
tags: Chapter 4 quiz: Endocrine Responses to Resistance Exercise and Training

questions.question: An athlete on a heavy 1-3RM, long-rest program shows only modest acute hormone spikes yet still gains strength and size. Which explanation reconciles the small hormonal response with the real adaptation?
options: It removes the need for muscle protein synthesis to occur
The scheme fails to recruit any motor units, so gains must come from elsewhere
It maximally recruits motor units and enhances receptor binding, while its low metabolic demand limits hormone surges
questions.answer_text: It maximally recruits motor units and enhances receptor binding, while its low metabolic demand limits hormone surges
questions.explanation_en: Heavy low-rep work maximally recruits motor units and enhances receptor binding, driving adaptation, while its low metabolic demand limits the acute hormone surge; it still recruits fibers and still requires protein synthesis.
tags: Chapter 4 quiz: Endocrine Responses to Resistance Exercise and Training

questions.question: A previously sedentary client adds 30 pounds to her back squat over her first three weeks of training, yet a limb-circumference measurement shows essentially no change in thigh girth. What best explains this rapid strength gain?
options: Early sarcomere addition that increases fiber size without changing limb girth
A rise in circulating testosterone that thickens the myofibrils
Improved neural function: greater motor unit recruitment, firing rate, and coordination
questions.answer_text: Improved neural function: greater motor unit recruitment, firing rate, and coordination
questions.explanation_en: Neural adaptations (recruitment, firing rate, coordination) dominate early strength gains before substantial hypertrophy appears.
tags: Chapter 5 quiz: Adaptations to Anaerobic Training

questions.question: As a lifter gradually increases the load on a curl from light to near-maximal, which sequence describes how the motor units of the biceps are brought into play, per Henneman's size principle?
options: Smaller, lower-threshold units are recruited first, with larger high-threshold units added as force demand rises
Units are activated in a rotating pattern to distribute fatigue evenly
The largest, highest-threshold units fire first, with smaller units added as load eases
questions.answer_text: Smaller, lower-threshold units are recruited first, with larger high-threshold units added as force demand rises
questions.explanation_en: Lower-threshold (smaller soma, Type I) motor units are recruited first, with higher-threshold (Type II) units added as force demand rises.
tags: Chapter 5 quiz: Adaptations to Anaerobic Training

questions.question: A muscle biopsy shows a fiber population that is highly fatigue resistant, rich in myoglobin, and served by motor neurons with the lowest activation thresholds. This fiber type is best classified as:
options: Type IIx, fast and white
Type I, slow and red
Type IIa, an intermediate fast-oxidative type
questions.answer_text: Type I, slow and red
questions.explanation_en: Type I fibers are slow, red, fatigue-resistant, and innervated by low-threshold motor neurons; Type II fibers are fast and white.
tags: Chapter 5 quiz: Adaptations to Anaerobic Training

questions.question: A sprinter in a lower-leg cast trains only the healthy leg for six weeks. At cast removal, the immobilized leg has lost less strength than expected and even tests slightly stronger than at injury. This carryover is termed:
options: The bilateral deficit, a shortfall when both limbs act together
Fiber-type transformation of Type II fibers into Type I
Cross-education, a strength gain in the untrained limb from training the opposite limb
questions.answer_text: Cross-education, a strength gain in the untrained limb from training the opposite limb
questions.explanation_en: Cross-education is the strength and neural activity increase in a resting contralateral limb when the opposite limb is trained.
tags: Chapter 5 quiz: Adaptations to Anaerobic Training

questions.question: An untrained athlete produces 40 kg pressing with only the right leg and 40 kg with only the left, but just 72 kg when both legs press together. This shortfall relative to the summed single-leg efforts illustrates:
options: The bilateral deficit, in which combined force is less than the sum of separate limb efforts
Increased antagonist coactivation caused by an unstable surface
A training effect showing bilateral work is superior to unilateral
questions.answer_text: The bilateral deficit, in which combined force is less than the sum of separate limb efforts
questions.explanation_en: In untrained individuals, force produced by both limbs together is lower than the sum of their separate unilateral efforts.
tags: Chapter 5 quiz: Adaptations to Anaerobic Training

questions.question: After several months of consistent heavy resistance training, a repeat biopsy of an athlete's vastus lateralis is expected to show a shift in fiber subtype in which direction?
options: No detectable change in subtype proportions
Toward the more oxidative subtype, IIx converting toward IIa
Toward the less oxidative subtype, IIa converting toward IIx
questions.answer_text: Toward the more oxidative subtype, IIx converting toward IIa
questions.explanation_en: Training shifts fibers toward more oxidative subtypes (IIx to IIa); detraining reverses this and can overshoot toward IIx.
tags: Chapter 5 quiz: Adaptations to Anaerobic Training

questions.question: Two fiber populations in the same muscle are exposed to identical resistance training. Which typically enlarges more, and how should a coach expect the growth to distribute?
options: Both enlarge equally, so growth is uniform across fiber types
Type I fibers enlarge more, so growth favors the slow-twitch pool
Type II fibers enlarge more, so hypertrophy is not uniform between the types
questions.answer_text: Type II fibers enlarge more, so hypertrophy is not uniform between the types
questions.explanation_en: Type II fibers manifest greater increases in size than Type I; hypertrophy is not uniform between the two.
tags: Chapter 5 quiz: Adaptations to Anaerobic Training

questions.question: A coach has an athlete perform chest presses seated on a Swiss ball instead of a stable bench, expecting to boost pressing power. Compared with the stable surface, what happens to agonist force output?
options: Peak force and rate of force development both fall
Force is unchanged because the same muscles do the work
Peak force and rate of force development both rise
questions.answer_text: Peak force and rate of force development both fall
questions.explanation_en: Instability raises antagonist coactivation and core demand while reducing agonist activation, lowering peak force and rate of force development.
tags: Chapter 5 quiz: Adaptations to Anaerobic Training

questions.question: For a loading program to trigger new bone formation, the strain must exceed the minimal essential strain. As a fraction of the force that would fracture the bone, that threshold is approximately:
options: One-half of the fracture force
One-tenth of the fracture force
One-hundredth of the fracture force
questions.answer_text: One-tenth of the fracture force
questions.explanation_en: The MES is thought to be roughly one-tenth of the force required to fracture the bone.
tags: Chapter 5 quiz: Adaptations to Anaerobic Training

questions.question: A coach wants to maximize the osteogenic stimulus for a young athlete's spine and hips. Which choice best accomplishes that goal?
options: High-repetition isolated assistance work with light loads
Seated single-joint leg extensions performed to fatigue
Multijoint structural lifts such as squats and deadlifts that direct load through the spine and hips
questions.answer_text: Multijoint structural lifts such as squats and deadlifts that direct load through the spine and hips
questions.explanation_en: Multijoint structural exercises that direct force through the spine and hip provide a stronger osteogenic stimulus than isolated machine work.
tags: Chapter 5 quiz: Adaptations to Anaerobic Training

questions.question: A coach wants to increase the collagen content and stiffness of an athlete's patellar tendon. Which loading prescription is most appropriate?
options: Heavy loads near 80% of 1RM
Load magnitude is irrelevant as long as volume is high
Light loads near 20% of 1RM performed for high repetitions
questions.answer_text: Heavy loads near 80% of 1RM
questions.explanation_en: Heavy loads (around 80% 1RM) increase tendon stiffness; light loads (around 20% 1RM) do not markedly change collagen.
tags: Chapter 5 quiz: Adaptations to Anaerobic Training

questions.question: A bodybuilder completes a block of heavy, high-volume hypertrophy training that markedly enlarges fiber cross-sectional area. What happens to the mitochondrial density measured per unit of fiber volume?
options: It rises as mitochondria proliferate to match the larger fiber
It falls because fiber volume grows faster than mitochondria are added
It is unchanged because mitochondria scale exactly with fiber size
questions.answer_text: It falls because fiber volume grows faster than mitochondria are added
questions.explanation_en: The fiber cross-sectional area grows faster than mitochondria proliferate, so mitochondrial density per unit volume decreases.
tags: Chapter 5 quiz: Adaptations to Anaerobic Training

questions.question: A sprinter repeatedly drains ATP and creatine phosphate with maximal-effort sets over weeks. What adaptation occurs in the resting concentrations of these substrates?
options: Resting stores are unchanged because these substrates cannot be stockpiled
Resting stores fall as the substrates are chronically depleted
Resting stores rise through a supercompensation response
questions.answer_text: Resting stores rise through a supercompensation response
questions.explanation_en: Repeated depletion triggers a supercompensation effect that raises resting stores of ATP, creatine phosphate, and glycogen.
tags: Chapter 5 quiz: Adaptations to Anaerobic Training

questions.question: An echocardiogram of a long-term heavy resistance-trained athlete is compared with that of a distance runner. The resistance-trained heart most characteristically shows:
options: Increased left ventricular wall thickness with little change in chamber size
No structural difference from an untrained heart
A greatly enlarged left ventricular chamber volume with normal wall thickness
questions.answer_text: Increased left ventricular wall thickness with little change in chamber size
questions.explanation_en: Resistance training increases left ventricular wall thickness while chamber size changes little; chamber enlargement is more an aerobic adaptation.
tags: Chapter 5 quiz: Adaptations to Anaerobic Training

questions.question: An athlete layers high-intensity, high-volume aerobic endurance running onto an existing heavy strength and power program. Which quality is the concurrent aerobic work most likely to blunt?
options: Joint flexibility
Explosive power development
Bone mineral density
questions.answer_text: Explosive power development
questions.explanation_en: Concurrent training most readily blunts power development, which is more susceptible to interference than slow-velocity strength.
tags: Chapter 5 quiz: Adaptations to Anaerobic Training

questions.question: A coach sees strength gains stalling in an athlete who does both resistance and aerobic endurance work. Which adjustment best reduces the interference effect?
options: Routinely place a hard aerobic bout immediately before the heavy lifting
Schedule both modes back-to-back on six consecutive days
Allow more recovery time between the resistance and aerobic sessions
questions.answer_text: Allow more recovery time between the resistance and aerobic sessions
questions.explanation_en: Increasing the recovery period between sessions decreases the incompatibility between strength and aerobic endurance training.
tags: Chapter 5 quiz: Adaptations to Anaerobic Training

questions.question: A strength athlete is sidelined by a non-training-related illness and does no resistance work for about four weeks. On return testing, his maximal strength is most likely to be:
options: Largely retained, remaining near pre-layoff levels
Dropped below his original pretraining baseline
Higher than before the layoff due to extra rest
questions.answer_text: Largely retained, remaining near pre-layoff levels
questions.explanation_en: Strength is readily maintained for up to about four weeks of inactivity and rarely falls below pretraining values.
tags: Chapter 5 quiz: Adaptations to Anaerobic Training

questions.question: After a period of detraining, biopsies are taken from an athlete's leg. Which fiber population is expected to have lost cross-sectional area first and fastest?
options: Slow-twitch Type I fibers, which atrophy earliest
Fast-twitch Type II fibers, which atrophy earliest
Both fiber types, atrophying at identical rates from day one
questions.answer_text: Fast-twitch Type II fibers, which atrophy earliest
questions.explanation_en: Fast-twitch fiber CSA declines first and fastest with detraining, while slow-twitch fibers initially show little change.
tags: Chapter 5 quiz: Adaptations to Anaerobic Training

questions.question: A coach argues that only very heavy loads let an athlete grow the full spectrum of muscle fibers. What is the correct physiological reason heavy resistance training can hypertrophy fibers across all motor units?
options: Anabolic hormones enlarge fibers directly, so recruitment is not required
Only Type I fibers respond to heavy loads, so they alone carry the growth
Generating high force recruits fibers across all motor units, and a fiber must be activated to receive the growth signal
questions.answer_text: Generating high force recruits fibers across all motor units, and a fiber must be activated to receive the growth signal
questions.explanation_en: Producing high force requires recruiting fibers across all motor units, and a fiber must be activated to receive the growth signal.
tags: Chapter 5 quiz: Adaptations to Anaerobic Training

questions.question: A once-competitive lifter returns after a long layoff and regains his former strength far faster than an equally strong novice builds it. This residual training effect is best described as:
options: Muscle memory: a residual effect that lets strength be reacquired rapidly on retraining
Conversion of atrophied muscle tissue into bone during the layoff
A total loss of adaptation requiring the athlete to rebuild strength from zero
questions.answer_text: Muscle memory: a residual effect that lets strength be reacquired rapidly on retraining
questions.explanation_en: Resistance training leaves a residual effect, so returning athletes regain strength quickly, consistent with muscle memory.
tags: Chapter 5 quiz: Adaptations to Anaerobic Training

questions.question: After a year of endurance training, a runner's maximal oxygen uptake has risen sharply. Which underlying cardiovascular change is chiefly responsible for delivering that extra oxygen?
options: A greater maximal cardiac output, driven mainly by increased stroke volume
A higher resting blood pressure pushing more blood to the muscles
A higher maximal heart rate driving more beats per minute
questions.answer_text: A greater maximal cardiac output, driven mainly by increased stroke volume
questions.explanation_en: The hallmark change is increased maximal cardiac output, resulting primarily from a higher stroke volume, not a higher max heart rate.
tags: Chapter 6 quiz: Adaptations to Aerobic Endurance Training

questions.question: A cyclist retested after two years of endurance training shows a much higher stroke volume and cardiac output. What is expected to have happened to her maximal heart rate over that same period?
options: It rose substantially to match the higher cardiac output
It stayed about the same or decreased slightly
It roughly doubled
questions.answer_text: It stayed about the same or decreased slightly
questions.explanation_en: Maximal heart rate generally remains unaltered or decreases slightly, partly due to increased parasympathetic tone.
tags: Chapter 6 quiz: Adaptations to Aerobic Endurance Training

questions.question: A trained endurance athlete has a resting heart rate of 44 beats per minute. Which pairing of mechanisms best accounts for this bradycardia?
options: A smaller, weaker heart that pumps less blood per beat
A reduced total blood volume requiring fewer beats
Increased parasympathetic tone slowing the SA node, combined with a larger stroke volume
questions.answer_text: Increased parasympathetic tone slowing the SA node, combined with a larger stroke volume
questions.explanation_en: Increased parasympathetic tone slows the SA node discharge, and a larger stroke volume means fewer beats are needed per minute.
tags: Chapter 6 quiz: Adaptations to Aerobic Endurance Training

questions.question: A biopsy panel from elite competitors in several sports is compared. The elite distance runners are distinguished by the highest proportion of which fiber type?
options: Type I, slow and red
Type IIx, fast and white
Type IIa transitioning toward IIx
questions.answer_text: Type I, slow and red
questions.explanation_en: Type I fibers are slow, red, and highly oxidative; elite distance runners show a higher proportion of them.
tags: Chapter 6 quiz: Adaptations to Aerobic Endurance Training

questions.question: Endurance training improves a muscle's ability to extract and use oxygen. Which set of cellular changes primarily accounts for this?
options: A rise in glycolytic enzyme activity that boosts anaerobic power
Increased mitochondrial size and number along with more myoglobin
Denser myofibrillar packing that raises contractile protein content
questions.answer_text: Increased mitochondrial size and number along with more myoglobin
questions.explanation_en: Aerobic training raises mitochondrial size and number and myoglobin, enhancing the muscle's capacity to extract and use oxygen.
tags: Chapter 6 quiz: Adaptations to Aerobic Endurance Training

questions.question: Two marathoners have laboratory-measured maximal oxygen uptakes that are essentially equal, yet one consistently races faster. Which combination best explains the performance gap?
options: A higher maximal heart rate allowing a faster finish
A greater proportion of Type IIx fibers
A higher lactate threshold together with better exercise economy
questions.answer_text: A higher lactate threshold together with better exercise economy
questions.explanation_en: With equal VO2max, a higher lactate threshold and better exercise economy let an athlete sustain a higher pace and perform better.
tags: Chapter 6 quiz: Adaptations to Aerobic Endurance Training

questions.question: A coach starts two athletes on aerobic training: a truly untrained beginner and an already elite endurance competitor. Which pattern of maximal oxygen uptake improvement should the coach expect?
options: About 20% for the untrained athlete versus about 5-10% for the elite athlete
About 50% for the untrained athlete versus about 40% for the elite athlete
Roughly the same percentage gain for both
questions.answer_text: About 20% for the untrained athlete versus about 5-10% for the elite athlete
questions.explanation_en: Untrained individuals may raise VO2max by up to about 20%, while elite athletes typically see only about 5-10%.
tags: Chapter 6 quiz: Adaptations to Aerobic Endurance Training

questions.question: An endurance athlete's maximal oxygen uptake has plateaued after roughly 6 to 12 months, yet his race times keep dropping. Where do these continued performance gains mainly come from?
options: A steadily rising maximal heart rate
Improved exercise economy and a higher lactate threshold
Ongoing large increases in maximal oxygen uptake
questions.answer_text: Improved exercise economy and a higher lactate threshold
questions.explanation_en: Once VO2max plateaus, performance continues to improve through better exercise economy and an increased lactate threshold.
tags: Chapter 6 quiz: Adaptations to Aerobic Endurance Training

questions.question: An athlete recovering from a stress fracture wants an aerobic mode that also loads the skeleton to help build bone. Which choice provides the strongest osteogenic stimulus?
options: Stationary cycling
Lap swimming
Running, which is high-impact and weight-bearing
questions.answer_text: Running, which is high-impact and weight-bearing
questions.explanation_en: Running's repetitive high-impact weight-bearing loading promotes bone growth more than weight-supported cycling or swimming.
tags: Chapter 6 quiz: Adaptations to Aerobic Endurance Training

questions.question: A competitive cyclist who trains almost exclusively on the bike gets a DXA scan. What is a plausible finding regarding bone density at sites not loaded during cycling?
options: Reduced density at non-locomotor sites, such as the lower spine
Density unchanged at every skeletal site
Uniformly increased density from the high training volume
questions.answer_text: Reduced density at non-locomotor sites, such as the lower spine
questions.explanation_en: Non-weight-bearing activity places minimal skeletal strain and can reduce bone density, for example lower-spine density in cyclists.
tags: Chapter 6 quiz: Adaptations to Aerobic Endurance Training

questions.question: At a given submaximal running pace, a well-trained endurance athlete relies on a different fuel mix than an untrained person. The training-induced shift is toward:
options: Near-exclusive reliance on protein for fuel
Greater fat oxidation with sparing of carbohydrate stores
Greater carbohydrate oxidation with sparing of fat stores
questions.answer_text: Greater fat oxidation with sparing of carbohydrate stores
questions.explanation_en: Trained muscle oxidizes more fat and spares glycogen, allowing higher-intensity exercise to be sustained longer.
tags: Chapter 6 quiz: Adaptations to Aerobic Endurance Training

questions.question: A distance runner relocates to a high-altitude camp for several weeks. Which chronic adaptation should the coach expect as the body compensates for the lower oxygen pressure?
options: Decreased capillary density in the working muscle
Reduced red blood cell production to conserve iron
Increased hemoglobin and red blood cell production
questions.answer_text: Increased hemoglobin and red blood cell production
questions.explanation_en: Chronic altitude exposure increases hemoglobin formation, red blood cell production, and capillarization to offset reduced oxygen pressure.
tags: Chapter 6 quiz: Adaptations to Aerobic Endurance Training

questions.question: A team has trained and fully acclimatized at moderate altitude before an event held at the same elevation, well above 3,900 feet. Compared with sea level, their aerobic performance there will generally be:
options: Still reduced relative to sea level
Identical to sea level once acclimatized
Better than at sea level thanks to acclimatization
questions.answer_text: Still reduced relative to sea level
questions.explanation_en: Arterial oxygen saturation falls at altitude, so VO2max and aerobic performance remain reduced versus sea level even after acclimatizing.
tags: Chapter 6 quiz: Adaptations to Aerobic Endurance Training

questions.question: A soccer team spends two weeks training in the heat before a hot-climate tournament. Which cluster of chronic adaptations should the staff expect from successful heat acclimatization?
options: Elevated resting and exercising core temperature
Expanded plasma volume, lower exercising heart rate and core temperature, and a higher sweat rate
Reduced plasma volume with decreased sweating to conserve fluid
questions.answer_text: Expanded plasma volume, lower exercising heart rate and core temperature, and a higher sweat rate
questions.explanation_en: Heat acclimatization expands plasma volume, lowers heart rate and core temperature, and increases sweat rate and evaporative cooling.
tags: Chapter 6 quiz: Adaptations to Aerobic Endurance Training

questions.question: An athlete finishes a heat-acclimation block, then trains in cool conditions for the next month with no heat exposure. What becomes of the heat adaptations?
options: They continue to strengthen even without heat exposure
They persist permanently once established
They are transient and decay over days to weeks
questions.answer_text: They are transient and decay over days to weeks
questions.explanation_en: Heat acclimation adaptations are transient and begin to dissipate within days to weeks, typically lost within about a month without exposure.
tags: Chapter 6 quiz: Adaptations to Aerobic Endurance Training

questions.question: A coach is comparing why altitude camps and heat camps help endurance athletes. Which statement correctly contrasts their primary physiological mechanisms?
options: Altitude mainly drives red cell and hemoglobin increases, while heat mainly expands plasma volume
Both operate through the identical adaptive pathway
Both act primarily by expanding plasma volume
questions.answer_text: Altitude mainly drives red cell and hemoglobin increases, while heat mainly expands plasma volume
questions.explanation_en: Altitude (hypoxia) stimulates erythropoietin and red cell mass, while heat acclimation mainly expands plasma volume; the mechanisms differ.
tags: Chapter 6 quiz: Adaptations to Aerobic Endurance Training

questions.question: An athlete can afford one environmental training camp before a key competition held in hot, humid, low-altitude conditions. What should most guide the choice between an altitude and a heat protocol?
options: Selecting whichever camp costs less, regardless of the event setting
Matching the protocol to the environment the athlete will compete in
Combining altitude and heat exposure to stack every possible benefit
questions.answer_text: Matching the protocol to the environment the athlete will compete in
questions.explanation_en: Nonhematological adaptations are specific to the environment, so the protocol should match the conditions of the competition.
tags: Chapter 6 quiz: Adaptations to Aerobic Endurance Training

questions.question: A client who has switched from smoking to vaping asks whether it is cardiovascularly harmless. Which documented short-term effect should you cite?
options: Decreases in heart rate and blood pressure
A reduction in systemic inflammation
Increases in heart rate and diastolic blood pressure
questions.answer_text: Increases in heart rate and diastolic blood pressure
questions.explanation_en: Nicotine-stimulated catecholamine release raises heart rate and diastolic blood pressure; vaping has clear short-term negative effects.
tags: Chapter 6 quiz: Adaptations to Aerobic Endurance Training

questions.question: An endurance athlete who smokes has a normal hemoglobin level yet delivers less oxygen to working muscle than expected. Why does the carbon monoxide in cigarette smoke impair aerobic performance?
options: It binds hemoglobin more strongly than oxygen does, cutting the oxygen actually carried
It raises the blood's oxygen-carrying capacity but blocks release at the tissues
It dilates the airways and hyperventilates the athlete
questions.answer_text: It binds hemoglobin more strongly than oxygen does, cutting the oxygen actually carried
questions.explanation_en: Carbon monoxide has a higher affinity for hemoglobin than oxygen, forming carboxyhemoglobin and reducing oxygen delivery to muscle.
tags: Chapter 6 quiz: Adaptations to Aerobic Endurance Training

questions.question: A multisport athlete stops training entirely for four weeks. Which of her adaptations will regress the most, and for what reason, given that maximal oxygen uptake can fall 4-14% in that short a span?
options: Maximal strength, because it is purely neural and quickly lost
Aerobic endurance adaptations, because of their enzymatic basis
Bone mineral density, because bone has slow turnover
questions.answer_text: Aerobic endurance adaptations, because of their enzymatic basis
questions.explanation_en: Aerobic endurance adaptations are most sensitive to inactivity owing to their enzymatic basis, with VO2max falling 4-14% in just four weeks.
tags: Chapter 6 quiz: Adaptations to Aerobic Endurance Training

questions.question: A coach records that a 12-year-old has advanced markedly toward the mature state of several body systems, even though he has not gotten much taller this year. Which term specifically captures this system-by-system progression toward the adult biological state?
options: Growth
Maturation
Development
questions.answer_text: Maturation
questions.explanation_en: Maturation is progress toward the mature biological state of the body's systems; growth is an increase in size, and development is the prenatal-to-adult progression.
tags: Chapter 7 quiz: Age-Related Differences and Their Implications for Resistance Training

questions.question: A practitioner tracks a young athlete's stature over several years and wants to identify the single point that reflects the fastest growth of the pubertal spurt. Peak height velocity is best described as which of the following?
options: The predicted final adult stature the athlete will reach
The chronological age at which the epiphyseal plates fully close
The age at the maximum rate of growth during the pubertal growth spurt
questions.answer_text: The age at the maximum rate of growth during the pubertal growth spurt
questions.explanation_en: PHV is the age at the maximum rate of growth during the pubertal growth spurt; predicted adult height and epiphyseal closure are separate concepts.
tags: Chapter 7 quiz: Age-Related Differences and Their Implications for Resistance Training

questions.question: A coach oversees a mixed group of 11- to 14-year-olds and notices the girls hitting their growth spurt well before the boys. On average, how does the timing of peak height velocity differ by sex?
options: Girls reach PHV about two years before boys
Both sexes reach PHV at essentially the same age
Boys reach PHV about two years before girls
questions.answer_text: Girls reach PHV about two years before boys
questions.explanation_en: Girls reach PHV roughly two years earlier than boys (mean about 11.9 years vs 13.8 years).
tags: Chapter 7 quiz: Age-Related Differences and Their Implications for Resistance Training

questions.question: Two athletes on a youth team are both exactly 13 years old, yet one is clearly far more physically mature than the other. Why does this make chronological age a poor basis for classifying developmental stage?
options: Children of the same age all mature at a constant, predictable rate
Two children of the same chronological age can differ biologically by up to five years
Chronological age is too difficult to measure accurately in youth
questions.answer_text: Two children of the same chronological age can differ biologically by up to five years
questions.explanation_en: Large interindividual variation means two children of the same chronological age can differ biologically by up to five years, so programs must account for maturation.
tags: Chapter 7 quiz: Age-Related Differences and Their Implications for Resistance Training

questions.question: A pediatric researcher needs the single most accurate index of a child's biological maturation, cost and convenience aside. Which method is the gold standard?
options: Somatic assessment using serial stature measurements
Sexual maturation (secondary sex characteristic) staging
Skeletal age assessment from a left-wrist radiograph
questions.answer_text: Skeletal age assessment from a left-wrist radiograph
questions.explanation_en: Skeletal age, determined by comparing wrist radiographs against reference standards, is the gold standard for biological maturation, though impractical for most field settings.
tags: Chapter 7 quiz: Age-Related Differences and Their Implications for Resistance Training

questions.question: A high school coach with no medical equipment or budget wants a noninvasive, practical way to estimate the biological age of her athletes. Which approach best fits these constraints?
options: Somatic assessment based on height measures
Skeletal age assessment via X-ray imaging
Sexual age assessment of secondary sex characteristics
questions.answer_text: Somatic assessment based on height measures
questions.explanation_en: Somatic (stature-based) assessments are noninvasive, low-cost, and practical for field practitioners, unlike radiographs or intrusive sexual maturation staging.
tags: Chapter 7 quiz: Age-Related Differences and Their Implications for Resistance Training

questions.question: In a growing child's long bone, one region acts as the primary ossification center and forms the central shaft. Which structure is this?
options: The epiphysis, the growth region near the joint surface
The diaphysis, the central shaft of the bone
The apophysis, the site where a tendon inserts
questions.answer_text: The diaphysis, the central shaft of the bone
questions.explanation_en: The diaphysis is the central shaft and primary ossification center of a long bone; the epiphysis and apophysis are separate growth-cartilage sites.
tags: Chapter 7 quiz: Age-Related Differences and Their Implications for Resistance Training

questions.question: A clinician explaining injury-vulnerable regions to a youth coach notes that growth cartilage (the secondary ossification centers) sits at more than one site in a child's bones. Where is it found?
options: Distributed uniformly throughout the entire bone
Only at the central shaft (diaphysis) of the bone
At the epiphyseal plate, the joint surface, and the apophyseal insertions
questions.answer_text: At the epiphyseal plate, the joint surface, and the apophyseal insertions
questions.explanation_en: Growth cartilage occupies three sites: the epiphyseal plate, the joint (articular) surface, and the apophyseal insertions of muscle-tendon units.
tags: Chapter 7 quiz: Age-Related Differences and Their Implications for Resistance Training

questions.question: A 9-year-old completes 12 weeks of supervised resistance training and gets clearly stronger, yet shows little change in limb girth. Which system is chiefly responsible for these gains?
options: The neuromuscular system
The endocrine system, through elevated androgens
The skeletal system
questions.answer_text: The neuromuscular system
questions.explanation_en: Preadolescents gain strength mainly through neural factors (improved motor unit activation, recruitment, and firing) rather than hypertrophy, because circulating androgens are low.
tags: Chapter 7 quiz: Age-Related Differences and Their Implications for Resistance Training

questions.question: A parent asks why her prepubescent son is getting stronger from training but not visibly building muscle like his older brother. What is the primary physiological reason?
options: His nervous system is fully myelinated and can no longer adapt
He has inadequate levels of circulating anabolic hormones such as testosterone
He lacks the muscle fibers required for any hypertrophy
questions.answer_text: He has inadequate levels of circulating anabolic hormones such as testosterone
questions.explanation_en: Low circulating testosterone, growth hormone, and IGF in preadolescents limit hypertrophy, so their strength gains are predominantly neural.
tags: Chapter 7 quiz: Age-Related Differences and Their Implications for Resistance Training

questions.question: A youth sport parent voices the usual concerns about kids and weights. Which of the following statements is actually TRUE and consistent with the evidence?
options: Children gain no benefit from resistance training until they have entered puberty
Properly loaded resistance training stunts long-bone growth in children
With correct technique, appropriate loading, and supervision, resistance training is safe for youth
questions.answer_text: With correct technique, appropriate loading, and supervision, resistance training is safe for youth
questions.explanation_en: The claims that training stunts growth or must wait until puberty are myths; with proper technique, loading, and instruction, resistance training is safe and beneficial for youth.
tags: Chapter 7 quiz: Age-Related Differences and Their Implications for Resistance Training

questions.question: A new coach plans to run his 11-year-olds through a scaled-down version of his adult powerlifting program. Which principle, captured by 'children are not miniature adults,' should redirect his approach?
options: Adult programs and training philosophies should not simply be superimposed on youth
Youth should train at adult intensities so they adapt faster
Once technique is learned, youth no longer need direct supervision
questions.answer_text: Adult programs and training philosophies should not simply be superimposed on youth
questions.explanation_en: Adult programs are often too severe for children; youth programming must be matched to a child's physical, technical, and maturity level.
tags: Chapter 7 quiz: Age-Related Differences and Their Implications for Resistance Training

questions.question: A trainer is uncertain how much load a child new to resistance training can handle. Which starting philosophy best protects the child?
options: Overestimate the child's abilities to accelerate early progress
Underestimate the child's abilities and progress volume and intensity gradually
Assign adult loads early to build the child's confidence
questions.answer_text: Underestimate the child's abilities and progress volume and intensity gradually
questions.explanation_en: It is safer to underestimate a child's abilities and raise volume and intensity gradually than to risk injury by starting too heavy.
tags: Chapter 7 quiz: Age-Related Differences and Their Implications for Resistance Training

questions.question: An older client shows progressive, generalized loss of skeletal muscle that his physician links to his recent falls and elevated mortality risk. Which condition does this describe?
options: Osteoporosis
Dynapenia driven by muscle hypertrophy
Sarcopenia
questions.answer_text: Sarcopenia
questions.explanation_en: Sarcopenia is the progressive, generalized loss of skeletal muscle mass associated with adverse outcomes such as falls, fractures, and mortality; osteoporosis concerns bone, not muscle.
tags: Chapter 7 quiz: Age-Related Differences and Their Implications for Resistance Training

questions.question: A coach designing training for seniors notes that the ability to rise quickly from a chair fades faster than the ability to lift a heavy load slowly. How do power and strength change with aging?
options: Power declines at a faster rate than strength
Strength declines at a faster rate than power
Power and strength decline at essentially the same rate
questions.answer_text: Power declines at a faster rate than strength
questions.explanation_en: Power recedes faster than strength with aging, which matters because many daily tasks demand rapid force production.
tags: Chapter 7 quiz: Age-Related Differences and Their Implications for Resistance Training

questions.question: A DXA scan reports a client's bone mineral density at -2.8 standard deviations below the young adult mean. Which diagnostic category does this value place her in?
options: Osteopenia
Osteoporosis
Normal bone density
questions.answer_text: Osteoporosis
questions.explanation_en: A BMD below -2.5 SD of the young adult mean defines osteoporosis; -1 to -2.5 SD is osteopenia.
tags: Chapter 7 quiz: Age-Related Differences and Their Implications for Resistance Training

questions.question: A 72-year-old hypertensive client is straining and breath-holding during heavy leg press. Which practice should the coach specifically discourage in this senior trainee?
options: Light static stretching after the session
A low-intensity aerobic warm-up before lifting
The Valsalva maneuver
questions.answer_text: The Valsalva maneuver
questions.explanation_en: The Valsalva maneuver is discouraged in seniors because it causes a sudden spike in systolic and diastolic blood pressure.
tags: Chapter 7 quiz: Age-Related Differences and Their Implications for Resistance Training

questions.question: A facility markets a seniors' program claiming that lifting weights by itself will keep members from falling. What is the accurate view of resistance training as a stand-alone fall-prevention method?
options: Resistance training alone does not prevent falls and must be paired with balance and flexibility work
Resistance training increases fall risk in older adults and should be avoided
Resistance training on its own reliably prevents falls
questions.answer_text: Resistance training alone does not prevent falls and must be paired with balance and flexibility work
questions.explanation_en: Resistance training alone does not prevent falls; it must be accompanied by balance and flexibility training.
tags: Chapter 7 quiz: Age-Related Differences and Their Implications for Resistance Training

questions.question: An older adult wants to increase muscular strength, power, and muscle mass. Of aerobic, balance, and resistance training, which modality uniquely delivers all three of those adaptations?
options: All three modalities produce them equally
Resistance training
Aerobic training
questions.answer_text: Resistance training
questions.explanation_en: All three modalities benefit older adults, but only resistance training increases muscular strength, power, and muscle mass.
tags: Chapter 7 quiz: Age-Related Differences and Their Implications for Resistance Training

questions.question: A coach is writing the opening resistance prescription for a previously untrained 68-year-old. Which starting point is most appropriate before gradual progression?
options: 5 sets of 1 rep at about 95 percent 1RM beginning in the first session
Maximal singles paired with the Valsalva maneuver for trunk stability
1 set of 8 to 12 reps at about 40 to 50 percent 1RM, progressing later toward higher volume and intensity
questions.answer_text: 1 set of 8 to 12 reps at about 40 to 50 percent 1RM, progressing later toward higher volume and intensity
questions.explanation_en: Seniors should begin around 1 set of 8 to 12 reps at 40 to 50 percent 1RM and progress gradually toward 3 sets at 60 to 80 percent 1RM.
tags: Chapter 7 quiz: Age-Related Differences and Their Implications for Resistance Training

questions.question: A coach compares average anthropometric profiles when adapting a program written for men to a group of women. Relative to adult males, which body composition profile do adult females tend to show on average?
options: Less body fat, more muscle, and higher bone mineral density
Equal body fat and muscle but higher bone mineral density
More body fat, less muscle, and lower bone mineral density
questions.answer_text: More body fat, less muscle, and lower bone mineral density
questions.explanation_en: On average, adult females carry more body fat, less muscle, and lower bone mineral density than males, and are lighter.
tags: Chapter 8 quiz: Sex-Related Differences and Their Implications for Resistance Training

questions.question: A strength coach working with young adult women wants to account for structural changes that are still ongoing into early adulthood. Which statement accurately describes this timeline?
options: Growth plates typically close around age 20 and peak bone density is reached around age 30
Bone mineral density peaks at puberty and declines immediately afterward
The number of muscle fibers roughly doubles during a woman's twenties
questions.answer_text: Growth plates typically close around age 20 and peak bone density is reached around age 30
questions.explanation_en: Growth plates generally close by about age 20 and peak bone mineral density is reached around age 30.
tags: Chapter 8 quiz: Sex-Related Differences and Their Implications for Resistance Training

questions.question: A 34-year-old woman who has never done structured resistance training asks when, left unaddressed, her muscle mass and bone density will start to slip. What is the typical pattern?
options: They do not begin declining until after age 70
They begin declining in the mid-30s and accelerate after about age 50
They begin declining immediately after puberty
questions.answer_text: They begin declining in the mid-30s and accelerate after about age 50
questions.explanation_en: Without a sustained resistance program, muscle mass and bone density begin declining in the mid-30s and accelerate after about age 50, particularly with menopause.
tags: Chapter 8 quiz: Sex-Related Differences and Their Implications for Resistance Training

questions.question: An athletic trainer reviews injury data across comparable sports. Although more ACL tears occur in males in absolute numbers, how does the relative rate of ACL injury in female athletes compare with males?
options: It is about half that of males
It is about the same as males
It is about two times higher than males
questions.answer_text: It is about two times higher than males
questions.explanation_en: Absolute ACL injury frequency is higher in males, but in comparable sports the female athletes' relative rate is about two times higher than males'.
tags: Chapter 8 quiz: Sex-Related Differences and Their Implications for Resistance Training

questions.question: A coach designing an ACL-injury-reduction program for female athletes wants to target the factor believed to contribute most to their elevated risk. Which factor should the program address?
options: A neuromuscular deficiency that produces abnormal biomechanics such as increased dynamic knee valgus
Femoral notch size alone
Their higher absolute muscle mass
questions.answer_text: A neuromuscular deficiency that produces abnormal biomechanics such as increased dynamic knee valgus
questions.explanation_en: Anatomical factors like notch size play a role, but a neuromuscular deficiency leading to dynamic knee valgus is considered the most significant, and it is trainable.
tags: Chapter 8 quiz: Sex-Related Differences and Their Implications for Resistance Training

questions.question: A clinic tracks anterior knee pain among its athletes. Compared with male athletes, how often does patellofemoral pain syndrome occur in female athletes?
options: At the same rate
More than two times as often
About half as often
questions.answer_text: More than two times as often
questions.explanation_en: Female athletes are more than two times as likely to experience patellofemoral pain syndrome as male athletes.
tags: Chapter 8 quiz: Sex-Related Differences and Their Implications for Resistance Training

questions.question: A researcher re-expresses raw strength scores relative to each participant's fat-free mass rather than total body mass. What happens to the apparent strength difference between the sexes?
options: It stays essentially unchanged
It increases substantially
It tends to disappear
questions.answer_text: It tends to disappear
questions.explanation_en: When strength is normalized to fat-free mass, sex-related differences tend to disappear, indicating the raw gap largely reflects body composition.
tags: Chapter 8 quiz: Sex-Related Differences and Their Implications for Resistance Training

questions.question: A coach compares a female athlete's absolute strength with male norms and finds one region much nearer to male values than the other. Which comparison is accurate on average?
options: Lower body strength is closer to male values than upper body strength
Upper body strength is closer to male values than lower body strength
Upper and lower body strength are equally close to male values
questions.answer_text: Lower body strength is closer to male values than upper body strength
questions.explanation_en: Female lower body strength is generally closer to male values, whereas upper body strength remains relatively further below.
tags: Chapter 8 quiz: Sex-Related Differences and Their Implications for Resistance Training

questions.question: A trainer runs identical 12-week hypertrophy blocks for a man and a woman of similar training status. How does their relative muscle hypertrophy over this short-term period compare?
options: Relative hypertrophy is greater in the female
Relative hypertrophy is similar between the sexes
Meaningful hypertrophy is not possible in the female
questions.answer_text: Relative hypertrophy is similar between the sexes
questions.explanation_en: Over short-term programs (up to about 16 weeks), relative hypertrophy is similar between sexes, though absolute hypertrophy is greater in males.
tags: Chapter 8 quiz: Sex-Related Differences and Their Implications for Resistance Training

questions.question: An endurance coach notes that, on average, her female runners fatigue more slowly and rely more on fat oxidation. Which average fiber-type distribution helps explain this?
options: A greater proportion of type II glycolytic fibers
A fiber distribution identical to males
A greater proportion of type I oxidative fibers
questions.answer_text: A greater proportion of type I oxidative fibers
questions.explanation_en: Females average a greater proportion of type I oxidative fibers, so they oxidize more fat and are more fatigue resistant; males average slightly more type II fibers.
tags: Chapter 8 quiz: Sex-Related Differences and Their Implications for Resistance Training

questions.question: A physiologist measures the cortisol response to an identical acute training bout in matched male and female athletes. How does the female response typically compare?
options: It is attenuated relative to males
It is entirely absent in females
It is greatly amplified relative to males
questions.answer_text: It is attenuated relative to males
questions.explanation_en: The acute cortisol response is attenuated in females, in part because female sex hormones lower cortisol responsivity and sensitivity differs.
tags: Chapter 8 quiz: Sex-Related Differences and Their Implications for Resistance Training

questions.question: A coach reads that men show a sharp acute testosterone spike after heavy lifting and wonders whether the same holds for his female athletes after a single session. What does the evidence indicate?
options: Females show an immediate two- to fourfold acute rise in testosterone
Females do not show significant acute elevations in testosterone
Females' testosterone drops to undetectable levels after the bout
questions.answer_text: Females do not show significant acute elevations in testosterone
questions.explanation_en: Females do not exhibit significant acute testosterone elevations after a resistance bout, although prolonged training can produce some acute increases.
tags: Chapter 8 quiz: Sex-Related Differences and Their Implications for Resistance Training

questions.question: In a female athlete, blood is sampled shortly after a high-total-work resistance session. Which hormonal change is most expected in her circulating growth hormone?
options: It falls below resting levels
It remains completely unchanged
It increases roughly two- to fourfold
questions.answer_text: It increases roughly two- to fourfold
questions.explanation_en: Circulating growth hormone rises about two- to fourfold after an acute resistance bout in females, with magnitude depending on the stimulus and total work.
tags: Chapter 8 quiz: Sex-Related Differences and Their Implications for Resistance Training

questions.question: A coach explains to a female client why maintaining normal menstrual and hormonal function supports her training. What is estradiol's effect on skeletal muscle?
options: It promotes protein synthesis over degradation and has a protective effect
It increases muscle damage and cell death with training
It negatively influences muscle contractile properties
questions.answer_text: It promotes protein synthesis over degradation and has a protective effect
questions.explanation_en: Estradiol supports muscle mass by favoring protein synthesis over degradation and exerts a protective, antioxidant-like effect on muscle.
tags: Chapter 8 quiz: Sex-Related Differences and Their Implications for Resistance Training

questions.question: A coach proposes rigidly periodizing every female athlete's loading to her menstrual cycle phase. What does the most recent evidence say about this practice?
options: Programs should always be periodized to the menstrual cycle
Current evidence does not support modifying prescription based on cycle phase
Training should be stopped entirely during menstruation
questions.answer_text: Current evidence does not support modifying prescription based on cycle phase
questions.explanation_en: Recent meta-analyses found no systematic relationship between cycle phase and performance, so current evidence does not support phase-based prescription changes.
tags: Chapter 8 quiz: Sex-Related Differences and Their Implications for Resistance Training

questions.question: A pregnant client in her second trimester wants to keep training core and upper body. Which modification is recommended as pregnancy advances?
options: Emphasize supine core work to support the spine
Routinely train above 90 percent of maximum heart rate
Avoid supine positions in favor of incline, side-lying, or vertical positions
questions.answer_text: Avoid supine positions in favor of incline, side-lying, or vertical positions
questions.explanation_en: Supine positions later in pregnancy reduce venous return and cardiac output, so incline, side-lying, or vertical positions are recommended instead.
tags: Chapter 8 quiz: Sex-Related Differences and Their Implications for Resistance Training

questions.question: A coach reviews pelvic health data for her female athletes. Compared with sedentary females, urinary incontinence in female athletes occurs at roughly what rate?
options: About 2.7 times more often
About half as often
At the same rate
questions.answer_text: About 2.7 times more often
questions.explanation_en: Urinary incontinence is reported about 2.7 times more often in female athletes than in sedentary females, and about 5 times more than in male athletes.
tags: Chapter 8 quiz: Sex-Related Differences and Their Implications for Resistance Training

questions.question: A return-to-play coordinator compares concussion outcomes between male and female athletes. How do female athletes' recovery patterns typically compare?
options: Shorter recovery with fewer symptoms
Longer recovery with more prolonged symptoms
Identical recovery across all sports
questions.answer_text: Longer recovery with more prolonged symptoms
questions.explanation_en: Female athletes tend to have longer recovery time and more prolonged symptoms after a concussion than males.
tags: Chapter 8 quiz: Sex-Related Differences and Their Implications for Resistance Training

questions.question: A sport organization reviews athlete mental health research to allocate support resources. What does the evidence suggest about elite female athletes and depression?
options: They report depression at about half the rate of male athletes
They show no difference in reported depression from male athletes
They are about twice as likely as male athletes to self-report depressive symptoms
questions.answer_text: They are about twice as likely as male athletes to self-report depressive symptoms
questions.explanation_en: Elite female athletes are about twice as likely to self-report depressive symptoms, and collegiate data show high rates of reported overwhelming anxiety.
tags: Chapter 8 quiz: Sex-Related Differences and Their Implications for Resistance Training

questions.question: A coach is deciding how to build a resistance program for a specific female athlete. Given everything known about sex-related differences, what should most govern the design?
options: Individualization to her specific needs, goals, and characteristics
Generalization based on typical demands of her sport
Matching her program to that of a comparable male teammate
questions.answer_text: Individualization to her specific needs, goals, and characteristics
questions.explanation_en: As with any athlete, individualization to the specific female athlete's needs is the most important design consideration.
tags: Chapter 8 quiz: Sex-Related Differences and Their Implications for Resistance Training

questions.question: A coach describes an athlete as being at a '3 out of 10' before a morning lift and a '9 out of 10' before a championship final, without judging either state as good or bad. The coach is describing which construct?
options: Arousal, a value-neutral level of physiological and psychological activation on a continuum
State anxiety, the athlete's moment-to-moment sense of threat
Anxiety, since a heightened pre-competition state involves worry
questions.answer_text: Arousal, a value-neutral level of physiological and psychological activation on a continuum
questions.explanation_en: Arousal is simply activation intensity, ranging from deep sleep to high excitement, and is not inherently pleasant or unpleasant.
tags: Chapter 9 quiz: Psychological Foundations of Performance

questions.question: An athlete reports a racing mind and pounding heart before a match and clearly perceives the feeling as unpleasant. How is this state best classified relative to arousal?
options: As arousal, which is itself one specific form of the broader category of anxiety
As anxiety, a negatively perceived subset of arousal with cognitive and somatic components
As a construct entirely separate from arousal and driven only by external threat
questions.answer_text: As anxiety, a negatively perceived subset of arousal with cognitive and somatic components
questions.explanation_en: Anxiety is a negatively perceived form of arousal that includes a cognitive component (worry) and a somatic component (physical symptoms).
tags: Chapter 9 quiz: Psychological Foundations of Performance

questions.question: An athlete reads threat into a wide range of unrelated situations year after year, on and off the field, regardless of the actual stakes. This enduring pattern reflects a high level of what?
options: Eustress, a facilitative interpretation of demanding situations
State anxiety, an intense reaction confined to a specific threatening moment
Trait anxiety, a stable personality disposition to perceive many situations as threatening
questions.answer_text: Trait anxiety, a stable personality disposition to perceive many situations as threatening
questions.explanation_en: Trait anxiety is a personality disposition, whereas state anxiety is the moment-to-moment experience of apprehension.
tags: Chapter 9 quiz: Psychological Foundations of Performance

questions.question: Right before the start gun, a sprinter notices tense muscles, a pounding heart, and a churning stomach, but no specific worried thoughts. Which component of anxiety is being reported?
options: Somatic anxiety, the physical and physiological manifestations of the state
Achievement motivation, the drive to master a challenging task
Cognitive anxiety, the worry and negative thoughts about performance
questions.answer_text: Somatic anxiety, the physical and physiological manifestations of the state
questions.explanation_en: Somatic anxiety is the physical reaction; cognitive anxiety refers to the mental worries and negative thoughts.
tags: Chapter 9 quiz: Psychological Foundations of Performance

questions.question: As an athlete's activation climbs from calm toward moderate, performance improves; but as it keeps rising past a certain point, performance falls off. Which explanation matches this pattern?
options: Drive theory, in which performance keeps rising as arousal rises
The inverted-U relationship, with performance peaking at a moderate, optimal level of arousal
Reversal theory, in which the effect of arousal depends on how it is interpreted
questions.answer_text: The inverted-U relationship, with performance peaking at a moderate, optimal level of arousal
questions.explanation_en: The inverted-U theory (Yerkes and Dodson) describes a curvilinear relationship with an optimal midpoint of arousal.
tags: Chapter 9 quiz: Psychological Foundations of Performance

questions.question: A coach claims that pumping athletes up more and more will always yield better and better performance. Which theory does this reasoning reflect, and what relationship does it assume?
options: Catastrophe theory, which assumes a sudden collapse once arousal passes a threshold
IZOF, which assumes an optimal bandwidth of functioning rather than a single trend
Drive theory, which assumes performance rises directly and linearly with arousal
questions.answer_text: Drive theory, which assumes performance rises directly and linearly with arousal
questions.explanation_en: Drive theory holds that as arousal increases, performance increases linearly, which is now seen as overly simplistic.
tags: Chapter 9 quiz: Psychological Foundations of Performance

questions.question: Two teammates perform their best at clearly different arousal levels, and neither peaks at the same intensity as the other. Which theory best accounts for this, and why?
options: IZOF, because ideal performance falls within an individualized bandwidth of arousal that differs by athlete
Drive theory, because within a sport the optimal arousal level is essentially identical for everyone
The inverted-U, because everyone peaks precisely at the exact midpoint of the arousal continuum
questions.answer_text: IZOF, because ideal performance falls within an individualized bandwidth of arousal that differs by athlete
questions.explanation_en: IZOF holds that ideal performance occurs within a small individualized range of arousal rather than at a single universal point.
tags: Chapter 9 quiz: Psychological Foundations of Performance

questions.question: Two athletes feel the same racing heart before a final; one calls it 'excitement' and thrives, the other calls it 'dread' and struggles. Which theory best explains why identical arousal produces opposite results?
options: Catastrophe theory, which stresses a sharp performance drop when cognitive anxiety is high
Reversal theory, which holds that the effect of arousal depends on how the individual interprets it
Drive theory, which holds that higher arousal directly raises performance
questions.answer_text: Reversal theory, which holds that the effect of arousal depends on how the individual interprets it
questions.explanation_en: Kerr's reversal theory emphasizes that one athlete may read high arousal as excitement while another reads it as anxiety.
tags: Chapter 9 quiz: Psychological Foundations of Performance

questions.question: A beginner is drilling a brand-new, coordination-heavy lift for the first time. Compared with an expert performing a well-learned skill, where should the beginner's optimal arousal generally sit, and why?
options: Higher, because a novice needs extra activation to compensate for weak technique
The same, because optimal arousal is set by the task and is unaffected by skill level
Lower, because worry competes for the attention the beginner still needs for motor details
questions.answer_text: Lower, because worry competes for the attention the beginner still needs for motor details
questions.explanation_en: Less skilled athletes have a lower optimal arousal point because worry competes with attention already occupied by motor details.
tags: Chapter 9 quiz: Psychological Foundations of Performance

questions.question: An athlete keeps training hard purely because she loves the sport and feels competent doing it, even after her scholarship and prize money were cut. This best illustrates what?
options: Intrinsic motivation, arising from within and tied to competence and self-determination
Negative reinforcement, which removes an aversive stimulus to sustain behavior
Extrinsic motivation, driven by tangible external rewards
questions.answer_text: Intrinsic motivation, arising from within and tied to competence and self-determination
questions.explanation_en: Intrinsic motivation comes from within and is tied to competence and self-determination rather than external rewards.
tags: Chapter 9 quiz: Psychological Foundations of Performance

questions.question: An athlete high in the motive to avoid failure repeatedly ducks challenging matchups and downplays effort. According to this construct, what is he fundamentally trying to escape?
options: Any external reward that might make the outcome feel less personal
The sense of shame and embarrassment that accompanies failing
Easy contests that offer little chance to demonstrate skill
questions.answer_text: The sense of shame and embarrassment that accompanies failing
questions.explanation_en: MAF is less about avoiding failure itself and more about avoiding the shame associated with failing.
tags: Chapter 9 quiz: Psychological Foundations of Performance

questions.question: After the team hustles hard in practice, the coach announces they can skip the dreaded conditioning sprints they normally run. Hustle increases going forward. This best illustrates which operant principle?
options: Positive reinforcement, adding a rewarding stimulus to increase a desired behavior
Positive punishment, adding an aversive consequence to reduce a behavior
Negative reinforcement, removing an aversive stimulus to increase a desired behavior
questions.answer_text: Negative reinforcement, removing an aversive stimulus to increase a desired behavior
questions.explanation_en: Negative reinforcement removes an aversive stimulus to increase the likelihood of a desired behavior.
tags: Chapter 9 quiz: Psychological Foundations of Performance

questions.question: A batter learns to tune out crowd noise and the scoreboard so he can lock onto the pitcher's release point. This deliberate filtering of task-irrelevant cues is called:
options: Selective attention, the suppression of task-irrelevant stimuli to process relevant cues
Counterconditioning, replacing one learned response with an incompatible one
Diaphragmatic breathing, a controlled technique for lowering arousal
questions.answer_text: Selective attention, the suppression of task-irrelevant stimuli to process relevant cues
questions.explanation_en: Selective attention, commonly called focus, filters out distractions within the limited capacity of working memory.
tags: Chapter 9 quiz: Psychological Foundations of Performance
