questions.question: In a PNF hamstring stretch, the athlete first contracts the hamstrings against resistance, and moments later that same muscle relaxes and lengthens further. The relaxation of the previously contracting muscle is termed:
options: Reciprocal inhibition, occurring in the opposing muscle group
Reciprocal inhibition, occurring in an unrelated stabilizing muscle
Autogenic inhibition, occurring in the same muscle that generated the tension
questions.answer_text: Autogenic inhibition, occurring in the same muscle that generated the tension
questions.explanation_en: Autogenic inhibition is relaxation occurring in the same muscle that built up tension, mediated by the GTO.
tags: Chapter 15 quiz: Performance Preparation, Mobility, and Flexibility

questions.question: To relax a tight hamstring during a stretch, an athlete actively contracts the quadriceps and the hamstring lets go, allowing greater range. This use of reciprocal inhibition works by contracting which muscle?
options: The quadriceps, the muscle opposing the one being stretched
Both the hamstring and quadriceps maximally at the same time
The hamstring itself, the muscle being passively stretched
questions.answer_text: The quadriceps, the muscle opposing the one being stretched
questions.explanation_en: Reciprocal inhibition results from contracting the muscle opposing the one being passively stretched, relaxing the stretched muscle.
tags: Chapter 15 quiz: Performance Preparation, Mobility, and Flexibility

questions.question: A coach wants the PNF variation that draws on both autogenic and reciprocal inhibition to maximize range-of-motion gains. Which technique should be selected?
options: Contract-relax, using a concentric contraction of the stretched muscle only
Hold-relax with agonist contraction, adding a contraction of the opposing muscle
Hold-relax, using a static contraction of the stretched muscle only
questions.answer_text: Hold-relax with agonist contraction, adding a contraction of the opposing muscle
questions.explanation_en: Hold-relax with agonist contraction is most effective because it uses both reciprocal and autogenic inhibition.
tags: Chapter 15 quiz: Performance Preparation, Mobility, and Flexibility

questions.question: An athlete asks how long to hold each position when doing static stretching to develop range of motion. What is the generally recommended hold duration per stretch?
options: About 60 to 90 seconds
About 1 to 5 seconds
About 10 to 30 seconds
questions.answer_text: About 10 to 30 seconds
questions.explanation_en: A static stretch is generally held for about 10 to 30 seconds; evidence supports holds around 30 seconds, with diminishing returns beyond that.
tags: Chapter 15 quiz: Performance Preparation, Mobility, and Flexibility

questions.question: Two athletes both stretch a tight muscle group, but one holds each stretch far longer per repetition while the other accumulates more stretching across the week. Regarding gains in range of motion, which factor is suggested to matter more than the length of any single stretch?
options: The total weekly stretching time and frequency
The specific time of day at which stretching is performed
The athlete's total body weight
questions.answer_text: The total weekly stretching time and frequency
questions.explanation_en: Evidence suggests weekly stretching time and frequency may matter more than the duration of any single stretch.
tags: Chapter 15 quiz: Performance Preparation, Mobility, and Flexibility

questions.question: A coach evaluates two athletes: one is notably stiff with restricted range, the other is extremely lax with joints that move well beyond normal limits. What is the correct view of how flexibility relates to injury risk?
options: More flexibility always lowers injury risk, so the lax athlete is the safer of the two
Both insufficient flexibility and excessive hyperflexibility can raise injury risk, so an activity-appropriate range is the goal
Flexibility bears no meaningful relationship to injury risk in either athlete
questions.answer_text: Both insufficient flexibility and excessive hyperflexibility can raise injury risk, so an activity-appropriate range is the goal
questions.explanation_en: Both inflexibility and hyperflexibility can raise injury risk; an optimal ROM for the activity is the goal.
tags: Chapter 15 quiz: Performance Preparation, Mobility, and Flexibility

questions.question: A lifter sets up for a barbell curl with the palms facing up and the knuckles pointing toward the floor. Which grip is being used?
options: A pronated, or overhand, grip
A supinated, or underhand, grip
A hook grip
questions.answer_text: A supinated, or underhand, grip
questions.explanation_en: The supinated, or underhand, grip has palms up and knuckles down.
tags: Chapter 16 quiz: Exercise Technique for Free Weight and Machine Training

questions.question: A weightlifter grips the bar overhand but then tucks the thumb against the bar first and wraps the index and middle fingers over the thumb to secure it. Compared with a standard pronated grip, what defines this hook grip?
options: One hand is supinated while the other is pronated
The palms are turned to face up rather than down
The thumb is positioned under the fingers against the bar
questions.answer_text: The thumb is positioned under the fingers against the bar
questions.explanation_en: The hook grip is like a pronated grip except the thumb is placed under the fingers to give a stronger grip.
tags: Chapter 16 quiz: Exercise Technique for Free Weight and Machine Training

questions.question: Preparing for a heavy deadlift, a lifter turns one palm to face backward and the other to face forward on the bar. This grip is best described as:
options: An alternated grip, with one hand pronated and the other supinated
A neutral grip, with both palms facing each other
A double hook grip, with both thumbs tucked under the fingers
questions.answer_text: An alternated grip, with one hand pronated and the other supinated
questions.explanation_en: In an alternated grip one hand is pronated and the other is supinated.
tags: Chapter 16 quiz: Exercise Technique for Free Weight and Machine Training

questions.question: A coach notices a lifter benching with the thumbs resting on the same side of the bar as the fingers rather than wrapped around it. What term describes this grip, and how does it differ from a closed grip?
options: It is a false grip, meaning the thumb is tucked under the fingers as in a hook grip
It is an open or false grip; a closed grip has the thumb wrapped around the bar while this one does not
It is a false grip that is defined by being wider than any closed grip
questions.answer_text: It is an open or false grip; a closed grip has the thumb wrapped around the bar while this one does not
questions.explanation_en: In a closed grip the thumb wraps around the bar; an open or false grip leaves the thumb off.
tags: Chapter 16 quiz: Exercise Technique for Free Weight and Machine Training

questions.question: A coach cues a lifter to establish the five-point body contact position before pressing on a bench. Which set of contact points is correct?
options: Head, both hands, and both feet
Shoulders, hips, both knees, and one foot
Head, shoulders and upper back, buttocks, right foot, and left foot
questions.answer_text: Head, shoulders and upper back, buttocks, right foot, and left foot
questions.explanation_en: The five points are the head, shoulders/upper back, buttocks, right foot, and left foot.
tags: Chapter 16 quiz: Exercise Technique for Free Weight and Machine Training

questions.question: A lifter grinds through the hardest part of a bench press rep. Following the standard breathing recommendation for most resistance exercises, when should the exhalation occur?
options: Through the sticking point of the concentric phase
Only while briefly holding the breath at the top of the movement
During the eccentric, lowering phase as the bar descends
questions.answer_text: Through the sticking point of the concentric phase
questions.explanation_en: Athletes should typically exhale through the sticking point of the concentric phase and inhale during the less stressful phase.
tags: Chapter 16 quiz: Exercise Technique for Free Weight and Machine Training

questions.question: An experienced lifter briefly braces before a maximal squat, and a coach explains that the resulting rigid trunk helps support the spine. Which action produces this bracing effect?
options: Rapid, shallow breathing maintained throughout the lift
Expiring against a closed glottis so the trunk musculature creates rigid compartments
Inhaling fully and simply holding that air for the entire set
questions.answer_text: Expiring against a closed glottis so the trunk musculature creates rigid compartments
questions.explanation_en: The Valsalva maneuver is expiring against a closed glottis, which with abdominal and rib cage muscle action stiffens the torso to support the spine.
tags: Chapter 16 quiz: Exercise Technique for Free Weight and Machine Training

questions.question: A lifter uses the Valsalva maneuver on a heavy squat. Because of its effect on blood pressure, what precaution governs how long the breath-holding phase should last?
options: It should be released and re-applied several times within a single rep
It should extend across the entire repetition from start to finish
It should be quite transient, lasting only about 1 to 2 seconds at most
questions.answer_text: It should be quite transient, lasting only about 1 to 2 seconds at most
questions.explanation_en: Because blood pressure can rise sharply, the breath-holding phase should be transient, only about 1 to 2 seconds at most.
tags: Chapter 16 quiz: Exercise Technique for Free Weight and Machine Training

questions.question: A coach must decide when to have an athlete wear a weight belt. For which of the following is a belt most clearly appropriate?
options: A back squat or deadlift performed with a near-maximal or maximal load
A lat pulldown performed with a light load
A standing biceps curl with a moderate load
questions.answer_text: A back squat or deadlift performed with a near-maximal or maximal load
questions.explanation_en: A weight belt is recommended for exercises stressing the lower back performed with near-maximal or maximal loads.
tags: Chapter 16 quiz: Exercise Technique for Free Weight and Machine Training

questions.question: An athlete wears a weight belt for nearly every set of every session, including light accessory work. What is the main drawback of relying on the belt this heavily?
options: It raises the likelihood of losing control of and dropping the bar
It reduces the training stimulus to the abdominal and lower back musculature over time
It makes performing the Valsalva maneuver impossible during the lift
questions.answer_text: It reduces the training stimulus to the abdominal and lower back musculature over time
questions.explanation_en: Overusing a belt reduces the training stimulus to the abdominal and lower back muscles.
tags: Chapter 16 quiz: Exercise Technique for Free Weight and Machine Training

questions.question: A coach reviews which lifts in a session require an over-the-bar spotter and which do not. For which exercise should the athlete NOT be spotted, and instead be taught to miss safely?
options: The barbell bench press
The back squat
The power clean
questions.answer_text: The power clean
questions.explanation_en: Power exercises are not spotted; instead athletes are taught how to safely miss and get away from the bar.
tags: Chapter 16 quiz: Exercise Technique for Free Weight and Machine Training

questions.question: A spotter prepares to assist a lifter on a barbell exercise where the bar travels over the face, such as a lying triceps extension. Which grip should the spotter use on the bar?
options: A closed, alternated grip, usually placed narrower than and inside the athlete's grip
A pronated grip positioned wider than the athlete's hands
A supinated grip placed outside the athlete's hands
questions.answer_text: A closed, alternated grip, usually placed narrower than and inside the athlete's grip
questions.explanation_en: Over-the-face barbell exercises are spotted with an alternated grip, usually narrower than and inside the athlete's grip.
tags: Chapter 16 quiz: Exercise Technique for Free Weight and Machine Training

questions.question: A spotter assists a lifter performing heavy dumbbell chest presses. To keep the athlete safest if the elbows begin to collapse, where should the spotter apply support?
options: At the athlete's elbows or upper arms
At the forearms, close to the wrists
Directly beneath the athlete's chest under the dumbbells
questions.answer_text: At the forearms, close to the wrists
questions.explanation_en: Spotting at the forearms near the wrists is safer; spotting at the elbows risks the dumbbells striking the athlete if the elbows collapse.
tags: Chapter 16 quiz: Exercise Technique for Free Weight and Machine Training

questions.question: A load is light enough that one competent spotter can handle it safely. Why is using that single spotter often preferred over recruiting two or more?
options: Regulations prohibit two people from spotting the same lift together
A single spotter is inherently stronger than any pair of spotters
Adding spotters means coordinating timing, which increases the chance of a spotting error
questions.answer_text: Adding spotters means coordinating timing, which increases the chance of a spotting error
questions.explanation_en: As the number of spotters increases, so does the chance of a timing or technique error, so one is preferred when feasible.
tags: Chapter 16 quiz: Exercise Technique for Free Weight and Machine Training

questions.question: Before a bench press, a spotter helps move the loaded bar out of the uprights and into position over the lifter's chest so the set can begin. This action is referred to as:
options: A liftoff, moving the bar from the upright supports to the athlete's start position
Reaching the peak of the concentric phase of the lift
The athlete jumping clear of a missed bar
questions.answer_text: A liftoff, moving the bar from the upright supports to the athlete's start position
questions.explanation_en: A liftoff is moving the bar from the upright supports into the position where the athlete begins the exercise.
tags: Chapter 16 quiz: Exercise Technique for Free Weight and Machine Training

questions.question: A lifter sets up a back squat with the bar carried in the high bar position. Where does the bar sit and how wide is the grip?
options: On the anterior deltoids and clavicles, with a narrow grip
Above the posterior deltoids at the base of the neck, with a grip only slightly wider than shoulder width
Across the posterior deltoids at the mid-trapezius, with a wide grip
questions.answer_text: Above the posterior deltoids at the base of the neck, with a grip only slightly wider than shoulder width
questions.explanation_en: High bar position places the bar above the posterior deltoids at the base of the neck with a grip only slightly wider than shoulder width.
tags: Chapter 16 quiz: Exercise Technique for Free Weight and Machine Training

questions.question: During the upward phase of a deadlift, a coach watches the lifter's hips shoot up faster than the shoulders, so the bar drifts and the back rounds. Which cue corrects this fault?
options: Allow the bar to travel forward, away from the shins, as it rises
Deliberately let the hips rise ahead of the shoulders to clear the bar path
Keep the torso-to-floor angle constant so the hips and shoulders rise together
questions.answer_text: Keep the torso-to-floor angle constant so the hips and shoulders rise together
questions.explanation_en: The deadlift requires keeping the torso-to-floor angle constant so the hips do not rise before the shoulders.
tags: Chapter 16 quiz: Exercise Technique for Free Weight and Machine Training

questions.question: A lifter transitions from back squats to front squats and must reposition the bar. Where is the bar racked for the front squat?
options: On top of the anterior deltoids and clavicles, using a parallel-arm or crossed-arm hold
Across the posterior deltoids on the upper back, as in a back squat
In the crease of the flexed elbows in front of the body
questions.answer_text: On top of the anterior deltoids and clavicles, using a parallel-arm or crossed-arm hold
questions.explanation_en: The front squat racks the bar on the anterior deltoids and clavicles using either a parallel-arm or crossed-arm position.
tags: Chapter 16 quiz: Exercise Technique for Free Weight and Machine Training

questions.question: A lifter performing good mornings bends the knees deeply and drops into a squat-like pattern, and the coach flags this as a common technique error. What movement pattern should the good morning actually be?
options: An overhead pressing movement of the loaded bar
A hip hinge in which the buttocks travel straight back with minimal knee flexion
A deep, knee-dominant squat driven by bending the knees
questions.answer_text: A hip hinge in which the buttocks travel straight back with minimal knee flexion
questions.explanation_en: The good morning is a hip hinge; flexing the knees too much turns it into a squat, which is a common error.
tags: Chapter 16 quiz: Exercise Technique for Free Weight and Machine Training

questions.question: A coach breaks down the power clean from the floor into its constituent phases for a new athlete. Which sequence correctly lists those phases in order?
options: Setup, press, lockout, then lower
Dip, drive, catch, then recovery
First pull, transition, second pull, then catch
questions.answer_text: First pull, transition, second pull, then catch
questions.explanation_en: The power clean consists of the first pull, transition, second pull, and catch, performed in one continuous motion.
tags: Chapter 16 quiz: Exercise Technique for Free Weight and Machine Training

questions.question: A strength coach notices an experienced athlete briefly holding his breath while grinding out the final rep of a heavy squat set. Under the general guidelines for these training methods, how should the coach evaluate this breathing pattern?
options: It is appropriate only during the eccentric phase of light single-joint exercises
It is a technique fault that should be corrected on every rep of any bodyweight movement
It is a reasonable, often unavoidable technique with heavy loads at or above 80 percent of maximal voluntary contraction or with lighter loads taken to failure
questions.answer_text: It is a reasonable, often unavoidable technique with heavy loads at or above 80 percent of maximal voluntary contraction or with lighter loads taken to failure
questions.explanation_en: The Valsalva maneuver helps maintain spinal stability and may be unavoidable at loads at or above 80 percent of maximal voluntary contraction or with lighter loads taken to failure.
tags: Chapter 17 quiz: Exercise Technique for Alternative Modes and Nontraditional Implement Training

questions.question: A lean, well-conditioned gymnast performs high volumes of push-ups, pull-ups, and dips but has plateaued in raw force production. What best explains why this style of training does little to advance absolute strength?
options: The external resistance can never exceed the individual's own body weight
The movements demand specialized equipment that most athletes lack
The movements are open-chain and isolate single joints, limiting overload
questions.answer_text: The external resistance can never exceed the individual's own body weight
questions.explanation_en: Because the resistance is capped at the individual's body weight, bodyweight training develops relative strength but does little for absolute strength.
tags: Chapter 17 quiz: Exercise Technique for Alternative Modes and Nontraditional Implement Training

questions.question: During a suspension-trainer row, an athlete wants to reduce the challenge of the exercise mid-set without changing the anchor or the device. What adjustment of the center of mass relative to the anchor point will accomplish this?
options: Adjust the strap length, because body position does not change the load
Shift the center of mass farther from the anchor point
Shift the center of mass closer to the anchor point
questions.answer_text: Shift the center of mass farther from the anchor point
questions.explanation_en: Generally, as the athlete's center of mass moves farther from the anchor point, the resistance to which the athlete is exposed decreases.
tags: Chapter 17 quiz: Exercise Technique for Alternative Modes and Nontraditional Implement Training

questions.question: When explaining what the anatomical core actually encompasses, which description is most complete and accurate?
options: The pelvic and shoulder girdles that link the axial and appendicular skeletons
The abdominal wall musculature, chiefly the rectus abdominis and obliques
The axial skeleton plus all soft tissues with proximal attachments originating on the axial skeleton
questions.answer_text: The axial skeleton plus all soft tissues with proximal attachments originating on the axial skeleton
questions.explanation_en: The anatomical core is defined as the axial skeleton plus all the soft tissues with proximal attachments that originate on the axial skeleton.
tags: Chapter 17 quiz: Exercise Technique for Alternative Modes and Nontraditional Implement Training

questions.question: A coach is deciding whether to add dedicated isolation core drills for an athlete who already squats and deadlifts heavy from the floor. What does the evidence suggest about core recruitment during those free weight lifts?
options: It is similar to, and in most cases greater than, that of traditional isolation core drills
It is negligible, since only isolation drills meaningfully recruit the core
It is far lower than in isolation core drills, so the added drills are essential
questions.answer_text: It is similar to, and in most cases greater than, that of traditional isolation core drills
questions.explanation_en: Ground-based free weight activities offer core activation that is similar to, or in most cases greater than, that seen with traditional isolation core exercises.
tags: Chapter 17 quiz: Exercise Technique for Alternative Modes and Nontraditional Implement Training

questions.question: A healthy, resistance-trained athlete asks whether performing squats on a wobble board or stability platform will boost his power output. What does the evidence indicate for this population?
options: The instability maximizes force and power output over stable-surface lifting
The instability mutes performance gains and lowers force, power, and rate of force development
The instability is necessary to build the sport-specific core stability he needs
questions.answer_text: The instability mutes performance gains and lowers force, power, and rate of force development
questions.explanation_en: Training on unstable devices reduces force, power, and rate of force development and produces muted performance improvements compared with stable free weight training.
tags: Chapter 17 quiz: Exercise Technique for Alternative Modes and Nontraditional Implement Training

questions.question: An athlete drapes heavy chains over a loaded barbell for the back squat. As he descends and the chain links accumulate on the floor, how does the total resistance behave, and where is it lowest?
options: Resistance stays essentially constant because the chains simply hang from the bar
Resistance is lowest at lockout, where the bar is farthest from the floor
Resistance is lowest at the bottom, where the links pile on the floor and unload the bar
questions.answer_text: Resistance is lowest at the bottom, where the links pile on the floor and unload the bar
questions.explanation_en: At the bottom of the movement the chain links pile on the floor, reducing the load and allowing the athlete to accelerate the bar.
tags: Chapter 17 quiz: Exercise Technique for Alternative Modes and Nontraditional Implement Training

questions.question: A coach measures that a band adds 20 lb of resistance at the bottom and 60 lb at the top of a bench press, and wants a target bar-plus-band load of 200 lb. How should the fixed plate load on the bar be determined?
options: Load the bar to the target minus the average of the top and bottom resistances
Load the bar to the target minus the sum of the top and bottom resistances
Load the bar to the target minus only the top-position resistance
questions.answer_text: Load the bar to the target minus the average of the top and bottom resistances
questions.explanation_en: The absolute resistances at the top and bottom are summed and averaged, and that average is subtracted from the target load on the bar.
tags: Chapter 17 quiz: Exercise Technique for Alternative Modes and Nontraditional Implement Training

questions.question: Two athletes use the same resistance band, but one anchors it so it is stretched much farther at the start position. Applying Hooke's law, what primarily governs the difference in band tension they experience?
options: The manufacturer's color coding of the band
The band's stiffness multiplied by how far it is deformed (stretched)
The body weight each athlete brings to the movement
questions.answer_text: The band's stiffness multiplied by how far it is deformed (stretched)
questions.explanation_en: Band tension equals stiffness (k) multiplied by deformation (d), so tension rises as the band is stretched farther.
tags: Chapter 17 quiz: Exercise Technique for Alternative Modes and Nontraditional Implement Training

questions.question: Accentuated eccentric loading applies extra load only during the lowering phase and removes it before the lift. Which property of muscle action does this method specifically capitalize on?
options: Eccentric and concentric maximal force are essentially equal across the range
Muscles are weaker eccentrically than concentrically, so lowering is the limiting phase
Muscles generate more force eccentrically than concentrically, so a constant load leaves the eccentric phase underloaded
questions.answer_text: Muscles generate more force eccentrically than concentrically, so a constant load leaves the eccentric phase underloaded
questions.explanation_en: Muscles are stronger eccentrically than concentrically, so a constant load underloads the eccentric phase, which AEL addresses by adding load only during lowering.
tags: Chapter 17 quiz: Exercise Technique for Alternative Modes and Nontraditional Implement Training

questions.question: A coach is considering which of three lifters is the best candidate for accentuated eccentric loading. For whom is this method generally most appropriate?
options: A lifter with extensive resistance training experience and a strong strength base
An athlete in the early return-to-play phase of rehabilitation
A novice still learning basic lifting technique
questions.answer_text: A lifter with extensive resistance training experience and a strong strength base
questions.explanation_en: AEL is an advanced training tactic that should be reserved for athletes with extensive resistance training experience and adequate strength.
tags: Chapter 17 quiz: Exercise Technique for Alternative Modes and Nontraditional Implement Training

questions.question: A coach wants to use accentuated eccentric loading to potentiate the concentric phase of a countermovement jump, releasing the added load before takeoff. What eccentric load, expressed as a percentage of body mass, is recommended?
options: About 5 to 10 percent of body mass
About 20 to 30 percent of body mass
About 50 to 60 percent of body mass
questions.answer_text: About 20 to 30 percent of body mass
questions.explanation_en: Loads of 20 to 30 percent of body mass applied eccentrically and released before the concentric phase improve plyometric jump performance.
tags: Chapter 17 quiz: Exercise Technique for Alternative Modes and Nontraditional Implement Training

questions.question: An athlete using the shoulders-against-the-tire flip technique keeps rounding his back and stalling at the start. The coach sees his feet are jammed up against the tire. What is the correct fix?
options: Keep the feet close but round the back further to shorten the lever to the tire
Pull the tire straight upward rather than driving the hips and chest forward
Move the feet back from the tire and drive through a forceful triple extension to raise the chest and tire
questions.answer_text: Move the feet back from the tire and drive through a forceful triple extension to raise the chest and tire
questions.explanation_en: Placing the feet too close forces a rounded back; the correction is to move the feet back and use a forceful triple extension to raise the chest and tire off the ground.
tags: Chapter 17 quiz: Exercise Technique for Alternative Modes and Nontraditional Implement Training

questions.question: Research compared the log lift with the barbell clean and jerk. Given the log's larger diameter, which pattern of differences was actually observed?
options: The log produced greater impulse and hip and trunk range of motion but lower vertical velocity and power
The two lifts were statistically indistinguishable across all measured variables
The log produced greater vertical bar velocity and greater power output
questions.answer_text: The log produced greater impulse and hip and trunk range of motion but lower vertical velocity and power
questions.explanation_en: The log lift produced significantly greater impulse and hip and trunk range of motion but less vertical velocity and power, reflecting the greater diameter of the log.
tags: Chapter 17 quiz: Exercise Technique for Alternative Modes and Nontraditional Implement Training

questions.question: A coach adds farmer's walks and yoke walks to a program. What is the primary training adaptation these loaded carries are chosen to develop?
options: Isolated hypertrophy of a single small muscle group
Total body and trunk stability, with high anterior-posterior and vertical impulse demands
Cardiovascular endurance with essentially no strength or stability demand
questions.answer_text: Total body and trunk stability, with high anterior-posterior and vertical impulse demands
questions.explanation_en: Weighted carries develop total body and trunk stability, grip strength, and the ability to produce high anterior-posterior and vertical impulse.
tags: Chapter 17 quiz: Exercise Technique for Alternative Modes and Nontraditional Implement Training

questions.question: An athlete wants to replace his barbell work with kettlebell swings and cleans to build maximal strength and vertical jump. How should the coach frame kettlebell training relative to traditional weightlifting?
options: The two approaches produce equivalent maximal strength and jump adaptations
Kettlebells outperform traditional weightlifting for both maximal strength and jumping
Kettlebells yield smaller gains, so they suit general preparation while traditional weightlifting drives strength and jumping
questions.answer_text: Kettlebells yield smaller gains, so they suit general preparation while traditional weightlifting drives strength and jumping
questions.explanation_en: Kettlebell training increases strength and jump performance less than traditional weightlifting, so kettlebells are best used as general preparation exercise.
tags: Chapter 17 quiz: Exercise Technique for Alternative Modes and Nontraditional Implement Training

questions.question: As an athlete walks a loaded yoke across the floor, the coach cues spinal posture. Which position should be maintained throughout the carry?
options: A predominantly neutral, vertical spine with no substantial hyperextension, flexion, or lateral flexion
A deliberately hyperextended spine to increase bracing against the load
A spine laterally flexed toward the side bearing more of the load
questions.answer_text: A predominantly neutral, vertical spine with no substantial hyperextension, flexion, or lateral flexion
questions.explanation_en: The athlete should keep a predominantly neutral and vertical spine with no substantial hyperextension, flexion, or lateral flexion while carrying.
tags: Chapter 17 quiz: Exercise Technique for Alternative Modes and Nontraditional Implement Training

questions.question: A coach observes that the sum of an athlete's separate single-leg press outputs exceeds his two-leg press output. This bilateral deficit is most characteristic of which type of individual, who may therefore gain from unilateral training?
options: Highly trained, stronger athletes
Untrained, weaker, or injured individuals
Elite powerlifters exclusively
questions.answer_text: Untrained, weaker, or injured individuals
questions.explanation_en: Untrained, weaker, or injured athletes tend to show a bilateral deficit, so unilateral methods may be useful for their strength development.
tags: Chapter 17 quiz: Exercise Technique for Alternative Modes and Nontraditional Implement Training

questions.question: A coach anchors one end of a barbell in a pivoting floor sleeve and loads the free end. What kind of training is this landmine setup primarily suited to deliver?
options: Pure aerobic endurance conditioning
Maximal isometric holds against a fixed bar
Loaded rotational and multiplanar resistance exercises using the bar as a lever
questions.answer_text: Loaded rotational and multiplanar resistance exercises using the bar as a lever
questions.explanation_en: The landmine anchors one end of a barbell through a pivot so it can be used as a lever for loaded rotational and multiplanar movements.
tags: Chapter 17 quiz: Exercise Technique for Alternative Modes and Nontraditional Implement Training

questions.question: A sprint coach wants to use heavy sled pulls to potentiate a subsequent 15 m sprint (a PAPE effect). What loading range, expressed as a percentage of body mass, does research associate with that effect?
options: About 66 to 75 percent of body mass
About 150 to 200 percent of body mass
About 10 to 20 percent of body mass
questions.answer_text: About 66 to 75 percent of body mass
questions.explanation_en: Sled pulls with loads between roughly 66 and 75 percent of body mass had the potential to produce 15-meter sprint PAPE effects in running athletes.
tags: Chapter 17 quiz: Exercise Technique for Alternative Modes and Nontraditional Implement Training

questions.question: Before writing a resistance training program, a coach first studies the movement patterns, injury sites, and physiological demands of the sport, then evaluates the individual athlete's training age, test results, and goals. These two activities make up which process, and in what order?
options: Evaluating the sport, then assessing the athlete
Setting session frequency, then ordering exercises
Selecting exercises, then assigning loads
questions.answer_text: Evaluating the sport, then assessing the athlete
questions.explanation_en: A needs analysis evaluates the requirements and characteristics of the sport and then assesses the individual athlete's status and goals.
tags: Chapter 18 quiz: Program Design for Resistance Training

questions.question: A coach explains that if an athlete trains slowly with heavy loads, he adapts toward strength rather than speed. This idea, closely tied to specificity, is captured by the acronym SAID, which stands for what?
options: Strength and intensity development
Specific adaptation to imposed demands
Sets and intervals during deloads
questions.answer_text: Specific adaptation to imposed demands
questions.explanation_en: SAID means specific adaptation to imposed demands: the type of demand placed on the body dictates the adaptation that occurs.
tags: Chapter 18 quiz: Program Design for Resistance Training

questions.question: An athlete has adapted to his current program and stops progressing, so the coach increases the load beyond what the athlete is accustomed to in order to drive new adaptation. Which training principle is the coach applying?
options: Individualization
Reversibility
Overload
questions.answer_text: Overload
questions.explanation_en: Overload is applying a stimulus beyond the athlete's accustomed level to produce adaptation past baseline abilities.
tags: Chapter 18 quiz: Program Design for Resistance Training

questions.question: A coach wants to prioritize the exercises with the greatest carryover for a team sport. Which combination of features identifies an exercise as a core (rather than assistance) exercise?
options: One or more large muscle areas acting across two or more primary joints
An isometric hold that stabilizes the trunk without joint movement
A small muscle area acting across a single primary joint
questions.answer_text: One or more large muscle areas acting across two or more primary joints
questions.explanation_en: Core exercises recruit one or more large muscle areas and involve two or more primary joints, giving them priority in selection.
tags: Chapter 18 quiz: Program Design for Resistance Training

questions.question: An exercise loads the spine directly and is performed explosively, such as a power clean. Within the exercise classification scheme, how is it best categorized?
options: An assistance exercise
A power exercise
A muscular endurance exercise
questions.answer_text: A power exercise
questions.explanation_en: A structural exercise that is performed very quickly or explosively is considered a power exercise.
tags: Chapter 18 quiz: Program Design for Resistance Training

questions.question: A coach is setting weekly training frequency for a highly experienced athlete in a demanding phase. What resistance training frequency is appropriate for this advanced level?
options: 2 to 3 sessions per week
3 to 4 sessions per week
4 to 7 sessions per week, potentially with multiple sessions in a day
questions.answer_text: 4 to 7 sessions per week, potentially with multiple sessions in a day
questions.explanation_en: Advanced athletes can train 4 to 7 times per week and may include multiple sessions per day depending on the phase.
tags: Chapter 18 quiz: Program Design for Resistance Training

questions.question: A session includes power cleans, back squats, and biceps curls. Because the cleans are the most skill- and fatigue-sensitive, where in the order should they be placed?
options: First, while the athlete is still fresh and unfatigued
In the middle, after the assistance work is done
Last, to finish the session on a high-intensity note
questions.answer_text: First, while the athlete is still fresh and unfatigued
questions.explanation_en: Power exercises require high skill and are prone to fatigue, so they are performed first while the athlete is fresh, then other core, then assistance.
tags: Chapter 18 quiz: Program Design for Resistance Training

questions.question: A coach sequences a bench press immediately followed by a bent-over row, then a shoulder press followed by a lat pulldown. What is the main rationale for this push-pull arrangement?
options: It improves the accuracy of one-repetition-maximum testing
It avoids using the same muscle group in two consecutive exercises, limiting fatigue there
It removes the need to schedule rest periods between sets
questions.answer_text: It avoids using the same muscle group in two consecutive exercises, limiting fatigue there
questions.explanation_en: A push-pull arrangement keeps the same muscle group from being used in two exercises in a row, reducing fatigue in those muscles.
tags: Chapter 18 quiz: Program Design for Resistance Training

questions.question: An athlete finishes a set of barbell biceps curls and, with no other exercise between, immediately performs hammer curls for the same muscle group. Which term describes this pairing?
options: Circuit training
A superset
A compound set
questions.answer_text: A compound set
questions.explanation_en: A compound set sequentially performs two different exercises for the same muscle group; a superset instead pairs an agonist and its antagonist.
tags: Chapter 18 quiz: Program Design for Resistance Training

questions.question: A coach wants to estimate a load from a rep max using the percent-1RM-to-reps relationship as reliably as possible. Under which condition is that relationship most accurate?
options: Loads greater than 75 percent of the 1RM for fewer than 10 repetitions
Any load, since the relationship holds equally across the whole range
Loads under 50 percent of the 1RM for more than 20 repetitions
questions.answer_text: Loads greater than 75 percent of the 1RM for fewer than 10 repetitions
questions.explanation_en: The relationship is most accurate for loads greater than 75 percent of the 1RM and fewer than 10 repetitions, improving further at lower reps.
tags: Chapter 18 quiz: Program Design for Resistance Training

questions.question: A coach programs a core exercise with the goal of maximizing maximal strength. Which load and repetition prescription fits that goal?
options: Less than 67 percent of the 1RM for 12 or more repetitions
At least 85 percent of the 1RM for 6 or fewer repetitions
67 to 80 percent of the 1RM for 8 to 12 repetitions
questions.answer_text: At least 85 percent of the 1RM for 6 or fewer repetitions
questions.explanation_en: Strength training in core exercises uses loads at or above 85 percent of the 1RM for 6 or fewer repetitions.
tags: Chapter 18 quiz: Program Design for Resistance Training

questions.question: A coach designing a block aimed primarily at muscle cross-sectional growth consults the standard load-repetition assignments. Which prescription targets hypertrophy?
options: Less than 67 percent of the 1RM for 12 or more repetitions
At least 85 percent of the 1RM for 6 or fewer repetitions
67 to 80 percent of the 1RM for 8 to 12 repetitions
questions.answer_text: 67 to 80 percent of the 1RM for 8 to 12 repetitions
questions.explanation_en: The table assigns roughly 67 to 80 percent of the 1RM for 8 to 12 repetitions to target hypertrophy, though a wide load range can work to failure.
tags: Chapter 18 quiz: Program Design for Resistance Training

questions.question: A coach wants an athlete to improve the ability to sustain repeated submaximal contractions. Which load and repetition prescription targets muscular endurance?
options: 67 percent of the 1RM or less for 12 or more repetitions
At least 85 percent of the 1RM for 6 or fewer repetitions
67 to 80 percent of the 1RM for 8 to 12 repetitions
questions.answer_text: 67 percent of the 1RM or less for 12 or more repetitions
questions.explanation_en: Muscular endurance training uses lighter loads at or below 67 percent of the 1RM for 12 or more repetitions per set.
tags: Chapter 18 quiz: Program Design for Resistance Training

questions.question: A coach is prescribing loads for single-joint assistance work like biceps curls and calf raises, aiming to limit isolative stress on the joint and connective tissue. What is the heaviest load these exercises should be assigned?
options: No heavier than a 2RM
No heavier than an 8RM
No heavier than a 15RM
questions.answer_text: No heavier than an 8RM
questions.explanation_en: Assistance exercises should be limited to loads no heavier than an 8RM to minimize isolative stress on the involved joint and connective tissue.
tags: Chapter 18 quiz: Program Design for Resistance Training

questions.question: An athlete's goal is 8 reps in his last set. He completes 10 reps in that set on Monday and 10 again on Wednesday. Applying the 2-for-2 rule, what should the coach do?
options: Increase the load after every workout regardless of how many reps he completes
Wait until he fails a repetition before making any load change
Increase the load, since he beat the goal by 2 or more reps on the last set for two consecutive workouts
questions.answer_text: Increase the load, since he beat the goal by 2 or more reps on the last set for two consecutive workouts
questions.explanation_en: The 2-for-2 rule adds load when the athlete completes 2 or more reps above the goal in the last set across two consecutive sessions.
tags: Chapter 18 quiz: Program Design for Resistance Training

questions.question: A coach programs strength work for a volleyball blocker, whose sport demands repeated maximal-effort jumps. For this multiple-effort power event, which loading is most appropriate?
options: 3 to 5 repetitions at 75 to 85 percent of the 1RM
12 or more repetitions at 50 percent of the 1RM
1 to 2 repetitions at 80 to 90 percent of the 1RM
questions.answer_text: 3 to 5 repetitions at 75 to 85 percent of the 1RM
questions.explanation_en: Multiple-effort power events use about 3 to 5 reps per set with loads of 75 to 85 percent of the 1RM.
tags: Chapter 18 quiz: Program Design for Resistance Training

questions.question: A coach assigns power cleans at a lighter load than the percent-1RM-to-rep relationship would predict for the target reps. What is the reasoning behind using the lighter load?
options: Heavy loads are considered unsafe for any athlete performing this lift
A lighter load lets the athlete move at maximum speed to develop power, because technique breaks down before true muscle failure
The lift is being programmed to build muscular endurance rather than power
questions.answer_text: A lighter load lets the athlete move at maximum speed to develop power, because technique breaks down before true muscle failure
questions.explanation_en: Power exercises cannot be maximally loaded because technique deteriorates before muscle failure, so lighter loads allow maximum-speed reps to develop power.
tags: Chapter 18 quiz: Program Design for Resistance Training

questions.question: An athlete performs 3 sets of 10 repetitions with 100 lb on the back squat. Using the standard definition, what is the volume-load for that exercise, and how is it derived?
options: The repetitions divided by the length of the rest period
The load divided by the number of sets performed
3,000 lb, from sets multiplied by repetitions multiplied by the load lifted
questions.answer_text: 3,000 lb, from sets multiplied by repetitions multiplied by the load lifted
questions.explanation_en: Volume-load is the total sets times reps times the load; 3 sets of 10 reps with 100 pounds equals 3,000 pounds.
tags: Chapter 18 quiz: Program Design for Resistance Training

questions.question: A coach building a hypertrophy-focused program wants an appropriate per-exercise set volume. Which number of sets is generally recommended for hypertrophy?
options: 3 to 6 sets per exercise
A minimum of 8 to 10 sets per exercise
1 set per exercise
questions.answer_text: 3 to 6 sets per exercise
questions.explanation_en: Hypertrophy is associated with higher volumes, commonly a moderate to high rep range with about 3 to 6 sets per exercise.
tags: Chapter 18 quiz: Program Design for Resistance Training

questions.question: A coach programming heavy strength and power work wants rest periods long enough to preserve load and technique across sets. What rest interval is recommended for strength or power training?
options: 60 to 90 seconds between sets
2 to 5 minutes between sets
30 seconds or less between sets
questions.answer_text: 2 to 5 minutes between sets
questions.explanation_en: Strength and power training uses 2 to 5 minute rest periods to permit greater work volume, heavier loads, and better adaptations.
tags: Chapter 18 quiz: Program Design for Resistance Training

questions.question: A coach wants a single training goal statement that captures what a plyometric exercise is actually built to develop. Which statement best fits?
options: Progressively lengthening tissue to expand joint range of motion through held end-range positions
Producing the greatest possible force in the least possible time by exploiting a rapid prestretch
Accumulating the most total mechanical work across a prolonged set to build work capacity
questions.answer_text: Producing the greatest possible force in the least possible time by exploiting a rapid prestretch
questions.explanation_en: Plyometric exercise is defined as a quick, powerful movement using a prestretch to reach maximal force in minimal time.
tags: Chapter 19 quiz: Program Design and Technique for Plyometric Training

questions.question: An athlete performs a fast rebound and much of the propulsion seems to come from stored elastic energy rather than fresh contractile effort. In the mechanical model of plyometrics, which structure is chiefly responsible for storing and returning that energy?
options: The Golgi tendon organ acting to recapture and release load
The parallel elastic component formed by the surrounding connective sheaths
The series elastic component, made up largely of tendon, behaving like a spring
questions.answer_text: The series elastic component, made up largely of tendon, behaving like a spring
questions.explanation_en: The series elastic component, made up largely of tendon, acts like a spring that stores and releases elastic energy.
tags: Chapter 19 quiz: Program Design and Technique for Plyometric Training

questions.question: Two athletes land and rebound; the one who rebounds faster shows a burst of reflexive muscle activity triggered by the rapid stretch. In the neurophysiological model, this potentiation is attributed mainly to which mechanism?
options: The stretch reflex driven by muscle spindles sensitive to rate and magnitude of stretch
A surge in anaerobic glycolytic energy supply meeting the sudden demand
Golgi tendon organ inhibition reducing tension to protect the tendon
questions.answer_text: The stretch reflex driven by muscle spindles sensitive to rate and magnitude of stretch
questions.explanation_en: The stretch reflex, mediated by muscle spindles sensitive to the rate and magnitude of stretch, reflexively increases muscle activity.
tags: Chapter 19 quiz: Program Design and Technique for Plyometric Training

questions.question: A coach is teaching a depth jump and wants to name the three phases in the exact order the athlete experiences them from box contact to takeoff. Which ordering is correct?
options: Concentric shortening, then amortization, then eccentric loading
Eccentric loading, then amortization, then concentric shortening
Amortization, then eccentric loading, then concentric shortening
questions.answer_text: Eccentric loading, then amortization, then concentric shortening
questions.explanation_en: The SSC proceeds eccentric (stretch), amortization (coupling pause), then concentric (shortening).
tags: Chapter 19 quiz: Program Design and Technique for Plyometric Training

questions.question: An athlete pauses noticeably on the ground between the landing and the jump. Why does coaching a shorter transition improve the outcome?
options: It lengthens ground contact so more total force can be applied against the surface
It lets the athlete recover more fully between repetitions before exploding upward
A prolonged transition dissipates stored elastic energy as heat and blunts the stretch reflex contribution
questions.answer_text: A prolonged transition dissipates stored elastic energy as heat and blunts the stretch reflex contribution
questions.explanation_en: If the amortization phase lasts too long, stored elastic energy is lost as heat and the stretch reflex no longer augments force.
tags: Chapter 19 quiz: Program Design and Technique for Plyometric Training

questions.question: A coach labels a squat jump as one category and a drop jump as another. What is the correct basis for that distinction?
options: The squat jump minimally involves stretch-shortening cycle contributions, whereas the drop jump depends on physiomechanical SSC contributions
The squat jump is inherently an upper body pattern while the drop jump is inherently a lower body pattern
The squat jump is loaded with heavier external resistance than the drop jump by definition
questions.answer_text: The squat jump minimally involves stretch-shortening cycle contributions, whereas the drop jump depends on physiomechanical SSC contributions
questions.explanation_en: Ballistic exercises like a squat jump minimally involve the SSC, whereas rebound exercises like drop jumps depend on SSC contributions.
tags: Chapter 19 quiz: Program Design and Technique for Plyometric Training

questions.question: A coach progresses an athlete from low box hops to high-intensity depth jumps. To keep the total stress appropriate, what should happen to the session volume as this intensity climbs?
options: It should be held exactly constant to standardize the workload
It should be reduced because higher-intensity drills stress tissues more per contact
It should climb in proportion so total training stimulus keeps rising
questions.answer_text: It should be reduced because higher-intensity drills stress tissues more per contact
questions.explanation_en: Higher intensity drills place more stress on tissues, so volume should be reduced as intensity rises.
tags: Chapter 19 quiz: Program Design and Technique for Plyometric Training

questions.question: A coach wants to log the dose of a lower body plyometric session in the way it is conventionally quantified. What should be recorded?
options: The peak heart rate reached across the drills
The cumulative time the working muscles spend under tension
The number of foot contacts completed during the session
questions.answer_text: The number of foot contacts completed during the session
questions.explanation_en: Lower body plyometric volume is normally expressed as the number of foot contacts per workout.
tags: Chapter 19 quiz: Program Design and Technique for Plyometric Training

questions.question: A coach declines to program depth jumps and high-impact lower body drills for a group of prepubescent children. What is the primary physiological reason?
options: Their epiphyseal growth plates have not yet closed, raising injury risk under high impact
They are developmentally incapable of following any movement instructions
Their muscles generate excessive force that the drills cannot safely absorb
questions.answer_text: Their epiphyseal growth plates have not yet closed, raising injury risk under high impact
questions.explanation_en: Because the epiphyseal plates of prepubescent children have not closed, high-impact depth jumps are contraindicated.
tags: Chapter 19 quiz: Program Design and Technique for Plyometric Training

questions.question: A coach setting up depth jumps wants to start most athletes at the height cited as the typical norm rather than the extremes of the usable range. Which height is that norm?
options: Roughly 6 to 12 inches, near the low end of the usable range
Roughly 30 to 32 inches
Roughly 48 to 60 inches, near the high end of the usable range
questions.answer_text: Roughly 30 to 32 inches
questions.explanation_en: Depth jump heights range from 16 to 42 inches, with 30 to 32 inches cited as the norm.
tags: Chapter 19 quiz: Program Design and Technique for Plyometric Training

questions.question: While filming landings, a coach flags one athlete whose pattern most strongly predicts ACL and patellofemoral injury. Which observed fault is that?
options: Landing with an active flat-foot contact
Knees tracking in line over the toes on contact
Inward collapse of the knees, a dynamic valgus pattern
questions.answer_text: Inward collapse of the knees, a dynamic valgus pattern
questions.explanation_en: Inward movement of the knees, called dynamic valgus, is a significant risk factor for ACL tears and knee injuries.
tags: Chapter 19 quiz: Program Design and Technique for Plyometric Training

questions.question: A coach must choose where to run lower body plyometrics from several available spaces. Which option provides appropriate shock absorption?
options: A grass field, a suspended floor, or a rubber mat
A poured concrete pad in the loading bay
Hardwood laid directly over a concrete slab
questions.answer_text: A grass field, a suspended floor, or a rubber mat
questions.explanation_en: Surfaces with adequate shock absorption such as grass, suspended floors, or rubber mats are recommended; concrete and tile are not.
tags: Chapter 19 quiz: Program Design and Technique for Plyometric Training

questions.question: An athlete has both plyometrics and aerobic endurance work scheduled for one session. To protect power output, how should the coach order them?
options: Aerobic work first so the muscles are thoroughly warmed before jumping
Plyometrics first, because preceding aerobic work can interfere with power production
Either order works equally well, so it can be left to preference
questions.answer_text: Plyometrics first, because preceding aerobic work can interfere with power production
questions.explanation_en: Because aerobic exercise can have an interfering effect on power, plyometrics should be performed before aerobic endurance training.
tags: Chapter 19 quiz: Program Design and Technique for Plyometric Training

questions.question: A coach is spacing an athlete's plyometric sessions across the week to allow adequate tissue recovery. What between-session interval is recommended?
options: About 5 to 7 days between sessions
About 12 to 24 hours between sessions
About 48 to 72 hours between sessions
questions.answer_text: About 48 to 72 hours between sessions
questions.explanation_en: Forty-eight to 72 hours between plyometric sessions is recommended to allow adequate recovery.
tags: Chapter 19 quiz: Program Design and Technique for Plyometric Training

questions.question: To combine resistance and plyometric work efficiently in one session without doubling stress on the same muscles, how should a coach pair lower body plyometrics?
options: With upper body resistance training that session
With lower body resistance training targeting the same muscles
With no resistance training, keeping plyometrics fully isolated
questions.answer_text: With upper body resistance training that session
questions.explanation_en: Guidelines suggest combining lower body resistance training with upper body plyometrics, and upper body resistance with lower body plyometrics.
tags: Chapter 19 quiz: Program Design and Technique for Plyometric Training

questions.question: Using ground contact time, a coach classifies a drill as a fast SSC action rather than a slow one. What approximate contact-time threshold marks that boundary?
options: About 2.5 seconds
About 0.25 seconds
About 1.0 second
questions.answer_text: About 0.25 seconds
questions.explanation_en: Slow SSC actions exceed 0.25 s of ground contact while fast SSC actions are under 0.25 s.
tags: Chapter 19 quiz: Program Design and Technique for Plyometric Training

questions.question: After months of progressive plyometric training, an athlete's motor units become more excitable partly because a protective proprioceptor has been blunted. Which structure is desensitized?
options: The Pacinian corpuscle, dulling its pressure sensitivity
The muscle spindle, reducing its stretch sensitivity
The Golgi tendon organ, raising the tension threshold at which it inhibits
questions.answer_text: The Golgi tendon organ, raising the tension threshold at which it inhibits
questions.explanation_en: Progressive plyometric training desensitizes the Golgi tendon organ, increasing the motor unit's excitability potential.
tags: Chapter 19 quiz: Program Design and Technique for Plyometric Training

questions.question: A coach wants to raise the intensity of a lower body plyometric drill through the movement demand itself. Which modification accomplishes that?
options: Adding a directional change that forces deceleration then redirected acceleration
Lowering the drop height the athlete works from
Switching from single-leg contacts to double-leg contacts
questions.answer_text: Adding a directional change that forces deceleration then redirected acceleration
questions.explanation_en: Directional changes require deceleration and redirected acceleration, increasing the impulse and intensity of the drill.
tags: Chapter 19 quiz: Program Design and Technique for Plyometric Training

questions.question: A coach programs medicine ball throws and slams for the upper body. In terms of movement classification, these drills are typically what?
options: Aerobic, sustaining low output over an extended period
Ballistic, projecting or accelerating an implement through release
Isometric, holding tension without joint movement
questions.answer_text: Ballistic, projecting or accelerating an implement through release
questions.explanation_en: Plyometrics for the upper body like throws and slams are typically ballistic in nature.
tags: Chapter 19 quiz: Program Design and Technique for Plyometric Training

questions.question: Two athletes perform the same drop jump from the same box onto the same surface. Which factor raises the relative intensity experienced by one of them?
options: Dropping from a shorter box height
Having a higher strength-to-body-weight ratio
Having greater body mass, which increases load on muscles, connective tissue, and joints
questions.answer_text: Having greater body mass, which increases load on muscles, connective tissue, and joints
questions.explanation_en: Greater body weight places more stress on muscles, connective tissues, and joints, raising drill intensity.
tags: Chapter 19 quiz: Program Design and Technique for Plyometric Training

questions.question: An athlete posts an excellent preplanned cone-drill time but repeatedly misreads defenders and cuts late in games. Using the standard definition, what does agility add that this athlete may be lacking?
options: A higher maximal sprint speed, since agility is essentially top-end velocity
A faster preplanned movement pattern, since agility is the rehearsed version of change of direction
A perceptual-cognitive response to a stimulus layered on top of change-of-direction ability
questions.answer_text: A perceptual-cognitive response to a stimulus layered on top of change-of-direction ability
questions.explanation_en: Agility requires perceptual-cognitive ability in combination with change-of-direction ability, responding to a stimulus.
tags: Chapter 20 quiz: Program Design and Technique for Speed and Agility Training

questions.question: An athlete has an excellent one-rep max but is beaten off the line because most of his sport actions last only a fraction of the time needed to reach that peak force. Which quality is more relevant to those brief actions?
options: Rate of force development, how quickly force can be produced
Maximal isometric strength, the peak force he can eventually reach
Aerobic capacity, his ability to sustain output over time
questions.answer_text: Rate of force development, how quickly force can be produced
questions.explanation_en: Maximal force takes at least 300 ms to develop, but sport actions are far shorter, so RFD is the more useful measure.
tags: Chapter 20 quiz: Program Design and Technique for Speed and Agility Training

questions.question: A coach wants the mechanical quantity that determines how much an athlete's momentum changes during a ground contact. Which description matches it?
options: Force divided by the time over which it acts
The product of force and the time it is applied, seen as the area under the force-time curve
Mass divided by acceleration during the contact
questions.answer_text: The product of force and the time it is applied, seen as the area under the force-time curve
questions.explanation_en: Impulse is force multiplied by time, represented as the area under the force-time curve, and it dictates change in momentum.
tags: Chapter 20 quiz: Program Design and Technique for Speed and Agility Training

questions.question: A coach is sorting sprint variables into vectors and scalars for a lecture. Which of these is a scalar, carrying magnitude but no direction?
options: Force, the push or pull applied against the ground
Velocity, how fast and in which direction the athlete moves
Speed, simply how fast the athlete moves
questions.answer_text: Speed, simply how fast the athlete moves
questions.explanation_en: Speed is a scalar describing only how fast an object moves; velocity and force are vectors with direction.
tags: Chapter 20 quiz: Program Design and Technique for Speed and Agility Training

questions.question: A coach wants to break sprint speed into the two variables whose interaction produces it, so each can be trained. Which pair is correct?
options: Step length and step frequency
Stride width and arm-swing amplitude
Ground contact time and body mass
questions.answer_text: Step length and step frequency
questions.explanation_en: Sprint speed is determined by the interaction of step length and step frequency.
tags: Chapter 20 quiz: Program Design and Technique for Speed and Agility Training

questions.question: Comparing an elite and a novice sprinter at top speed, force-plate data show the key difference. What most distinguishes the elite sprinter?
options: Markedly faster repositioning of the swing leg between steps
Greater vertical force applied to the ground within a shorter ground contact
Longer ground contact times that allow more force to accumulate
questions.answer_text: Greater vertical force applied to the ground within a shorter ground contact
questions.explanation_en: Elite sprinters apply greater vertical force in a shorter ground contact; their swing-leg repositioning times are similar to slower sprinters.
tags: Chapter 20 quiz: Program Design and Technique for Speed and Agility Training

questions.question: In the spring-mass model of sprinting, how is the stance leg represented as it goes from contact to push-off?
options: As a purely passive shock absorber that only dampens impact
As a rigid lever that transmits force without deforming
As a spring that compresses at contact and rebounds at push-off
questions.answer_text: As a spring that compresses at contact and rebounds at push-off
questions.explanation_en: The spring-mass model depicts the leg as a spring that compresses during midstance and returns energy at push-off.
tags: Chapter 20 quiz: Program Design and Technique for Speed and Agility Training

questions.question: An athlete plants and cuts through an angle sharper than about 45 degrees, requiring heavy braking. How is that action generally categorized?
options: A slower SSC action with longer ground contact due to greater braking demand
An action with no meaningful SSC involvement
A fast SSC action with very brief ground contact
questions.answer_text: A slower SSC action with longer ground contact due to greater braking demand
questions.explanation_en: COD over 45 degrees generally involves slower SSC actions with longer ground contact due to greater braking demands.
tags: Chapter 20 quiz: Program Design and Technique for Speed and Agility Training

questions.question: Because arresting momentum is central to sharp cuts, which muscle-action capacity should a coach prioritize when training change of direction and agility?
options: Slow concentric-only actions performed under control
High-velocity, high-force eccentric muscle actions for braking
Isometric holds performed at fixed joint angles
questions.answer_text: High-velocity, high-force eccentric muscle actions for braking
questions.explanation_en: Effective braking requires high-velocity and high-force eccentric muscle actions, which recruit different pathways than concentric work.
tags: Chapter 20 quiz: Program Design and Technique for Speed and Agility Training

questions.question: During a cut, one step does the decisive work of turning the athlete. What is the main function of that plant step?
options: To passively recover the swing leg before the next stride
To attain the athlete's maximal sprint velocity
To deflect the center of mass, transitioning from deceleration into reacceleration
questions.answer_text: To deflect the center of mass, transitioning from deceleration into reacceleration
questions.explanation_en: The plant phase is the main step that achieves deflection of the center of mass between deceleration and reacceleration.
tags: Chapter 20 quiz: Program Design and Technique for Speed and Agility Training

questions.question: A coach cues an athlete on posture to improve cutting. Which combination of trunk and body-position cues is recommended?
options: Lower the center of mass and keep trunk motion controlled
Lean the trunk forward aggressively while decelerating into the plant
Raise the center of mass to lengthen the stride into the cut
questions.answer_text: Lower the center of mass and keep trunk motion controlled
questions.explanation_en: A lower center of mass increases stability, and controlling trunk motion during deceleration improves COD performance.
tags: Chapter 20 quiz: Program Design and Technique for Speed and Agility Training

questions.question: A coach argues that the Illinois agility run and L-run measure maneuverability rather than sharp change of direction. What is the basis for that claim?
options: They include a reactive stimulus the athlete must respond to
They require rounding objects to preserve velocity rather than aggressively decelerating and repushing
They are too brief to impose any metabolic demand
questions.answer_text: They require rounding objects to preserve velocity rather than aggressively decelerating and repushing
questions.explanation_en: These longer tests require bending around objects to maintain velocity and impose higher metabolic demand, characteristic of maneuverability.
tags: Chapter 20 quiz: Program Design and Technique for Speed and Agility Training

questions.question: Two athletes post identical 5-0-5 times, but one is a much faster linear sprinter. To isolate true turning ability and fairly compare them, what should a coach calculate?
options: Each athlete's VO2max to gauge aerobic contribution
Each athlete's vertical jump height as a power proxy
The COD deficit, subtracting the 10 m linear sprint time from the 5-0-5 time
questions.answer_text: The COD deficit, subtracting the 10 m linear sprint time from the 5-0-5 time
questions.explanation_en: The COD deficit subtracts the 10 m linear sprint time from the 5-0-5 time to isolate change-of-direction ability.
tags: Chapter 20 quiz: Program Design and Technique for Speed and Agility Training

questions.question: A coach adds sled load for resisted sprints but wants to preserve sprinting mechanics. Roughly how much velocity reduction should the load generally not exceed?
options: About 10 percent
About 50 percent
About 75 percent
questions.answer_text: About 10 percent
questions.explanation_en: Loads are typically chosen to keep velocity decrements modest, around 10 to 12 percent, to preserve sprinting biomechanics.
tags: Chapter 20 quiz: Program Design and Technique for Speed and Agility Training

questions.question: A coach is considering assisted overspeed sprinting to raise an athlete's top speed. Which is a recognized drawback of the method?
options: It reliably produces faster ground contacts and cleaner mechanics
It can rush the stance phase, reduce muscle activation and propulsive force, and cause faulty technique
It is strongly and extensively supported by the research base
questions.answer_text: It can rush the stance phase, reduce muscle activation and propulsive force, and cause faulty technique
questions.explanation_en: Assisted sprinting can prematurely rush the stance phase, decrease muscle activation and propulsive force, and produce chop steps; little research supports it.
tags: Chapter 20 quiz: Program Design and Technique for Speed and Agility Training

questions.question: A coach reports that an athlete ran 9 m/s heading due north; a teammate ran 9 m/s but was constantly changing heading. Velocity differs from speed by adding which property that separates these cases?
options: Temperature of the environment
Mass of the moving athlete
Direction of the motion
questions.answer_text: Direction of the motion
questions.explanation_en: Velocity is speed with a direction, making it a vector quantity.
tags: Chapter 20 quiz: Program Design and Technique for Speed and Agility Training

questions.question: This chapter's framework declines to use power as the primary training target and prefers its underlying variables. What is the reasoning?
options: Power is a derived construct, so measuring its underlying characteristics, force and velocity, is more practically useful
Power bears no meaningful relationship to sprinting performance
Power cannot be measured with available equipment
questions.answer_text: Power is a derived construct, so measuring its underlying characteristics, force and velocity, is more practically useful
questions.explanation_en: Power is a derived mechanical construct, so measuring its underlying characteristics, force and velocity, gives more practical insight.
tags: Chapter 20 quiz: Program Design and Technique for Speed and Agility Training

questions.question: Watching a sprint from the start to top speed, a coach notes how trunk posture evolves. Which description is correct?
options: The athlete leans backward to brake as speed increases
Forward lean is greatest early in acceleration and gradually becomes upright by maximum velocity
The trunk is fully upright from the very first step onward
questions.answer_text: Forward lean is greatest early in acceleration and gradually becomes upright by maximum velocity
questions.explanation_en: Acceleration begins with forward inclination that gradually reduces to an upright posture by maximum velocity.
tags: Chapter 20 quiz: Program Design and Technique for Speed and Agility Training

questions.question: A basketball athlete improves T-test times over an offseason. Which anthropometric change is regarded as a predictor of that improved change-of-direction performance?
options: Greater limb length providing longer levers
Increased body fat adding overall mass to push against the ground
Increased muscle mass combined with decreased body fat, improving functional mass
questions.answer_text: Increased muscle mass combined with decreased body fat, improving functional mass
questions.explanation_en: Improving functional mass through more muscle and less fat predicts better COD performance, as in T-test results for basketball players.
tags: Chapter 20 quiz: Program Design and Technique for Speed and Agility Training

questions.question: An athlete jams a stiff, extended leg into the ground when cutting and struggles to absorb the load. Which lower-limb cue should the coach teach to tolerate braking forces?
options: Use triple flexion at the hip, knee, and ankle to dissipate eccentric loads
Keep the knees locked on contact to create a firm base
Maintain a stiff-legged braking style to transmit force quickly
questions.answer_text: Use triple flexion at the hip, knee, and ankle to dissipate eccentric loads
questions.explanation_en: Athletes should use triple flexion at the hip, knee, and ankle to dissipate eccentric braking loads and avoid a stiff-legged style.
tags: Chapter 20 quiz: Program Design and Technique for Speed and Agility Training

questions.question: A coach is drafting an aerobic endurance program from scratch and wants to set the variables in the sequence the program design process prescribes. Which order should be followed?
options: Choose the exercise mode first, then frequency, then intensity, then duration, then plan progression
Choose frequency first, then mode, then duration, then intensity, then plan progression
Choose intensity first, then duration, then frequency, then mode, then plan progression
questions.answer_text: Choose the exercise mode first, then frequency, then intensity, then duration, then plan progression
questions.explanation_en: The program design steps are (1) exercise mode, (2) frequency, (3) intensity, (4) duration, and (5) progression, in that order.
tags: Chapter 21 quiz: Program Design and Technique for Aerobic Endurance Training

questions.question: Two distance runners share nearly identical VO2max values, yet one consistently outperforms the other in long races. Which profile most likely explains the better performer's advantage?
options: A greater proportion of type IIx fibers and a higher glycolytic capacity
A higher lactate threshold, better exercise economy, and a greater proportion of type I fibers
A larger muscle cross-sectional area combined with greater anaerobic power output
questions.answer_text: A higher lactate threshold, better exercise economy, and a greater proportion of type I fibers
questions.explanation_en: When VO2max is matched, a high lactate threshold, good exercise economy, high fat utilization, and a high percentage of type I fibers become decisive for endurance performance.
tags: Chapter 21 quiz: Program Design and Technique for Aerobic Endurance Training

questions.question: During an incremental treadmill test, a technician notes the running speed at which blood lactate first climbs meaningfully above the athlete's resting concentration. Which variable has been identified?
options: The maximum heart rate the athlete can hold for one hour
The speed at which the athlete reaches VO2max
The lactate threshold
questions.answer_text: The lactate threshold
questions.explanation_en: The lactate threshold is the running speed (or percentage of VO2max) at which blood lactate begins rising above resting levels.
tags: Chapter 21 quiz: Program Design and Technique for Aerobic Endurance Training

questions.question: A cyclist rides at the highest steady power output she can sustain while her blood lactate stays elevated but stable rather than continuing to climb. This intensity is best labeled as:
options: The intensity where maximal lactate production is matched by maximal lactate clearance
The intensity where blood lactate first rises above zero
The point where lactate production outpaces clearance and rises until failure
questions.answer_text: The intensity where maximal lactate production is matched by maximal lactate clearance
questions.explanation_en: Maximal lactate steady state is the intensity at which maximal lactate production equals maximal clearance; it is synonymous with critical power and critical speed.
tags: Chapter 21 quiz: Program Design and Technique for Aerobic Endurance Training

questions.question: Two runners hold the exact same pace, but one consumes less oxygen and expends less energy to do so. That runner is said to have superior:
options: Maximal aerobic capacity
Exercise economy
Lactate tolerance
questions.answer_text: Exercise economy
questions.explanation_en: Exercise economy is the energy cost of holding a given velocity; better economy means less energy expended to maintain the same pace.
tags: Chapter 21 quiz: Program Design and Technique for Aerobic Endurance Training

questions.question: A coach increases the intensity of an athlete's aerobic sessions and must adjust duration accordingly. What is the expected relationship between the two?
options: They are set independently, so duration need not change
Raising intensity allows a longer sustainable duration
Raising intensity requires a shorter duration
questions.answer_text: Raising intensity requires a shorter duration
questions.explanation_en: Intensity and duration are inversely related; higher-intensity work must be shorter, while lower-intensity work can be sustained longer.
tags: Chapter 21 quiz: Program Design and Technique for Aerobic Endurance Training

questions.question: Using the age-predicted maximal heart rate formula (Fox), what maximal heart rate would a coach estimate for a 30-year-old athlete?
options: 190 beats per minute
160 beats per minute
220 beats per minute
questions.answer_text: 190 beats per minute
