questions.explanation_en: Age-predicted maximal heart rate equals 220 minus age, so 220 minus 30 gives 190 beats per minute.
tags: Chapter 21 quiz: Program Design and Technique for Aerobic Endurance Training

questions.question: A coach wants a target heart rate that accounts for the athlete's resting heart rate, computing it as heart rate reserve multiplied by the desired intensity and then adding resting heart rate. Which method is this?
options: The percentage of maximal heart rate method
The Karvonen (heart rate reserve) method
The metabolic equivalent (MET) method
questions.answer_text: The Karvonen (heart rate reserve) method
questions.explanation_en: The Karvonen method uses heart rate reserve: target HR equals (HRR times intensity) plus resting HR.
tags: Chapter 21 quiz: Program Design and Technique for Aerobic Endurance Training

questions.question: An athlete performs a two-hour run held below 65 percent of VO2max to build an aerobic base. Which category of aerobic training does this session represent?
options: Interval training performed near VO2max
High-intensity interval training
Long slow distance (extensive endurance) training
questions.answer_text: Long slow distance (extensive endurance) training
questions.explanation_en: Long slow distance (extensive endurance) training is the longest-duration, lowest-intensity work, typically performed below about 65 percent of VO2max.
tags: Chapter 21 quiz: Program Design and Technique for Aerobic Endurance Training

questions.question: A distance coach prescribes sustained efforts at an intensity right at the athlete's threshold, which is why the workout is sometimes called threshold training. This corresponds most closely to which physiological marker?
options: An intensity at or slightly above the maximal lactate steady state
An intensity above VO2max
An intensity well below the lactate threshold
questions.answer_text: An intensity at or slightly above the maximal lactate steady state
questions.explanation_en: Pace/tempo (threshold) training is performed at or slightly above the maximal lactate steady state, which is why it is also called threshold training.
tags: Chapter 21 quiz: Program Design and Technique for Aerobic Endurance Training

questions.question: A coach programs VO2max interval work using 4-minute work bouts and needs to set the rest interval. For traditional interval training in this bout range, what work-to-rest ratio is recommended?
questions.explanation_en: For 3- to 5-minute interval work bouts, rest should roughly equal the work interval, yielding a 1:1 work-to-rest ratio.
tags: Chapter 21 quiz: Program Design and Technique for Aerobic Endurance Training

questions.question: An athlete performs an extremely intense cycling protocol of repeated all-out bouts, each followed by a rest interval half as long as the work bout, reaching exhaustion in roughly 7 to 8 repetitions. Which structure matches the classic Tabata protocol?
options: 60 seconds of work followed by 60 seconds of rest
3 minutes of work followed by 1 minute of rest
20 seconds of work followed by 10 seconds of rest
questions.answer_text: 20 seconds of work followed by 10 seconds of rest
questions.explanation_en: The classic Tabata protocol uses very high intensity with 20 seconds of work and 10 seconds of rest, reaching exhaustion in about 7 to 8 repetitions.
tags: Chapter 21 quiz: Program Design and Technique for Aerobic Endurance Training

questions.question: During one continuous run, an athlete freely mixes easy jogging, sustained threshold-pace segments, and short fast surges based on feel. This unstructured blending of intensities within a single session is called:
options: Fartlek training
Pace/tempo training
Long slow distance (extensive endurance) training
questions.answer_text: Fartlek training
questions.explanation_en: Fartlek, Swedish for speed play, combines long slow distance, pace/tempo, and interval-style efforts within a single workout.
tags: Chapter 21 quiz: Program Design and Technique for Aerobic Endurance Training

questions.question: A coach wants to advance an endurance athlete safely without provoking overtraining or injury. What is the general guideline for progressing frequency, intensity, or duration?
options: Double the training load each week
Increase only one variable at a time by no more than about 10 percent per week
Increase by at least 25 percent per week to force adaptation
questions.answer_text: Increase only one variable at a time by no more than about 10 percent per week
questions.explanation_en: To limit overtraining and injury risk, increase frequency, intensity, or duration by no more than about 10 percent per week, and only one variable at a time.
tags: Chapter 21 quiz: Program Design and Technique for Aerobic Endurance Training

questions.question: An endurance athlete is months away from her key race and spends this block on long, low-intensity volume. What is the primary objective of this off-season (base) training?
options: Maximize race-pace speed work
Peak specifically for the most important competition
Develop a large base of cardiorespiratory conditioning
questions.answer_text: Develop a large base of cardiorespiratory conditioning
questions.explanation_en: Off-season base training builds a large cardiorespiratory base primarily through long-duration, low-intensity work.
tags: Chapter 21 quiz: Program Design and Technique for Aerobic Endurance Training

questions.question: A runner recovering from a repetitive-stress issue substitutes cycling and swimming for some running mileage. What is the primary rationale for this cross-training?
options: To maintain general conditioning while reducing overuse injury risk during reduced running or injury
To permanently replace all sport-specific training year-round
To maximize race-specific performance adaptations
questions.answer_text: To maintain general conditioning while reducing overuse injury risk during reduced running or injury
questions.explanation_en: Cross-training maintains general conditioning and distributes stress to different muscle groups, lowering overuse injury risk.
tags: Chapter 21 quiz: Program Design and Technique for Aerobic Endurance Training

questions.question: An athlete stops training for several weeks due to a scheduling conflict and returns noticeably less fit. This decline is best described as:
options: Retention of adaptations regardless of the layoff
Detraining, the progressive loss of training-induced physiological adaptations
Continued improvement occurring without any training
questions.answer_text: Detraining, the progressive loss of training-induced physiological adaptations
questions.explanation_en: Detraining is the progressive loss of training-induced physiological adaptations when training is reduced or stopped.
tags: Chapter 21 quiz: Program Design and Technique for Aerobic Endurance Training

questions.question: Ahead of a championship, a coach cuts an athlete's training volume roughly in half in one move and then holds that reduced volume steady through the final days. Which tapering strategy is this?
options: An increase in training volume immediately before competition
A gradual, linear reduction in daily training volume
A step taper: an abrupt, substantial volume reduction held constant thereafter
questions.answer_text: A step taper: an abrupt, substantial volume reduction held constant thereafter
questions.explanation_en: A step taper is an abrupt, considerable reduction in volume (often at least 50 percent) that is then maintained without fluctuation throughout the taper.
tags: Chapter 21 quiz: Program Design and Technique for Aerobic Endurance Training

questions.question: A coach wants an athlete to gain the hematological benefits of altitude while keeping training quality high. Which arrangement correctly describes the live high, train low approach?
options: Live at moderate altitude for acclimatization but train at or near sea level
Live at sea level but travel up to train at high altitude
Both live and train at extreme altitude
questions.answer_text: Live at moderate altitude for acclimatization but train at or near sea level
questions.explanation_en: Live high, train low has athletes living at moderate altitude (about 2,000 to 3,000 m) for acclimatization while training near sea level to preserve training quality.
tags: Chapter 21 quiz: Program Design and Technique for Aerobic Endurance Training

questions.question: After several weeks of a heat acclimation protocol, which physiological change would a coach expect to observe in the athlete?
options: A reduced plasma volume
Sweating that begins at a lower core temperature
A delayed onset and reduced overall sweat rate
questions.answer_text: Sweating that begins at a lower core temperature
questions.explanation_en: Heat acclimation increases plasma volume and sweat rate and shifts the onset of sweating earlier, to a lower core temperature.
tags: Chapter 21 quiz: Program Design and Technique for Aerobic Endurance Training

questions.question: A strength coach maps out a full year of training blocks and separately decides the exact exercises, methods, and loads inside each block. Which statement correctly distinguishes these two activities?
options: They are identical terms and can be used interchangeably
Periodization is the macro-level scaffold, while programming is the micro-level management of modes, methods, and loads
Programming is the year-long overview, while periodization sets each day's sets and reps
questions.answer_text: Periodization is the macro-level scaffold, while programming is the micro-level management of modes, methods, and loads
questions.explanation_en: Periodization is the macro-management scaffold of the training process; programming is the micro-management that defines the actual modes, methods, and loads.
tags: Chapter 22 quiz: Periodization

questions.question: Selye's model describes how an organism responds to a stressor across three sequential stages. Which set names those stages in order?
options: Preparation, competition, transition
Hypertrophy, strength, power
Alarm, resistance, exhaustion
questions.answer_text: Alarm, resistance, exhaustion
questions.explanation_en: The general adaptation syndrome consists of the alarm, resistance, and exhaustion stages.
tags: Chapter 22 quiz: Periodization

questions.question: An athlete begins a demanding new training block and reports heavy soreness and a temporary dip in performance in the first days. According to the general adaptation syndrome, which phase does this reflect?
options: The alarm phase, in which performance generally decreases from fatigue and soreness
The resistance phase, in which performance rises above baseline
A steady state in which performance stays exactly at baseline
questions.answer_text: The alarm phase, in which performance generally decreases from fatigue and soreness
questions.explanation_en: The alarm phase is marked by fatigue, soreness, and a reduced performance capacity in response to a novel or more intense stress.
tags: Chapter 22 quiz: Periodization

questions.question: An athlete is subjected to unrelenting high training and psychoemotional stress for too long and fails to adapt, showing signs of overtraining. Which general adaptation syndrome phase has been entered?
options: A supercompensation phase
The exhaustion phase
The resistance phase
questions.answer_text: The exhaustion phase
questions.explanation_en: Persistent excessive stress that exceeds the athlete's ability to adapt drives entry into the exhaustion phase, often reflecting overreaching or overtraining.
tags: Chapter 22 quiz: Periodization

questions.question: Under the fitness-fatigue paradigm, a coach wants to estimate an athlete's readiness to perform on a given day. Preparedness is best modeled as:
options: The fitness aftereffect only, with fatigue disregarded
The fatigue aftereffect only, with fitness disregarded
The summation of the fitness and fatigue aftereffects of training
questions.answer_text: The summation of the fitness and fatigue aftereffects of training
questions.explanation_en: Preparedness is the summation of the fitness and fatigue aftereffects produced by each training bout.
tags: Chapter 22 quiz: Periodization

questions.question: As competition nears, a coach deliberately lowers training load and the athlete's readiness climbs. Which mechanism explains why reducing load tends to raise preparedness?
options: Fatigue dissipates faster than fitness is lost
Both fatigue and fitness vanish instantly when load drops
Fitness is lost faster than fatigue clears
questions.answer_text: Fatigue dissipates faster than fitness is lost
questions.explanation_en: Because fatigue dissipates faster than fitness, a planned load reduction lets preparedness rise as fatigue clears while most fitness is retained.
tags: Chapter 22 quiz: Periodization

questions.question: A coach outlines a season using the traditional (Stone and colleagues) periodization model and needs the four sequential periods in order. Which list is correct?
options: Microcycle, mesocycle, macrocycle, annual plan
Preparatory, first transition, competitive, second transition
General, specific, peaking, maintenance
questions.answer_text: Preparatory, first transition, competitive, second transition
questions.explanation_en: The traditional model uses the preparatory, first transition, competitive, and second transition periods in that order.
tags: Chapter 22 quiz: Periodization

questions.question: Within the traditional model, the longest period is itself split into two subphases. Which pair correctly names them?
options: An alarm phase and a resistance phase
A peaking phase and a maintenance phase
A general preparatory phase and a specific preparatory phase
questions.answer_text: A general preparatory phase and a specific preparatory phase
questions.explanation_en: The preparatory period is subdivided into a general preparatory phase and a specific preparatory phase.
tags: Chapter 22 quiz: Periodization

questions.question: Early in the preparatory period, a coach prescribes higher-repetition sets at roughly 50 to 75 percent of 1RM to build work capacity and muscle mass. Which loading pattern describes this hypertrophy/strength-endurance phase?
options: Low to moderate intensity with high volume
Very high intensity with very low volume
Maximal singles at peaking loads
questions.answer_text: Low to moderate intensity with high volume
questions.explanation_en: The hypertrophy/strength-endurance phase uses low to moderate intensity (about 50 to 75 percent 1RM) and high volume to develop work capacity and muscle mass.
tags: Chapter 22 quiz: Periodization

questions.question: As an athlete progresses from the preparatory period toward competition in the traditional model, how do training volume and intensity generally trend relative to each other?
options: Volume rises while intensity falls
Volume falls while intensity rises
Volume and intensity both rise together
questions.answer_text: Volume falls while intensity rises
questions.explanation_en: Training generally shifts from high-volume, low-intensity work toward lower-volume, higher-intensity work as competition approaches.
tags: Chapter 22 quiz: Periodization

questions.question: A coach is nesting shorter training cycles inside longer ones for a full annual plan. Of a microcycle, a mesocycle, and a macrocycle, which spans the longest period of time?
options: The mesocycle
The microcycle
The macrocycle
questions.answer_text: The macrocycle
questions.explanation_en: The macrocycle is the longest of the three (several months up to a year), with mesocycles and microcycles nested within it.
tags: Chapter 22 quiz: Periodization

questions.question: A coach designs a mid-length training block and picks its most typical length. What is the usual range for a mesocycle, and what is its most common duration?
options: Two to six weeks, most commonly four weeks
Several months, most commonly six months
Several days, most commonly a single day
questions.answer_text: Two to six weeks, most commonly four weeks
questions.explanation_en: A mesocycle is a medium cycle of about two to six weeks, with four weeks being the most common duration.
tags: Chapter 22 quiz: Periodization

questions.question: A coach lays out the smallest recurring training cycle and uses its most typical length. How long does a microcycle most commonly last?
options: About four weeks
About one week (roughly 7 days)
A single day
questions.answer_text: About one week (roughly 7 days)
questions.explanation_en: A microcycle ranges from several days up to two weeks, but its most common duration is one week.
tags: Chapter 22 quiz: Periodization

questions.question: A coach plans a period that lasts a single day, may hold more than one training session, and is designed within the week-long cycle that contains it. Which unit is this?
options: The macrocycle
The annual plan
The training day
questions.answer_text: The training day
questions.explanation_en: A training day lasts one day, can contain multiple sessions, and is designed within the context of its microcycle.
tags: Chapter 22 quiz: Periodization

questions.question: When mapping the sport season onto the traditional periodization model, the off-season conditioning block corresponds to which period?
options: The preparatory period
The second transition period
The competitive period
questions.answer_text: The preparatory period
questions.explanation_en: The off-season maps to the preparatory period, which focuses on building a conditioning base.
tags: Chapter 22 quiz: Periodization

questions.question: The competitive period of the traditional model, during which the year's scheduled contests take place, aligns with which part of the sport season?
options: The off-season
The in-season
The postseason
questions.answer_text: The in-season
questions.explanation_en: The competitive period is the in-season, which contains all of the year's scheduled contests.
tags: Chapter 22 quiz: Periodization

questions.question: The period sitting between the end of the competitive season and the next preparatory period goes by which other name?
options: The basic strength phase
The peaking period
The active rest (restoration) period
questions.answer_text: The active rest (restoration) period
questions.explanation_en: The second transition period is also called the active rest or restoration period, bridging the competitive season and the next preparatory period.
tags: Chapter 22 quiz: Periodization

questions.question: A coach schedules the active rest block after the season and wants to avoid triggering detraining that would lengthen the next preparatory period. How long should this second transition generally last?
options: No longer than about four weeks
At least three months
A full year
questions.answer_text: No longer than about four weeks
questions.explanation_en: Active rest should generally last no longer than about four weeks; a longer layoff causes detraining and requires a longer preparatory period to recover.
tags: Chapter 22 quiz: Periodization

questions.question: A colleague calls the traditional model linear periodization. Why is that label considered technically inaccurate?
options: Because the model never alters intensity at any point
Because it still varies intensity and volume-load at the micro- and mesocycle level, making it nonlinear
Because it applies one unchanging training load for the entire plan
questions.answer_text: Because it still varies intensity and volume-load at the micro- and mesocycle level, making it nonlinear
questions.explanation_en: A core tenet of periodization is removing linearity; the traditional model varies intensity and volume-load within its micro- and mesocycles, so it is actually nonlinear.
tags: Chapter 22 quiz: Periodization

questions.question: Within one week, an athlete performs a heavy strength day, a hypertrophy day, and a power day, rotating focus session to session. Which periodization approach does this exemplify, and how does it differ from the traditional model?
options: It uses only one training session per month, unlike the traditional model
It holds load and focus identical every session, unlike the traditional model
It varies load, volume, and training focus within a single microcycle, rather than progressing gradually across mesocycles
questions.answer_text: It varies load, volume, and training focus within a single microcycle, rather than progressing gradually across mesocycles
questions.explanation_en: Daily undulating periodization makes large day-to-day fluctuations in load, volume, and focus within a microcycle, unlike the more gradual mesocycle progression of the traditional model.
tags: Chapter 22 quiz: Periodization

questions.question: A recovering athlete is cleared by the athletic trainer, who has run the daily rehab, but the coach wants to know whose sign-off is legally and professionally the final word before the athlete competes again. Who most often makes that determination?
options: The athletic trainer, because they supervised the rehabilitation
The strength and conditioning professional, who oversees reconditioning
The team physician, even though they do not run daily rehabilitation
questions.answer_text: The team physician, even though they do not run daily rehabilitation
questions.explanation_en: The team physician (MD or DO) most often makes the final return-to-play decision, even though they are not responsible for daily rehabilitation.
tags: Chapter 23 quiz: Rehabilitation, Reconditioning, and Medical Issues

questions.question: An athlete has anterior shoulder instability, and the athletic trainer directs the S and C coach to remove the barbell bench press from the program because that movement places the joint in a vulnerable position. In clinical terms, the bench press is best described for this athlete as a:
options: Contraindication
Indication
Macrotrauma
questions.answer_text: Contraindication
questions.explanation_en: A contraindication is an activity that is inadvisable or prohibited due to the given injury, such as bench pressing with anterior shoulder instability.
tags: Chapter 23 quiz: Rehabilitation, Reconditioning, and Medical Issues

questions.question: During a tackle an athlete's shoulder is forced so that the humeral head fully separates from the glenoid and stays out of position until reduced. When only the joint surfaces had partially separated and spontaneously returned, that lesser event would instead be called a subluxation. The complete-separation event is termed a:
options: Sprain
Dislocation
Subluxation
questions.answer_text: Dislocation
questions.explanation_en: A dislocation is complete displacement of the joint surfaces, whereas a subluxation is only partial displacement.
tags: Chapter 23 quiz: Rehabilitation, Reconditioning, and Medical Issues

questions.question: A distance runner who steadily raised weekly mileage without adding rest days develops a nagging injury from the repeated abnormal loading rather than any single traumatic event. This mechanism of injury is classified as:
options: Macrotrauma
A third-degree sprain
Microtrauma (overuse)
questions.answer_text: Microtrauma (overuse)
questions.explanation_en: Microtrauma, or overuse injury, results from repeated abnormal stress, in contrast to macrotrauma which is a single sudden overload episode.
tags: Chapter 23 quiz: Rehabilitation, Reconditioning, and Medical Issues

questions.question: On a manual muscle test after a hamstring injury, the athlete can generate almost no force yet reports little to no pain, and imaging shows a complete tear of the muscle fibers. This grading of muscle activity is consistent with a:
options: Third-degree strain
First-degree strain
Second-degree strain
questions.answer_text: Third-degree strain
questions.explanation_en: A third-degree strain is a complete tear of the fibers producing very weak, painless muscle activity; first-degree is strong but painful and second-degree is weak and painful.
tags: Chapter 23 quiz: Rehabilitation, Reconditioning, and Medical Issues

questions.question: A cross-country athlete who ramped up training volume too quickly develops localized, activity-related bone pain that imaging later confirms. This represents the most common overuse injury to bone, which is a:
options: Avulsion fracture
Stress fracture
Contusion
questions.answer_text: Stress fracture
questions.explanation_en: The most common overuse (microtrauma) injury to bone is a stress fracture, often from rapid increases in training volume.
tags: Chapter 23 quiz: Rehabilitation, Reconditioning, and Medical Issues

questions.question: An athlete has chronic Achilles pain, and imaging reveals disorganized collagen, tendon cell damage, and new vessel growth but little sign of active inflammation. This picture points to tendinopathy rather than tendinitis because tendinopathy is characterized by:
options: Acute inflammation of the tendon
A complete tendon rupture
A degenerative condition with minimal inflammation
questions.answer_text: A degenerative condition with minimal inflammation
questions.explanation_en: Tendinopathy is a degenerative condition with minimal inflammation, tendon cell damage or death, and neovascularization, unlike inflammatory tendinitis.
tags: Chapter 23 quiz: Rehabilitation, Reconditioning, and Medical Issues

questions.question: An S and C coach planning progressive reconditioning wants to time loading to the biology of healing. Regardless of tissue type, which sequence correctly orders the phases the tissue moves through?
options: Inflammatory response, then fibroblastic repair, then maturation-remodeling
Fibroblastic repair, then inflammatory response, then maturation-remodeling
Maturation-remodeling, then inflammatory response, then fibroblastic repair
questions.answer_text: Inflammatory response, then fibroblastic repair, then maturation-remodeling
questions.explanation_en: All tissues heal in the same basic order: inflammation first, then fibroblastic repair, then maturation-remodeling.
tags: Chapter 23 quiz: Rehabilitation, Reconditioning, and Medical Issues

questions.question: An athlete sustains an acute ankle sprain on Monday morning. Assuming an intact blood supply and no unusual severity, roughly when should the initial inflammatory phase be resolving?
options: By about two months after the injury
By about 72 hours after the injury
By about two weeks after the injury
questions.answer_text: By about 72 hours after the injury
questions.explanation_en: The inflammatory phase typically lasts about 72 hours, though it may last longer with compromised blood supply or more severe damage.
tags: Chapter 23 quiz: Rehabilitation, Reconditioning, and Medical Issues

questions.question: A few days into healing, a biopsy of the wound area shows freshly laid collagen that is disorganized and considerably weaker than the original tissue. This finding is characteristic of the fibroblastic repair phase, in which the collagen is primarily:
options: Type I collagen, aligned along the lines of stress
Fully matured collagen at normal tensile strength
Type III collagen, randomly oriented and weak
questions.answer_text: Type III collagen, randomly oriented and weak
questions.explanation_en: The repair phase produces type III collagen that is randomly deposited and weaker than the original tissue; alignment and strength come later in remodeling.
tags: Chapter 23 quiz: Rehabilitation, Reconditioning, and Medical Issues

questions.question: As a healed tendon is progressively loaded during the final phase of tissue healing, what happens to its collagen fibers?
options: They hypertrophy and realign along the lines of stress
They are broken down and removed by macrophages
They stay randomly oriented and transverse to the load
questions.answer_text: They hypertrophy and realign along the lines of stress
questions.explanation_en: With increased loading the collagen fibers hypertrophy and realign along the lines of stress, becoming stronger and allowing return to function.
tags: Chapter 23 quiz: Rehabilitation, Reconditioning, and Medical Issues

questions.question: A clinician managing a fresh soft-tissue injury wants the current acronym that updated the older PRICE model by adding an emphasis on controlled, graded loading rather than strict rest. Which approach is that?
options: MICE
POLICE
RICE
questions.answer_text: POLICE
questions.explanation_en: Evidence has shifted to POLICE (Protection, Optimal Loading, Ice, Compression, Elevation), emphasizing optimal loading over pure rest.
tags: Chapter 23 quiz: Rehabilitation, Reconditioning, and Medical Issues

questions.question: As an injury moves from the inflammatory phase into repair, growth factors that drive that transition are released from the injured area. Which cells release them?
options: Histamine and bradykinin
Fibroblasts and osteoblasts
Macrophages and platelets
questions.answer_text: Macrophages and platelets
questions.explanation_en: Macrophages and platelets within the injured area release growth factors that assist the transition to the fibroblastic repair phase.
tags: Chapter 23 quiz: Rehabilitation, Reconditioning, and Medical Issues

questions.question: A coach chooses the back squat and the push-up during reconditioning specifically because in both movements the foot or hand is planted against the ground and cannot move freely. This shared feature classifies them as closed kinetic chain exercises, defined by a terminal (distal) segment that is:
options: Fixed and meeting considerable resistance
Free to move against little resistance
Loaded only during the eccentric phase
questions.answer_text: Fixed and meeting considerable resistance
questions.explanation_en: In a closed kinetic chain exercise (e.g., squat, push-up) the distal segment is fixed and meets resistance that restrains its free motion.
tags: Chapter 23 quiz: Rehabilitation, Reconditioning, and Medical Issues

questions.question: A therapist wants to isolate the quadriceps at the knee with the foot free to swing through the movement, so she selects the seated leg (knee) extension. Based on the distal segment being free to move, this exercise is classified as:
options: Purely isometric
Open kinetic chain
Closed kinetic chain
questions.answer_text: Open kinetic chain
questions.explanation_en: The leg extension is an open kinetic chain exercise because the foot is free to move, allowing concentration on the quadriceps at the knee.
tags: Chapter 23 quiz: Rehabilitation, Reconditioning, and Medical Issues

questions.question: A clinician wants a resistance-training system that changes the working load from session to session according to how many repetitions the athlete completed, giving more individualization than the fixed DeLorme or Oxford schemes. Knight's DAPRE protocol fits because it:
options: Always progresses from heavy loads down to light loads
Relies exclusively on isometric contractions
Adjusts intensity and volume on a daily basis according to performance
questions.answer_text: Adjusts intensity and volume on a daily basis according to performance
questions.explanation_en: DAPRE (daily adjustable progressive resistive exercise) adjusts resistance daily based on reps performed, allowing more individualization than DeLorme or Oxford.
tags: Chapter 23 quiz: Rehabilitation, Reconditioning, and Medical Issues

questions.question: When screening an active population to predict who is most likely to get hurt in the coming season, which single factor is repeatedly cited as one of the most substantial predictors?
options: Having sustained a previous injury
Possessing a high aerobic capacity
Demonstrating strong neuromuscular control
questions.answer_text: Having sustained a previous injury
questions.explanation_en: Previous injury is repeatedly cited as one of the most substantial risk factors for future injury.
tags: Chapter 23 quiz: Rehabilitation, Reconditioning, and Medical Issues

questions.question: After an unusually intense session in the heat, an athlete reports severe muscle pain and weakness, and their urine is dark and cola-colored from myoglobin. These signs point to which condition?
options: Heat cramps
Rhabdomyolysis
Sickle cell trait crisis
questions.answer_text: Rhabdomyolysis
questions.explanation_en: Rhabdomyolysis is the breakdown of skeletal muscle releasing myoglobin into the blood, producing myalgia, weakness, and myoglobinuria with risk to the kidneys.
tags: Chapter 23 quiz: Rehabilitation, Reconditioning, and Medical Issues

questions.question: A lineman collapses in practice with a very high core temperature and altered mental status consistent with exertional heatstroke. Which management response is the recognized standard of care?
options: Passive static stretching of the large muscle groups
Oral rehydration alone while the athlete keeps exercising lightly
Immediate whole-body cooling such as cold-water immersion while activating EMS
questions.answer_text: Immediate whole-body cooling such as cold-water immersion while activating EMS
questions.explanation_en: Heatstroke is a medical emergency requiring immediate total body cooling (ice immersion), core temperature monitoring, and emergency medical services.
tags: Chapter 23 quiz: Rehabilitation, Reconditioning, and Medical Issues

questions.question: An athletic trainer teaches staff to catch heat illness early rather than treating each presentation as an unrelated surprise. This reflects the fact that heat illnesses are best understood as:
options: A continuum, with heatstroke typically preceded by cramps, syncope, and exhaustion
Isolated, unrelated events that give no warning signs beforehand
Conditions that arise almost exclusively in cold environments
questions.answer_text: A continuum, with heatstroke typically preceded by cramps, syncope, and exhaustion
questions.explanation_en: Heat illnesses exist on a continuum of thermoregulatory dysregulation, so heatstroke is usually preceded by heat cramps, heat syncope, and heat exhaustion.
tags: Chapter 23 quiz: Rehabilitation, Reconditioning, and Medical Issues

questions.question: An athlete shows elevated cortisol and depressed testosterone on bloodwork but is still hitting personal records. A coach argues this proves overtraining syndrome. What is actually required before overtraining syndrome can be said to exist?
options: A long-term (weeks to months) impairment in performance
Decreased testosterone together with increased cortisol
A run of poor results in competition
questions.answer_text: A long-term (weeks to months) impairment in performance
questions.explanation_en: Performance impairment (long-term, weeks to months) is the necessary requirement for overtraining syndrome; hormonal changes indicate stress but are not required.
tags: Chapter 24 quiz: Overreaching, Overtraining, and Recovery

questions.question: A coach uses the terms overtraining and the overtraining syndrome interchangeably. Which statement correctly separates the process from its outcome?
options: They are identical terms describing exactly the same phenomenon
Overtraining is the process; the overtraining syndrome is the resulting condition
The overtraining syndrome is the process; overtraining is the resulting condition
questions.answer_text: Overtraining is the process; the overtraining syndrome is the resulting condition
questions.explanation_en: Overtraining is the process (excessive volume/intensity), and the overtraining syndrome is the result (symptoms plus performance impairment).
tags: Chapter 24 quiz: Overreaching, Overtraining, and Recovery

questions.question: Two athletes both show a training-induced performance dip, but one is a milder case that resolves quickly while the other is a full-blown syndrome. Which statement captures how overreaching primarily differs from overtraining?
options: Overreaching invariably leaves a permanent performance decrement
Overreaching typically requires hospitalization to resolve
Overreaching is less severe and recovery is faster
questions.answer_text: Overreaching is less severe and recovery is faster
questions.explanation_en: Overreaching is a lesser form of stressful training; the condition is less severe and recovery is faster than with overtraining.
tags: Chapter 24 quiz: Overreaching, Overtraining, and Recovery

questions.question: A coach deliberately overloads a sprinter for a planned block, accepts a short-term drop in performance, then tapers and sees the athlete rebound above the pre-block level. This planned outcome is which phenomenon?
options: Functional overreaching, ending in supercompensation above baseline
Nonfunctional overreaching, requiring months to recover
Overtraining syndrome, which stalls performance at baseline
questions.answer_text: Functional overreaching, ending in supercompensation above baseline
questions.explanation_en: Functional overreaching causes a short-term decrement but, with appropriate recovery, leads to supercompensation and improved performance.
tags: Chapter 24 quiz: Overreaching, Overtraining, and Recovery

questions.question: After a heavy block an athlete recovers more slowly than expected and, when they finally return, their performance is no better than where they started. Compared with functional overreaching, this nonfunctional overreaching is distinguished by the fact that it:
options: Resolves without needing any recovery period
Produces no supercompensation, returning only to baseline
Reliably pushes performance above the previous baseline
questions.answer_text: Produces no supercompensation, returning only to baseline
questions.explanation_en: Nonfunctional overreaching involves greater fatigue and longer recovery with no supercompensation, so the athlete only returns to baseline.
tags: Chapter 24 quiz: Overreaching, Overtraining, and Recovery

questions.question: The overtraining framework borrows a stress model describing an alarm reaction, a resistance stage, and an adaptation or exhaustion stage. Which model, first proposed by Selye, is this?
options: The size principle of motor unit recruitment
The Henneman recruitment gradient
The general adaptation syndrome (GAS)
questions.answer_text: The general adaptation syndrome (GAS)
questions.explanation_en: Selye's general adaptation syndrome (alarm, resistance, adaptation) is the foundational model applied to overtraining.
tags: Chapter 24 quiz: Overreaching, Overtraining, and Recovery

questions.question: A strength-power athlete deep in high-intensity training shows an exaggerated catecholamine response to exercise and elevated resting sympathetic activity. This presentation is most consistent with which form of overtraining?
options: Sympathetic OTS, marked by an increased epinephrine response
Sympathetic OTS, marked by a lowered resting heart rate
Parasympathetic OTS, marked by decreased cortisol
questions.answer_text: Sympathetic OTS, marked by an increased epinephrine response
questions.explanation_en: Sympathetic OTS is marked by an increased epinephrine (catecholamine) response and is associated with high-intensity resistance/strength-power training.
tags: Chapter 24 quiz: Overreaching, Overtraining, and Recovery

questions.question: The parasympathetic form of overtraining, originally labeled the Addisonoid syndrome, tends to appear in a particular athlete type. Which athletes are most affected?
options: Sprinters performing short bouts of high-intensity work
Aerobic endurance athletes accumulating very large training volumes
Powerlifters repeatedly handling near-maximal loads
questions.answer_text: Aerobic endurance athletes accumulating very large training volumes
questions.explanation_en: Parasympathetic OTS, often accompanied by decreased cortisol, is most common in aerobic endurance athletes who use very large training volumes.
tags: Chapter 24 quiz: Overreaching, Overtraining, and Recovery

questions.question: In parasympathetic overtraining the sympathetic response to training becomes blunted, a state sometimes called adrenal exhaustion. What does that term specifically describe?
options: The adrenal glands secreting excessive epinephrine
Overgrowth and enlargement of the adrenal cortex
The adrenal glands failing to produce adequate epinephrine
questions.answer_text: The adrenal glands failing to produce adequate epinephrine
questions.explanation_en: Parasympathetic OTS shows a diminished sympathetic (epinephrine) response, termed adrenal exhaustion because the glands cannot produce adequate epinephrine.
tags: Chapter 24 quiz: Overreaching, Overtraining, and Recovery

questions.question: When evaluating an overtrained athlete, a coach maps out poor sleep, an inadequate diet, heavy travel, and job stress alongside the training itself. The cumulative wear and tear from all of these stressors together is called the:
options: Allostatic load
Volume-load
Autonomic dysfunction index
questions.answer_text: Allostatic load
questions.explanation_en: The allostatic load is the cumulative wear and tear from all stressors, including non-training factors like sleep, nutrition, travel, and job demands.
tags: Chapter 24 quiz: Overreaching, Overtraining, and Recovery

questions.question: An athlete's performance drops, and the staff immediately assumes overtraining. Which statement about underperformance should temper that assumption?
options: Underperformance and overtraining are effectively the same thing
Not all underperformance is due to overtraining or overreaching
All underperformance ultimately traces back to overtraining
questions.answer_text: Not all underperformance is due to overtraining or overreaching
questions.explanation_en: Overtraining is only one cause of underperformance; many other factors, such as mistimed peaking, can impair performance without overtraining.
tags: Chapter 24 quiz: Overreaching, Overtraining, and Recovery

questions.question: As an athlete begins to slide into overtraining in the weight room, the staff monitors several qualities to catch it early. Which physical performance generally deteriorates FIRST?
options: Maximal strength
Maximal oxygen uptake capacity
Speed, such as sprinting and other high-velocity work
questions.answer_text: Speed, such as sprinting and other high-velocity work
questions.explanation_en: When overtraining in the weight room, speed (sprinting) is most sensitive and decreases first, before power and well before maximal strength.
tags: Chapter 24 quiz: Overreaching, Overtraining, and Recovery

questions.question: In monitoring the same athlete for overtraining, which performance quality tends to hold up the longest and is one of the LAST to decline?
options: Maximal strength
Sprinting speed
Vertical jump power
questions.answer_text: Maximal strength
questions.explanation_en: Maximal strength is consistently one of the last performances to decline; strength is well-protected relative to speed and power.
tags: Chapter 24 quiz: Overreaching, Overtraining, and Recovery

questions.question: A coach wants to use cortisol and testosterone assays to confirm a diagnosis of overtraining syndrome. What do such hormonal variables actually indicate?
options: The precise timeline required for recovery
The presence of stress, not overtraining specifically
A definitive, confirmatory diagnosis of overtraining
questions.answer_text: The presence of stress, not overtraining specifically
questions.explanation_en: Hormonal variables indicate stress rather than overtraining specifically, so they are not by themselves diagnostic of OTS.
tags: Chapter 24 quiz: Overreaching, Overtraining, and Recovery

questions.question: An athlete diagnosed with overreaching (not the full syndrome) stops training to recover. Under favorable conditions, performance has been observed to return to original levels in as little as:
options: Three months
One year
One week
questions.answer_text: One week
questions.explanation_en: With overreaching, training cessation has permitted performance to return to original levels in as little as one week.
tags: Chapter 24 quiz: Overreaching, Overtraining, and Recovery

questions.question: An athlete is confirmed to have overtraining syndrome. Before adding recovery modalities or lab testing, what is the first and most important step in the recovery process?
options: Carefully revise the training program, cutting volume or intensity or ceasing training
Insert additional high-intensity sessions to push through the plateau
Order an extensive panel of blood biomarkers before changing anything
questions.answer_text: Carefully revise the training program, cutting volume or intensity or ceasing training
questions.explanation_en: Recovery begins with a careful revision of the training program, typically a rapid decrease in volume, intensity, or training cessation.
tags: Chapter 24 quiz: Overreaching, Overtraining, and Recovery

questions.question: A coach building a recovery plan wants to prioritize a strategy that carries strong supporting evidence rather than one whose evidence is weak. Which of these qualifies?
options: Red-light therapy
Quality sleep
Acupuncture
questions.answer_text: Quality sleep
questions.explanation_en: Quality sleep is rated as a strong-evidence recovery strategy, along with modifying the training program and the training taper.
tags: Chapter 24 quiz: Overreaching, Overtraining, and Recovery

questions.question: A staff wants to set up an athlete-monitoring program that will actually let them adjust training in time. Which combination of qualities should the monitoring tests have?
options: Expensive and intrusive, with slow but very detailed interpretation
Administered only once per season to establish a single benchmark
Valid, reliable, sensitive, and easy to administer with rapid turnaround
questions.answer_text: Valid, reliable, sensitive, and easy to administer with rapid turnaround
questions.explanation_en: Monitoring tests must be valid, reliable, sensitive to the training stimulus, and easy to incorporate with rapid turnaround so the program can be adjusted.
tags: Chapter 24 quiz: Overreaching, Overtraining, and Recovery

questions.question: A previously healthy endurance athlete shows overtraining-like symptoms, and screening also flags low energy availability. Why is relative energy deficiency in sport (RED-S), the successor concept to the female athlete triad, relevant to the overtraining picture?
options: It shares many symptoms with OTS and the two can be interrelated
It is entirely unrelated to overtraining and can be ruled out
It affects only maximal strength and nothing else
questions.answer_text: It shares many symptoms with OTS and the two can be interrelated
questions.explanation_en: RED-S shares many causes and symptoms with overtraining syndrome, and the two can be interrelated and contribute to each other.
tags: Chapter 24 quiz: Overreaching, Overtraining, and Recovery

questions.question: A coach is writing progression rules to help avoid overtraining. Which guideline regarding training volume is recommended?
options: Eliminate rest days entirely to maximize the training stimulus
Use caution with large volume jumps of more than about 30 percent
Push weekly volume up by at least 50 percent to force adaptation
questions.answer_text: Use caution with large volume jumps of more than about 30 percent
questions.explanation_en: Avoidance strategies include exercising caution with excessive volumes and large increases (greater than about 30 percent), while preserving critical rest days.
tags: Chapter 24 quiz: Overreaching, Overtraining, and Recovery

questions.question: A university hires you to help build a brand-new weight room from scratch. Before any blueprints are drawn or walls go up, you want to sequence the whole project correctly. Which ordering of the four project phases should guide the work?
options: Design, predesign, construction, preoperation
Predesign, design, construction, preoperation
Predesign, construction, design, preoperation
questions.answer_text: Predesign, design, construction, preoperation
questions.explanation_en: The phases run predesign, design, construction, then preoperation, each with its own objectives.
tags: Chapter 25 quiz: Facility Design, Layout, and Organization

questions.question: During early planning for a new facility, a consultant runs a SWOT analysis to confirm the investment will produce a sustainable financial return before committing funds. This SWOT work belongs to which predesign activity?
options: The needs analysis
The master plan
The feasibility study
questions.answer_text: The feasibility study
questions.explanation_en: The feasibility study uses a SWOT analysis to ensure the financial investment will yield a viable and sustainable return.
tags: Chapter 25 quiz: Facility Design, Layout, and Organization

questions.question: You expect a peak session of 18 athletes plus 2 coaches on the floor at once. Using the recommended per-person space allowance, what is the minimum floor area each individual should be allotted when planning capacity?
options: 100 square feet (9.3 m2)
144 square feet (13.4 m2)
70 square feet (6.5 m2)
questions.answer_text: 100 square feet (9.3 m2)
questions.explanation_en: The recommended minimum is 100 square feet (9.3 m2) per individual, including athletes, professionals, and any other staff present.
tags: Chapter 25 quiz: Facility Design, Layout, and Organization

questions.question: You are spacing out power racks and free-weight stations so a lifter and spotter can move safely and dumbbell users do not collide. What is the minimum clearance you should leave on each side of a rack and between free-weight sets?
options: 7 feet (2.1 m)
3 feet (0.9 m)
5 feet (1.5 m)
questions.answer_text: 3 feet (0.9 m)
questions.explanation_en: Racks, barbells, and dumbbells need a minimum of 3 feet between equipment for safe movement of the athlete and spotter.
tags: Chapter 25 quiz: Facility Design, Layout, and Organization

questions.question: When mapping out the main travel lanes that must keep exits clear and permit ADA wheelchair access, what width should you designate for those primary walkways?
options: more than 10 feet (3 m)
questions.explanation_en: Main walkways should be 5 to 7 feet wide to allow clear access to exits and ADA-required wheelchair access.
tags: Chapter 25 quiz: Facility Design, Layout, and Organization

questions.question: Athletes at the new facility will perform box jumps, standing vertical jumps, and overhead weightlifting movements. What clear ceiling height should you specify so these actions have adequate overhead room?
questions.explanation_en: A height of 12 to 14 feet gives enough clearance for box jumps, vertical jumps, and overhead weightlifting exercises.
tags: Chapter 25 quiz: Facility Design, Layout, and Organization

questions.question: You are setting the HVAC thermostat so training quality is not degraded by athletes overheating or getting chilled. Which climate-control range should you target for the training floor?
questions.explanation_en: A comfortable training temperature of roughly 68 to 74 F keeps athletes and staff comfortable so training quality is not affected.
tags: Chapter 25 quiz: Facility Design, Layout, and Organization

questions.question: To limit bacterial and microbial growth and keep steel equipment from rusting, you set a moisture ceiling for the training area. Relative humidity should be held at or below what level?
options: 80 percent
40 percent
60 percent
questions.answer_text: 60 percent
questions.explanation_en: Relative humidity should stay at or below 60 percent to prevent bacterial and microbial growth and to protect equipment from rust.
tags: Chapter 25 quiz: Facility Design, Layout, and Organization

questions.question: To keep the training floor free of odors and stagnant air, you specify the ventilation rate. What is the recommended air-exchange rate, including the optimal target?
options: 8 to 10 times per hour, optimally 12 to 15
20 to 25 times per hour
2 to 4 times per hour
questions.answer_text: 8 to 10 times per hour, optimally 12 to 15
questions.explanation_en: Air should be exchanged a minimum of 8 to 10 times per hour, optimally 12 to 15, to prevent odors and stagnant air.
tags: Chapter 25 quiz: Facility Design, Layout, and Organization

questions.question: You want music to energize the room but not drown out verbal coaching cues during lifts. Below what sound level should you cap the audio system?
options: 70 decibels
90 decibels
110 decibels
questions.answer_text: 90 decibels
questions.explanation_en: Sound volume should be less than 90 decibels so athletes can hear instructions and coaching cues.
tags: Chapter 25 quiz: Facility Design, Layout, and Organization

questions.question: You want the supervisor to be able to see everyone entering, exiting, and training at all times. Where should the supervision office be positioned in the layout?
options: Just outside the facility entrance for privacy
In a back corner away from traffic to limit distraction
In a central location with a clear line of sight, possibly elevated
questions.answer_text: In a central location with a clear line of sight, possibly elevated
questions.explanation_en: The supervision office should be central with a clear line of sight, sometimes elevated, so the supervisor can see everyone entering and exiting.
tags: Chapter 25 quiz: Facility Design, Layout, and Organization

questions.question: A proposed weight room sits on the second floor of a building, so it must tolerate heavy loaded equipment and dropped weights. What minimum load-bearing capacity should the floor be rated for?
options: 100 foot-pounds per square foot
200 foot-pounds per square foot
50 foot-pounds per square foot
questions.answer_text: 100 foot-pounds per square foot
questions.explanation_en: A floor above ground level should support at least 100 foot-pounds per square foot to handle heavy and dropped equipment.
tags: Chapter 25 quiz: Facility Design, Layout, and Organization

questions.question: You are mounting wall mirrors near a free-weight area where plates are set down and leaned against the wall. To keep rolling or dropped plates from shattering the glass, mirrors should start at least how far above the floor?
options: 12 inches (30 cm)
20 inches (51 cm)
30 inches (76 cm)
questions.answer_text: 20 inches (51 cm)
questions.explanation_en: Mirrors should be at least 20 inches off the floor so dropped or leaning weight plates do not roll into and break the glass.
tags: Chapter 25 quiz: Facility Design, Layout, and Organization

questions.question: You are arranging a row of selectorized resistance machines and want a comfortable safety cushion for athletes moving between them. What clearance should you leave between machines, and what is the preferred spacing?
options: 48 inches (122 cm)
18 inches (46 cm)
30 inches (76 cm), with 36 inches (91 cm) preferred
questions.answer_text: 30 inches (76 cm), with 36 inches (91 cm) preferred
questions.explanation_en: Machines should be at least 30 inches apart, preferably 36 inches, to provide a wide enough safety cushion.
tags: Chapter 25 quiz: Facility Design, Layout, and Organization

questions.question: In a busy facility with athletes constantly moving between stations, you must choose between inlaid platforms and raised platforms for the lifting area. What is the primary safety reason to favor inlaid platforms?
options: They sit flush with the floor and do not present a tripping hazard
They reduce the noise of dropped weights to zero
They are cheaper to install and maintain
questions.answer_text: They sit flush with the floor and do not present a tripping hazard
questions.explanation_en: Inlaid platforms sit flush with the surrounding floor, so they do not create the tripping hazard that raised platforms do.
tags: Chapter 25 quiz: Facility Design, Layout, and Organization

questions.question: You want a single supervisor to maintain sight lines across the entire training floor. When positioning equipment of differing heights, where should the shorter pieces generally go?
options: Along the perimeter walls
In the middle of the room
Inside the storage area
questions.answer_text: In the middle of the room
questions.explanation_en: Shorter equipment is best placed in the middle of the room so staff can see across the entire facility.
tags: Chapter 25 quiz: Facility Design, Layout, and Organization

questions.question: A small satellite training room is too tight to include dedicated walkways separating the equipment. How should you arrange the equipment to keep transitions safe and emergency exits unobstructed?
options: Clustered in the center of the room
Stacked against the emergency exit to save space
Bolted and secured around the perimeter with the center kept open
questions.answer_text: Bolted and secured around the perimeter with the center kept open
questions.explanation_en: Equipment should be bolted around the perimeter with the center open for transitions and unimpeded access to emergency exits.
tags: Chapter 25 quiz: Facility Design, Layout, and Organization

questions.question: You need durable floor covering for the main lifting area that protects the subfloor, cushions dropped loads, and is easy to sanitize. Which flooring is regarded as the premier choice for this zone?
options: Rubber flooring
Hardwood throughout
Carpet
questions.answer_text: Rubber flooring
questions.explanation_en: Rubber flooring is the premier option because it protects the subfloor, provides durable cushioning, and is easy to clean.
tags: Chapter 25 quiz: Facility Design, Layout, and Organization

questions.question: To limit the spread of skin infections, you set a cleaning schedule for mats, pads, and any surface that contacts athletes' skin. How often should these be wiped down with a germicidal cleaner?
options: Once a month
Daily
Only when visibly soiled
questions.answer_text: Daily
questions.explanation_en: Surfaces and pads that contact skin should be cleaned daily with a germicidal cleaner to limit the spread of infection.
tags: Chapter 25 quiz: Facility Design, Layout, and Organization

questions.question: A cable machine breaks mid-session and the repair vendor cannot come for several days. To minimize liability, how should you handle the unit in the meantime?
options: Discard it immediately without documentation
Leave it in place so athletes can work around it
Label it with an Out of Order sign, and move it to storage since repair is delayed
questions.answer_text: Label it with an Out of Order sign, and move it to storage since repair is delayed
questions.explanation_en: Broken equipment should be tagged Out of Order and, if there is a delay before repair, removed from the floor to storage to reduce liability.
tags: Chapter 25 quiz: Facility Design, Layout, and Organization

questions.question: Your facility manual states 'closed-toe athletic shoes are required at all times' and separately lays out the step-by-step process staff follow to enforce and document violations. Which statement correctly classifies these two items?
options: The shoe rule is a procedure; the enforcement steps are the policy
Both are the same thing, since policy and procedure are interchangeable
The shoe rule is a policy; the enforcement steps are a procedure that carries the policy out
questions.answer_text: The shoe rule is a policy; the enforcement steps are a procedure that carries the policy out
questions.explanation_en: Policies are essentially a facility's rules and regulations, while procedures describe how those policies are met or carried out.
tags: Chapter 26 quiz: Facility Policies, Procedures, and Legal Issues

questions.question: An athlete is injured and sues, claiming the strength coach was negligent. For the claim to succeed in court, which complete set of elements must be established?
options: Duty, breach of duty, proximate cause, and damages
Duty, breach, assumption of risk, and damages
Sovereign immunity, breach, proximate cause, and damages
questions.answer_text: Duty, breach of duty, proximate cause, and damages
questions.explanation_en: Negligence requires all four: a duty to act, a breach of that duty, proximate cause, and resulting damages.
tags: Chapter 26 quiz: Facility Policies, Procedures, and Legal Issues

questions.question: In a lawsuit, the court weighs whether the coach acted as a competent peer would have in the same situation. This benchmark of conduct is known as which of the following?
options: A signed waiver accepted before participation
What a reasonable and prudent person would do under similar circumstances
The maximum load an athlete can safely lift
questions.answer_text: What a reasonable and prudent person would do under similar circumstances
questions.explanation_en: Standard of care is the degree of caution and prudence a reasonable person would exercise in similar situations.
tags: Chapter 26 quiz: Facility Policies, Procedures, and Legal Issues

questions.question: A strength and conditioning professional owes their athletes a legal responsibility, duty, or obligation for their well-being. Which single term captures that legal responsibility?
options: Informed consent
Assumption of risk
Liability
questions.answer_text: Liability
questions.explanation_en: Liability is a legal responsibility, duty, or obligation owed to the athletes a professional serves.
tags: Chapter 26 quiz: Facility Policies, Procedures, and Legal Issues

questions.question: Every athlete signed an assumption-of-risk waiver before training. One is hurt and shows the coach failed to spot a maximal lift as a competent coach would. How does the waiver bear on the coach's exposure?
options: It may NOT shield the coach when negligence is established
It permanently transfers all liability onto the athlete
It fully shields the coach from all liability regardless of conduct
questions.answer_text: It may NOT shield the coach when negligence is established
questions.explanation_en: An assumption-of-risk waiver may not protect a professional from legal liability if they are found to be negligent.
tags: Chapter 26 quiz: Facility Policies, Procedures, and Legal Issues

questions.question: You supervise a college varsity team's lifting sessions and want to staff them at the recommended supervision level. What professional-to-athlete ratio applies at the collegiate level?
questions.explanation_en: Recommended ratios are 1:10 for junior high, 1:15 for high school, and 1:20 for college.
tags: Chapter 26 quiz: Facility Policies, Procedures, and Legal Issues

questions.question: You are assigned to supervise junior high athletes, the youngest group you train, which calls for the most conservative staffing. What professional-to-participant ratio is recommended for this age group?
questions.explanation_en: The junior high school ratio is 1:10, the most conservative of the three levels.
tags: Chapter 26 quiz: Facility Policies, Procedures, and Legal Issues

questions.question: A returning athlete reports lingering symptoms and asks when they can restart lifting. Staying within your scope of practice, who is authorized to grant medical clearance to begin the program?
options: The sports medicine staff, such as an athletic trainer, physician, or physical therapist
The head sport coach
The strength and conditioning professional
questions.answer_text: The sports medicine staff, such as an athletic trainer, physician, or physical therapist
questions.explanation_en: Only the sports medicine staff can provide medical clearance; diagnosing conditions is outside the S and C professional's scope of practice.
tags: Chapter 26 quiz: Facility Policies, Procedures, and Legal Issues

questions.question: A head coach wants athletes who miss a drill to run extra sprints and do push-ups as a consequence. From a legal and professional standpoint, how should the strength coach regard using conditioning as punishment?
options: It is encouraged as a way to build mental toughness
It is strictly prohibited because of the reckless or negligent conduct it represents
It is acceptable for a player's first offense only
questions.answer_text: It is strictly prohibited because of the reckless or negligent conduct it represents
questions.explanation_en: Using exercise or conditioning as punishment is strictly prohibited because of the reckless or negligent conduct it represents (e.g., hazing, mental abuse).
tags: Chapter 26 quiz: Facility Policies, Procedures, and Legal Issues

questions.question: When lawsuits arise from athletic injuries, one program factor is implicated far more than any other. Supervision was cited in roughly what share of such court cases?
options: 20 percent
50 percent
80 percent
questions.answer_text: 80 percent
questions.explanation_en: Supervision was cited in an estimated 80 percent of court cases in which athletic injuries occurred.
tags: Chapter 26 quiz: Facility Policies, Procedures, and Legal Issues

questions.question: You are drafting a mission statement for a new strength and conditioning program. Which quality reflects an effective mission statement?
options: It matches and stays within the organization's scope of practice
It is kept general and ambiguous to leave room for interpretation
It prescribes the specific means and methods of training to be used
questions.answer_text: It matches and stays within the organization's scope of practice
questions.explanation_en: A good mission statement is short, clear, does not prescribe means, and matches the organization's scope of practice.
tags: Chapter 26 quiz: Facility Policies, Procedures, and Legal Issues

questions.question: You are assembling a performance team of scientific-foundation experts to support your athletes. Which of these individuals would traditionally NOT be counted as a core member of that team?
options: Sports nutritionist
Athletic director
Exercise physiologist
questions.answer_text: Athletic director
questions.explanation_en: The performance team is built from scientific-foundation experts such as the nutritionist, sport psychologist, and exercise physiologist, not the athletic director.
tags: Chapter 26 quiz: Facility Policies, Procedures, and Legal Issues

questions.question: The person overseeing a collegiate strength and conditioning program coaches lifts on the floor while also managing budgets, staff, and the facility. This dual role is best described how?
options: Solely an administrator with no coaching duties
Strictly a practitioner who only coaches lifts
Both a practitioner and an administrator
questions.answer_text: Both a practitioner and an administrator
questions.explanation_en: The director is both a practitioner and an administrator responsible for the overall program, facility, equipment, and staff.
tags: Chapter 26 quiz: Facility Policies, Procedures, and Legal Issues

questions.question: In a negligence suit, the plaintiff must show that the coach's breach set off an unbroken chain of foreseeable events ending in the injury. Which element of negligence does that describe?
options: Proximate cause
Damages
Duty
questions.answer_text: Proximate cause
questions.explanation_en: Proximate cause is the direct, continuous sequence of reasonably foreseeable events that connects the breach to the resulting damages.
tags: Chapter 26 quiz: Facility Policies, Procedures, and Legal Issues

questions.question: Before an athlete enrolls, you walk them through what a testing-and-training program involves, including its inherent risks and expected benefits, so they can choose whether to take part. This process is called which of the following?
options: A government's immunity from being sued
Informed consent
An insurer's promise to defend the insured
questions.answer_text: Informed consent
questions.explanation_en: Informed consent describes a procedure or activity with its inherent risks and benefits so the individual can decide whether to participate.
tags: Chapter 26 quiz: Facility Policies, Procedures, and Legal Issues

questions.question: A colleague asks how long to keep old injury report forms, assuming they can be shredded after a year. What is the sound reason to retain such records indefinitely instead?
options: HIPAA mandates permanent retention of all such records
Equipment manufacturers require it to honor warranties
The statute of limitations for filing a lawsuit varies by location
questions.answer_text: The statute of limitations for filing a lawsuit varies by location
questions.explanation_en: The statute of limitations varies by location, so keeping records indefinitely protects the program if a suit is filed later.
tags: Chapter 26 quiz: Facility Policies, Procedures, and Legal Issues

questions.question: A coach welds an added handle onto a machine and later an athlete is hurt using it. Even though the coach did not manufacture the equipment, how can product liability reach them?
options: They can be named as codefendants, especially after modifying equipment or using it improperly
Only the athlete can ever be held responsible for equipment injuries
It cannot, because they did not manufacture the product
questions.answer_text: They can be named as codefendants, especially after modifying equipment or using it improperly
questions.explanation_en: Although professionals do not make products, modifying equipment or using it other than as intended can shift liability onto them and name them as codefendants.
tags: Chapter 26 quiz: Facility Policies, Procedures, and Legal Issues

questions.question: A new athlete shows up eager to start lifting today. Before you let them use the facility, what must be completed and documented regarding their health status?
options: A 1RM test to gauge their readiness to train
Preparticipation screening and medical clearance per the relevant governing bodies
Only a verbal statement from the athlete that they feel healthy
questions.answer_text: Preparticipation screening and medical clearance per the relevant governing bodies
questions.explanation_en: Preparticipation screening and clearance, documented on file, are required before an athlete is allowed to participate.
tags: Chapter 26 quiz: Facility Policies, Procedures, and Legal Issues

questions.question: You are training your staff on how to supervise the floor to minimize risk. Which of the following aligns with the recognized principles of supervision?
options: Focus supervision only on the most advanced lifters
Delegate supervisory authority freely to the athletes themselves
Always be there, be active and hands on, be prudent, and stay vigilant
questions.answer_text: Always be there, be active and hands on, be prudent, and stay vigilant
questions.explanation_en: Principles of supervision include always being there, being active and hands on, being prudent and prepared, and being vigilant.
tags: Chapter 26 quiz: Facility Policies, Procedures, and Legal Issues

questions.question: A 17-year-old athlete asks you to recommend a supplement. Under NSCA professional standards, which conditions must be met before you recommend or provide any substance?
options: It must be lawful, scientifically shown to be beneficial or at least not harmful, and provided only to those age 18 or older
You may provide any product from a reputable manufacturer
You may provide whatever supplement the athlete requests
questions.answer_text: It must be lawful, scientifically shown to be beneficial or at least not harmful, and provided only to those age 18 or older
questions.explanation_en: Standard 9.1 permits only lawful substances scientifically shown to be beneficial or at least not harmful, provided only to individuals age 18 or above.
tags: Chapter 26 quiz: Facility Policies, Procedures, and Legal Issues
